THE BABBLE OF THE Ba.BEL. I suppose if all the children Who have live through ages long Were collected and inspected, They would make a wondrous throng; Oh, the babble of the Babble! Oh, the flutter of the fuss! To begin with Cain and Abel, And to finish up with us! Think of all the men and women Who are neer and who have been, Every nation since creation That this world of oars has sees; And of all of them not any But was once a baby small; While of children, oh, how many Never have grown up at all! Some have never laughed or spoken, Never used their rosy feet; • Some have even flown to heaven Ere they knew that earth was sweet; And, indeed, I wonder whether, It we reckon ev'ry birth, And bring such a flock together, There is room for them on earth? Who will wash their smiling faces? Who their saucy ears will box? Who will dress them and caress them? Who will darn their little socks? Where are arms enough to hold them? Hands to pat each shining head? Who will praise them, who will scold them? Who will pack them off to bed? Little happy Christian children, Little savage children, too,. - In all stages, of all ages, That our planet ever knew! Little princes and princesses. Little beggars, wan ac.d faint, Some in very handsome dresses, • Naked some, bedaubed with paint. Only think of the confusion Such a motley crowd would make! And the clatter of their chatter, And the things that they would break! Oh, the babble of the Babel! Oh, the flatter of the fuss! To begin with Cain and Abel, And to finish off with us! --Leeds .111erclay Weekly.

----- When gals is very little it is their motrier's anxiety ter keep matches out ov their way, but when they gets bigger the motherly anxiety is all the other way. As a part of the marriage ceremony in Servia, the bride has to hold a piece of sugar between her lips as a sign that she will speak little and sweetly during her married life. A boy ken do wrong an' outlive it, but it aint often dat way wid a man. De colt can slip down an' jump up widout much injury, but when de obi hoss falls he's ap' ter hurt hisse'f. De 'oman what dresses to please herse'l shows sense, but de 'em en what dresses to displease some udder 'oman wid 'eperior finery, is got a salt spot sum users near de top o' her head. Little Mrs. Whedleim spent 45 minutes in a vain effort SO convince Mr. W. that a sealskin sacque was necessary to her existence. Then she startled him by the question : Jcljg4. hadn't you better sell me for a car-wheel ?" 6. Who', f' Recauir I've got a cast-iron Hub." She got the stCque. A Scotchuln at a Burns anniversary meeting, tilt other I Itgeeing, not far from Liverpool, delivered what he thought an eloquent little speech and was sadly put out when he sat down on not receiving very hearty applause. A light dawned upon him when a neighbour whispered—" Donald, moo, gin ye spier awa' like that agen, tho' I ken a' ye say mysel, justbring wi' ye an intairmeter." SOME BISHOPS OF CHESTEII.--Ett the Reformation Ches ter was deffinitely created a distinct diocese, and the die. established monastery of Wetburgh in the city turned into its episcopal palace. Its first occupant was John Bird, for- merly a Carmelite friar, who had earned the King's favour by preachihg before him a sermon against the Pops's supre• macy, and was translated, as were so many of his successors, from the diocese of Bangor. He WAS turned out by Queen Mary, for the crime of being married, and was succeded by George Cotts, mast-r of Balliol, and then by Cuthbert Sweet, a "froward person," who had distinguished himself at Cambridge by being "a busy man in the burning .of Bucer's bones." The fifth bishop was. William Chaderton, president of Queen's College Cambridge, a learned and witty man, of whom many good stories are told. While a don at Cambridge he had preached a wedding sermon, and then made this " merry comparison." He declared that the choice of a wife was a thing full of hazard, and not unlike to men groping for one fish in a barrel of serpents. "If he escape harm of the snake and light upon the fish, the man may be thought fortunate; yet let him not boast, for per- haps it may be but an eel." He was much beloved of the scholars at the university for his affable and courteous be- haviour; bat on one occasion, at least, he afterwards pushed his courtesy rather far. The seventh bishop was Richard Vaughan also translated, from Bangor, "a man of prompt and ready utteranee, and a sour enemy to all pretended miracles" He was once rather hard pressed on the subject Of miraculous cures for the king's evil, and being too loyal a man to absolutely deny the Royal power in this matter, at length declared his belief that the care was effected by the secret means of a precious- stone in the possession of the English Crown. This prelate died in 1606, having some time before "fallen into a drowsy disease of an apoplexy," which caused some amusement and joking at his expense. Dn. JOHNSON ON REYNOLDS.—The well-known sentence of Johnson's, that he was "the most invulnerable man he knew; whom, if he should quarrel with him he should find the most difficulty how to abase," implies in itself only a negative judgment, and might aptly fit a nature that was capable of inspiring no real affection. But Johnson found warmer terms in which to describe his friend. In the sum- mer of 1764, when Reynolds had been ill, he addressed him in words that he would not have used to a man he did not love, though the form in which he expresses himself may seem to us now somewhat ponderously polite. "Having bad no llarticular account of your disorder," he writes, "I know not in what state it has left you. If the amusement of my company can exhilarate the langour of a slow re eovery, I will not delay a day to come to you; for I know not how I can so effectually promote my own pleasure as by pleasing you, or my own interestby preserving you, in whom, if I should lose you, I should lose about the only man whom I call a friend." On another occasion, referring to his own melancholy, he lets fall an observation that throws a pleasant light upon the character of the painter. "Some men," he says, "and very thinking men too, have not these vexing thoughts. Sir Joshua Reynolds is the same all the year round." Even the occasional differences between the two friends have a touch of kindliness; and once when Johnson's rudeness had called forth Reynolds's dignity, the former grew soddenly humble, and with as near an approach to a blush as Boswell could bring himself to eecord, said; "Nay, don't be angry, I did not mean to offend you." The last vision we get of this happy friendship is Johnson's dying request that Reynolds would forgive him 130 which he had borrowed of him, as he wished to leave the money to a poor family.—English Illustrated Magazine. Tux BEST HORSES Is THE WORLD.—England—in which geographical expression Ireland, Wales, and Scotland are also, of course included—is the breeding ground, the original home, Of the best horses in the world. English- men invented, if one may be permitted to use so mechanical a term, the thoroughbred horse, which combines with mar- vellously increased size, speed, and power all the fire, cour- age, and quality of his Oriental ancestors—the Barb and the Arab. The EngliA thoroughbred is universally re- Ilognieed as the sole source of improvement for every variety of the horse tribe in Europe and America, save those used In the dull useful labour of heavy draught; and even the British draught-horse has been brought to perfection by the application of principles which were first employed, al- though recently neg•lected, in the breeding of the incompar- Able race-horse. At the present moment there is in Con- tinental gurope scarcely a State in which the character of the riding and light harness horse has not been materially ameliorated by cros-,es of English blood. The importations by private breeders and by the governing managers of Royal and National studs, which commenced soon after the close of the great war in 1815, have been carried on ever since with annually increasing care and vigour. The first ex- periments with English blood•aires were made, towards the middle of the eighteenth century, in those ancient breeding grounds of medixval war horses, Mecklenburgand Hanover. In the long peace which followed Waterloo, the merits Of the thoroughbred sire conquered the prejudices of nations inclined to detest everything English; and now In the State studs of France, of the several kingdoms and principalities which form the northern portion of the Get- man Empire, in the German dominions of the Austrian Kaiser, as well as in his horse loving kingdom of Hungary, In the newly-formed Royalty of united Italy, and under the Czar of all the Russians the English blood-horse holds the first place. "It may safely be assumed that at the great deocukstsinaenndtalfarzoiersm--ivlyitaerre emperors and kings, reigning ornmanders, appear on horse- back Surrounded by their brilliant irsttinst," distinguished of the chargers ridden by the personages have been bred in England, or are the in mediate produce of Eng. lish'tires. All the best horses in the United States are dffoomy discended from English thorough-brads, with lelight intermixture of Barbs or Arabs. Experts belonginga tri the Ani'erieen horse. #reat Anglo-Saxon Republic trace back the pedigrees of their best trotters—the speciality breeding —to Messenger, an imported blood-sire, the son of gray .Mambrino, who was bred by Lord Grosvenor, and painted by the celebrated George Stubbs, about 1774. It his been reserved for Out colonists in South Africa and Australia to prove that the English blood-horse, unpam.• pared, and trained for the purpose, while far exceeding the Arab-tn-size and general utility, can equal him in endurance and the power of completing great distances in journeys ex- tending over, many successive dept.—From The Book of froese".:for March. .11" medie'a or tessi m are ..ow 'ordering radbUrftt 00004 "."""raCe in hamanos of otAee. he-euse it contains more nutri- tious ruad r.nirt4 ...1...en 6 'hat, any other beverage. limn ie Preferable to LW, trnek archv no•sa ordinarily sold. div.head: NOTES ON AGRICULTURE, fIORTI-
div.p: NOTES ON AGRICULTURE, fIORTI-

CULTURE, &c. It has been resolved to change the name of the Cart-Horse Society to that of the Shire-Horse Society. Foot-and-mouth disease has broken out at Neoshofalls, in Texas and the United States Government is considering the advisability of prohibiting the importation of cattle from

_ Great Britain. • The decline in foot.and-mouth disease continues. At the close of the week ended March 1 there were 2,305 animals remained affected in Great Britain, together with 33 in Ireland at the close of the week ended February 23. This shows a decrease of 511 in Great Britain and a decrease of 24 in Ireland. RATHER HARD CHEESE.—The cheese made in Cumber- land used to be harder than buckhorn. In some places, ac- cording to a local authority, where the herdsmen wore clogs t shod with iron, it was no uncommon thing to supply the I place of the iron with the crust of a dry cheese. There is plenty of testimony to cheese striking fire like a flint. A soldier used a cheese.pariug for a flint, and a blacksmith at Cartmel, Harriet Martineau informs us, 'averred that he struck sparks from a cheese while cutting it up with an axe. A tract of dry heather burned without intermission for three weeks, having been kindled by sparks from a cheese which had rolled from a cart on the road above, and had bounded from crag to crag.—Girls' Own Paper.—To the above we might add the following :—Some wailers were engaged in the erection of farm buildings in High Furness, an rfeli short of slate pegs. They were in a dilemma, when a happy inspiration came to one of the men. Some cheese had been sent to them from sthe farm. They could not eat it, but they attacked it with their tools, converted it into slate pegs, and for anything we know, the .cheese pegs are still doing dote. WARBLES.—The secretary of the Newcastle Hide Inspec- tion Society writea to the Mark Lane Express :—" During I the preval-nce of the warble season, which embraces four or five months of the year, it is estimated that fully one- half of the hides are more or less warbled; and it is not too mush to say that the deoreciation in the value of such hiles will average three to four shillings each. In addition to the injury caused to the hide by warble holes, it is appa- rent that the gro Nth of the animals BO affected must be considerably retarded from the ,a ne cause. The Newcastle gide Inspection Society had the subject discussed at its last &reseal meeting, when it was euggested that the most likely means of attaining the obj4ct in view was to offer a pre- mium for the best essay on the subject. It is expected that in the course of the next few months this society will be in a position formally to invite the attention of veterinary ex- perts in the way indicated." ENSILAGE IN AMERICA.—At the Ensilage Congress, in New York, the discussion turned upon ensilage as a food for horses, and the evidence seemed to be decidedly un- favourable. Dr. Baxter, of Virginia, said that it had been tried with fatal results in his State, and that autopsies showed that death was due to the presence in the throat of stomach worms, which calved suffocation. This was due, he thought, to the acidity of the food, which drove the worms from the stomach. The experience of the Superin- tendent of the Greenfield Park Farm in Connecticut was somewhat similar. Of ten horses fed for a week on ensilage eight had died, the trouble appearing to be in the throat. Others contended that the plan worked well, but Mr. Post, a milk-dealer, declared it was better to feed horses on arsenic than ensilage. But for cattle the evidence was just the opposite. A representative was introduced from Theodore Havemeyer'e farm at Mahwah, N.J., where for a year the cattle have been fed largely upon eruailage. He said —"TO: each of 100 Jersey cows is given 20 pounds of ensilage in the morning, seven pounds of hay at noon, and 20 pounds of ensilageat night. Mixed with the ensilage is one quart of corn meal and one of ground oats. Under this fodder, the cattle have grown in weight from two to three ant a half pounds a day, while expenses have been reduced. Fier,e, are fecl en ensilage three times a week, and hogs Comet train No bad reitiltl have been experienced on the farm from overfeeding cattle with ensilage." THE MILK YIELD OF JERSETS.—There is at all times considerable difficulty in obtaining information as to the actual yield of Jersey cattle, and this is felt in America as well as in England. The American Dairyman publishes a well-attested case, particulars of which are here condensed. The cow Mary Anne of St. Lambert, owned by Mr. Faller, I of Hamilton, Ontario, was tested for the month of January 1 in this year-31 clear days. Her milk was kept apart and churned- whole. For the month she gave 6271 b. Boz. of milk; of unsalted butter, 631 b. 150 z.; of salted but- ter, 661 b. 2oz. The weight of marketable butter for 248 consecutive days was 7201 b. The animal was milked every night and morning, her average being in the morning about 111 b. and in the evening about 91b. of milk. This is an ex- ceedingly remarkable case, for the butter was about 10 per cent, of the milk; or in other words, one pound to each gallon. Now, as the average is about one pound to three gallon, or twelve quarts, it will be conceded that this is, perhaps, the most astonishing case on record. It would have been still more interesting had the owner given some particulars of the method of feeding. The case is attested by the manager of the farm, who made a solemn declaration before two commissioners in Her Majesty's court, so that there are really some grounds for believing the evidence to be thoroughly genuine. It is somewhat annoying that re- cords of this kind are never heard of in our own country; but the fact is there are so few persons who think it .worto while to keep any accounts with regard to their cattle, and until that system is more popular we need not expect to be much wiser than we are at present CHEAP RURAL RAILWAYS WANTED.—One of the best improvements, in my opinion, which has been brought out for farmers in districts where there is heavy cropping and heavy manuring such as we have in some districts of Lan- cashire and Cheshire is the balance railway invented by M. Lartique, and shown at the Paris Exhibition. We badly want Finale cheap method of conveying green crops to market and manure back to the land. That our present costly sys- I tern of railways are of small use to us witness the long trains of carts which stream into Manchester from Cheshire and South Lancashire laden with the fruits of the field and taking back manure, and this is perhaps more noticeable still from the Ormskirk direction in and out of Liverpool. The Fylde and Preston afford another instance. M. Lax- tique's balance railway, as described, meets the desideratum; it is cheaply laid, can be taken upon fields without skilled labour, and a pony can draw 20 to 30 of the basket-waggons. There is only one rail, which is raised a few feet above the ground, on iron trestles resting on a sleeper; the load is balanced on each side and is said to ride easily. The idea is an old one, as something similar was attempted more than half a century ago. Whether or not this will be adopted, some lightly constructed and cheaply worked system of a railway would be of the greatest service for distances, say, within fifteen miles of the market and the natural manure supplies. If we had cheap lines, we should not see tons upon tons of good manure which the land is yearning for being tipped into old clay pits and hollows near our large towns, in a few years to be built upon and become, not hot- beds for vegetable growth, but for pestilential fever. COUNTY ASSESSMENT COMMITTEES.—A correspondent writes to a contemporary:—" Having sat on a Board of Guardians, and seen how the wires are pulled, I must say that much undue pressure is brought to bear by county ma- gistrates, who by law are allowed to sit as es-officio guar- dians without election. For instance, supposing the rating of a certain mansion or mansions, for they have friends to serve, be brought before the Assessment Committee, the members of which are often tenants of some of the magis- trates on the board, and very often the chairman on the board is a magistrate, I ask, can the members of such As- sessment Committee be expected to give a fair, unbiassed opinion as to the ratable value of certain county houses or property brought before them? No, they do not; they are unwilling to speak out, in many cases being afraid to offend their landlord, knowing too well that if they act conscien- tiously matters referring to their farms May be made pretty hot for them as to cross-cropping, abatement of rent, and many other favours required. In short, when county ma- gistrates and landed proprietors have tenants in their power, as many just now unhappily have, they can indirectly bring much undue pressure to bear on them. I hope shortly that farmers will manage their own county business by boat and that we may have a county stipendiary magistracy. _ have conversed with many shrewd and practical farmers of both Liberal and Conservative principles, and could the Opinion of the whole body of tenant-farmers in the country be taken by ballot-voting, not otherwise, I am convin ed that they would be in favour of it. Farmers, or rather the farming interests, are beginning to be heard in the country ;,, and if the question he well agitated, this crying disgrace will be remedied." A PEMBROKESHIRE DAIRY.--" M.," in Agricultural Gazette, records the doings of a Welsh herd, of the breed known as the Pembrokeshire Blacks. The average number' of cows milked in 1883 was 151 [7]. and the total amount of butter actually churned within the twelve months was 3,94811b5., which would give over 2541b5. as the produce of each cow. Three of the cows were heifers after their first calf, and two others had slipped their calves. One four- yearsold cow was giving 231bs, of milk per day nearly six months after calving, her highest daily yield recorded being over 341bs. One of the heifers gave over 381bs. of milk in one day, and four months after' calving was giving over 231bs. of milk per day. Another cow was giving 221bs. of milk seven months after calving. Excepting one cow and a heifer (her half-sister) the herd is pare Blacks, the two exceptions being cross-bred, whose mother in the previous year was giving 50Ibs. of milk two months after calying, her milk when tested showing 15 per cent, of cream. The , average percentage of creed' from the whole is about 15 ; and 251bs. of milk will easily make 11b. of butter. We weigh the milk about every fortnight through the summer, and occasionally teat with the creamometer ; but as the cows graze during the spring at a considerable distance from the homestead, and are not brought home for a couple of months, it is impossible to take the weight of the milk during that time. The cows were, after calving, fed on what grass they could pick up in the 11610, supplemented with hay, and when gram Was very short, by a daily feed of I whole oats and crushed barley (about 41bs.) until April, after which they had nothing but grass. The slight frosts we have had during the week, and oi Nich we hope to see a recurrence, will prove most valuable, r whilst they cannot do much injury to vegetation, they /).11 'pulverise the surface of the soil, and assist in making iuitable seed beds. There are several crops of small seeds ' which may be deposited in the ground as opportunity oilers, and the requirements or taste of the cottager demands. Early Horn Carrot may be either sown broadcast or in drills 6in. distant. An ounce of seed should sow five rows of 10ft. each. We select the drilling system because it admits of a small hoe being run between the rows to destroy the weeds. To make the seeds separate readily, mix some sand with them; if it is moist it farther assists the opera- tion of sowing by adhering to the seeds, which increases their weight, causing them to drop more in accordance with the will of the sower, ingtead of being wafted by the slightest wind. For an early crop of carrots the soil should be friable and rich. They succeed best on land that has been well mannred for a previous crop, such as celery or potatoes. Our late crops, or those sown in April, are so un- satisfactory that we have to depend chiefly on our enuply from these early sowings, and to the ground occupied by both we give a dressing of soot or lime, whichever is at hand, but both must not be applied to the same piece of ground the same year. Mustard and Cress should be sown in a eheltered sunny position. The seed requires but a very slight covering of soil—a little more than their own thick- ness. Radishes should also occupy a similar position, and the ground for these can scarcely be too rich. The birds will steal every seed as they germinate and appear through the soil if they are not protected, or some measures taken to scare the birds. The French Breakfast is a good crisp radish, so is Wood's Frame and Scarlet Short Top. Parsley: If the autumn sown has perished, which it has with us, a small SO wing may be made at once, and a choice aspect is not so mach of a consideration as it is to some of the early sown seeds, so long as it is a fairly open one. The wet destroys more of oar parsley riots than severe frosts, and we hear of others suffering in a similar manner. We are in- clined to think that we could have been more successful had we sown in beds well elevated above the general sur- face, so as to have the crown of the plant above a water laden soil. _

SUIINJIIEI NoTES. The collection of meteorites t together by the late Professor J. Lawrence Smith, and said to be the largest ever made, has been secured for Harvard College University. The excavations made by the Coburg Anthropological Society in the old Germany pottery station found near Sonneberg have resulted in the discovery of some types of composition and form hitherto unknown.

_ At a recent meeting of the American Academy of Sciences Professor Eleilprin called attention to investigations which prove that the plants which appear earliest in any temperate region are strictly alpine in habit, and can be found flourish- ing at high elevations. Prof. Milne, of Japan, has established in the Takashima coal mine, near Nagasaki, an underground, or, as he prefers to call it, a cetachthonic observatory. This colliery is worked for some considerable distance under the sea, and it is purposed to establish a regular system of observations on temperature and pressure, and on the tides, earth tremors, and the escape of gas, carefully noting if any connection exists between them, and establishing a comparison between surface and sub terra lean pile mmena.

EXPERIMENTS WITH DYNAMITE AT UNDERLEY.—An ex- I periment has been made by Lord Healy° on a portion of his Underley gall esta,e which is of- some interest to i farmers. It is well known that considerable difficulty at- tends the removal of the roots of old trees, and it occurred ' to his lordship and his agent (Mr. Punchard) that probably dynamite might prove an efficient agent in removing the "old stumps" and big roots on his estate. Small pieces of this explosive were placed in several roots and fired. Tha result, however, did not answer the expectation and hope of Lord Bective. The soil surrounding the roots was blown in all directions, but the tough, far spreading rootlets proved too strong for the blasting operation, and it is not at all probable that dynamite will be used in future efforts to re- move tree roots.

THE FRONT GATULNIN.—A correspondent in one of the gardening journals enumerates quite MO plants which tre saw in flower in cottage gardens on the borders of Surrey A and Sussex a week ago. This must be delightful to all the passers-by who have a love of flowers. The names given are familiar to all growers of hardy flowers, and are really what may be termed old.fashioned. As is our wont when out abroad, we had just made a list of what we saw, and we shall be glad if any cottager would supply us with the names of any additional ones that they may have been flowering in their front gardens. Polyanthus and Prim- roses were the most prevalent. Next, the white and red varieties of double Daisies, which look well in rows round the beds or along the front sides of the borders. Crocuses of different colours are now at their best. The others just expanding were Arable Albida Aubretia Purpnrea, Erythro- nia Dias Canis (or dog's tooth violet), Muscari flotryoides (or grape hyacinth), with the blue and white Vinica hug- ging a few stones intentionally laid for them to embrace. Erica Elerbacea, a hardy heath, looked well in one garden. Snowdrops are universally bidding adieu to 1884. Christ- mas Roses appear to be scarce. We prefer the white variety, of which several thousands are annually imported to this country for forcing, when they are made Christmas flowers, if not a veritable rose. The gardening journals have for some weeks devoted considerable space in discuss- ing its various species and varieties. The white variety does not maintain its colour long in a smoky district, but with the most primitive 'glass contrivance it does; as well as flower a week or a fortnight in advance of uncovered ones; that is, presuming they are covered sufficiently early. One which we protected with a broken handlight flowered three weeks ago. Nasturtiums may be sown any time. The seeds are extremely hardy, and the plants are just as tender; for some self-sown ones that had already grown two inches were destroyed by the frost on Tuesday morning, when we had 11 deg. in the open or exposed position, with the ther- mometer as it ought to be, 3ft. from the ground. Nastur- tiums are best sown against walls or fences; so as to cover them. They flower more freely in such positions, especially if the aspect is south or south-west. TEM WINDOW.—In our notes last week on the fern case, we commended it as suitable for raising seedlings. For this purpose we should select one of the "pockets," or space in- tended for a plant, And with the peat and sand put some stones the size of filt-erts, which may be placed on the top and pressed three parts of their depth in; and when com- pleted, sow as directed last week. They require watering at first with a fine distributor, or it may be done by frequent dipping of the hand and holding it close to the surface, so that the water will fall without force. When the general watering of the case takes place, a piece of glass should be placed over the seed to avoid any sp'ashing. In about two months some of the young ferns will be seen, most probably clinging to the stones inserted in the soil. We have had more than one Whittle-stone covered with dozens of baby ferns. The dimensions of the stones should be more than a man would care about holding long on one hand. When we placed the stones where we did, we never anticipated such results, as they were not fixed for that purpose, though on reflection they were under favourable conditions particu- larly suitable. They had evidently been used for construct- ing a wall some years age, and were cons,goently covered with lichen or moss, and in this the fern spores found a nursery and established themselves a home and, Cuckoo- like, they elbowed the lichen away. It was the wrong sort to agree long with the lovers of a moist, close atmosphore.

One of George lll.'s first acts was to knight a gentleman named Day. " Now," said he. "I know that lam a king, for I have turned Day into knight." CURES FOR SEASICKNESS.—Dr. J. M. Kendall writing in the British Medical Journal, advocated a teaspoonful of Worcester sauce as a useful remedy in the earlier stages of seasickness. 01 drugs, he has found the most effectual to be bromide of sodium. "When bromide of sodium is given in doses of ten grains three times a day, the attacks entirely subside, the appetite improves, and the patient is able to Walk about with comfort." It is a very important point to keep the stomach full, and the best food for this purpose is fat bacon. According to Dr. Kendall, "it acts like a charm." Even better than bacon is curry, which is retained by the stomach when all other food has been rejected. Brandy, so far from being a cure, very often induces seasickness. A NEW VIEW OF TENNYSON.—" Mamma," said a fashion- able New York young lady to her mother, "the papers are making a great fuss over a Mr. Tennyson, of England." ",Yes," responded the mother, "he has been raised to the dear, delighted peerage." "He has been made a baron, I see," said the daughter. "Yes, and his wife will be a baroness, I suppose," reflected the old lady. "How ex snisitely beautiful it must be to be a baroness." "What has he been a-doing of to be a baron ?" asked the cultured young lady. " What has he been a doing of?" repeated the mother; "why, he is the sole survivor of the noble six hundred whofmade the famous charge at Balaclava."— American Paper. THE NATIONAL MUSIC OF SCOTLAND.—The music of Scotland-is of a much more extensive nature than might at first be supposed. If we were to reckon up all the vocal pieces—including many traditional ballad airs—pihrochs, strathspeys, reels, marches, hornpipes, jigs, and battle- piecess, the number would probably reach 7,000 or 8,000. Much has been done to preserve many of the finer melodies In book form, but there are numberless airs which have never yet appeared in musical notation, and are only to be heard in the secluded rural districts of the country. It is to be hoped that these will yet be rescued from the oblivion into which otherwise they are certain to fall with the spread of education, and with extended means of intercommunica- tion among the people. A collection embracing all that is worthy of preservation in Scottish music would be of great value, and would meet with acceptance from all lovers of !amine, heart-stirring melody.—Cassell's Family Maga. Me. WORDSWORTH AND BEAUMONT.—Of the long, intimate, ad unbroken friendship between William Wordsworth and iir George Beaumont we have many relics, but no adequate record. Perhaps the best known of the relics is a single line of verse— The light that never was on Pea or i and— which has come to do duty as a stock quotation, and which, like Milton's "fresh woods and pastures new," is almost always misquoted, "shore" being substituted for "land," just as " fields " is made to serve for the Mdtonic "woods." Probably in both cases the original sinner was some one who thought that the lines could be be improved by a little alteration ; and it may be taken for granted that very few' of those who have perpetuated the "see or shore" emenda- tion know even that the line was written by Wordsworth, mach less the name or nature of the poem in which it is to be found. Misquotation is inexcusable, because no one is called upon to quote if he cannot quote correctly.—The Magazine of Art. FREDERICK THE GREAT AND THE PASTY. 'During his stay in Amsterdam,the King wished to taste a Dutch pasty, which he had heard spoken of as particularly excellent. Hie, companion was directed to order one of the landlady of the house in which they lodged. On his application the woman eyed him with a look of some contemn- from head to foot, and said, .‘ Well, sir, as ye would like to eat a pasty, have ye the money to pay for one ? " Baldi assured the good woman that his companion could easily pay that sum, for .he was a virtuoso on the flute, and by playing a few hours he could get plenty of money. She then inquired what... virtuoso was. Baldi explained the meaning of the word, and told her that the stranger was an excellent performer on the flute, who was travelling to make money by his talent. "Oh, then, I mast hear him," said the hostess. Away she posted to the room where the King was, and, set- ting her arms akimbo,." Sir," said she, "as ye can pipe so cleverly, will ye just pipe a bit for me ? " At this unex- pected address, the King was rather taken by surprise, but italdi told him in a few words what had passed. Frederick cheerfully took the flute and played for some time in his best manner, so that the landlady, delighted with the per- formance, was fixed to the spot. When he had ceased, she said, "Sure enough, sir, ye can pipe nicely, and earn a penny. Now I'll go and make ye a pasty."—Magazine of Music. '

FAMILY ETIQUETTE.--In order to cultivate manners that will be really attractive and lasting, we must commence early labouring from the heart and soul outward, and they in their turn will react upon the heart,,and aid the growth and development of virtuous character. "If we wish to mould clay, or plaster of Paris, or metal into any shape, we mast not wait until it is half hard before we pat it into the mould, for then it will be fall of flaws and roughnessereand will not well take the desired form. So, if we wish to mould the heart and mind into good manners, we mast not wait until the child is half-grown before we begin the train- i big. We must begin with the young child. Greet its • waking with a smile and a loving word, that it may learn to wake up pleasantly. Teach it to take gently what is offered it, not snatching, and to return the look And word of ; thanks. Teach it to share its treasures, to pity and soothe anyone who is sick or sad, to pick up what is dropped by its elders, to lend its toys, to reply kindly, to say "please," "thank you," and "good bye"—indeed, there are hundreds of ways to teach a little one good manners. "Cultivate in your children the pleasant manners of a morning greeting, , saying "Good morning" with a smile and a bow; such a greeting makes the whole day go more pleasantly. Do not let the children gi to bed without a good-night kiss; they are never too old for that. And how do we know but that i _ . _

I JUBILEE FUND OF THE CONGREGATIONAL UNION.—An audited statement of accounts of this fund has just bees issued, showing that for the two years ending September last £114,205 passed through the books of the fund, of which £11,978 remains as a balance in hand. The total amount promised to the Meth of September was £270,970. This year both the spring and autumnal meetings of the Congregational Union of England and Wales are to be held in London, a circumstance which has not happened, with two exceptions, for nearly thirty years. The May assembly is to meet at the Memorial Hall and City Temple, under the presidency of the Rev. Jos. Parker, D.D. Mr. Frederic Harrison informs the Rev. J. P. Hoppa that he has no desire to enter the House of Commons, preferring. to assist in forming public opinion rather than to represent it in Parliament. Some of his political views might be thought too advanced and others too Conservative. On some

NEW DISESTABLISILMENT LITERATURE—The Liberation Society has just issued a series of new tracts and pamphlets, setting forth in brief the case for the three disestablishment motions, of which notice has been given for the present session of Parliament. They are clearly and forcibly writ- ten, and full of facts and arguments. There is one tract for each of the motions separately, and a fourth discussing the three motions together, and giving the argument for dises- tablishment, broadly as a matter of national policy. For friends and opponents alike, there is a great advantage in having the terms of these motions, together with an outline of the arguments in their favour, set forth in this brief but comprehensive form. But besides the tracts dealing speci- fically with the disestablishment motions, the new series in- cludes several dealing with the question of disestablishment in Wales, one of which consists largely of quotations from an address by the Dean of Bangor, and another of passages from recent speeches of Mr. H. Richard, M.P. These tracts and pamphlets will be extremely useful to all who wish to know what is said in support of their position by the friends of the disestablishment movement. • THE GARMOYLE BREACH OF PROMISE a...am—The statement of defence in the action for the breach of promise of marriage brought by Miss Finney (Miss Fortescue) against Lord darmoyle has now been duly delivered by Messrs. THE "STANDARD" AND THE Govnasimescr.—The lead- ing Conservative journal is offering advice to the Govern- ment on the subject of a dissolution. The Standard, having assumed that dissensions exist in the Cabinet, advises Mr. Gladstone that "a dissolution is the necessary remedy for the divisions of the Liberal party, and the weakness of the Liberal Administration." The Standard did not, so far as we remember, offer the same advice to Lord Beaconsfield at the periodical reconstructions of his Cabinet; nor does it offer more than the yagnest surmise that Mr. Gladstone and his colleagues are not thoroughly united. "A Conserva- tive," whose letter the Standard prints with the suggestive heading "Overdoing it," shows, on the other hand, that the Opposition leaders do not or will not lead. He says :—" I must confess that from being what would be designated a staunch Conservative, lam reluctantly becoming lukewarm, and fleet sure that my sentiments are felt by many other Conservatives, by the ridiculous and unwarrantable ob- struction shown to the Government by partisans of the Lord Randolph Churchill stemn. It is time that unprejudiced and right-feeling Englishmen should protest against this puely party factiousness, one might almost say spite." Tnis is a pretty accurate description of the tactics of the meaib)r for the late Duke of Marlborough. "A Conserva- tive" eor-s on to "pray that the Conservatives will, for the Country's into .est, cease from the useless hampering of the Governmonr," and to sue--eat that " unprejudiced Liberals and Cons,•l v ives" should unite and form "a strong Natianal party." ;.tiithlGN INTELLIGI'4Nc, E. OPERATIONS IN THE SOUDAN. The centre of interest in the Soudan has for the moment .Shifted from Suakim to Khartoum. The communication by telegraph southward of Shendy was cut a day or two ago, and on Sunday it had not been completely restored. The reports which were set whilst the telegraph was working are, it is said, very unsatisfactory with regard to the position of General Gordon, and it is feared that he is in much dan- ger. The I,!sr published telegram from Khartoum is dated the 11th inst. Wilting on that day the Times correspondent said that the Haggis, who liveon tha right bank of the Nile from Khartoum to Shendy, have thrown in their lot with General Gordon. This resolution had for the time etemmed the advance of the Shiekh el Obeid to the Nile. General Gordon hoped, therefore, to preserve the telegraph and his "iinnunications up to Berber intact, and, further, to take the offensive against the Shitlth El Obeid. General Gordon nad built a strong fortified camp on the opposite side of the Blue Nile, and stationed a strong force there to prevent the rebels from going further north on the line of communica- ntione. The £40,000, now famous as having been with tr *eneral Gordon, •• has not," says the correspondent, "to our Sorrow, yet reached Berber." Sir W. Hewett offered a reward for the capture or proof ef the death of 0.. and this was approved be the "friendly" Sheikhs who met the Admiral in council at Suakim. ['his proclamation was, however, disapproved by the British Government, who have ordered it to be with- !town. It is said that the chiefs near rani inieb have burnt this proclamation. Two chiefs who attempted to desert from Osman have been in.priseaed ; and this fate has also befallen the Sheik He, a, who fought against the British at Teb, the Mahrli's lieutenant condemning him for not hav- ing protected Toka. An advance was mai's by a small British force on Tues- tsar te the wells at liandouk, where a lsager is being formed. ao Arabs accompanied, wow, nor were any seen on the March or at Handoue. the Hussars are expected to advance to Otao, six miles beyond the 'eager, but whether any farther advance will be made in the direction of Berber or not ie unknown. What are Osman Digna's intentions is Uncertain, but rumour says that be is endeavauring to gather together sufficient followers to fight a third battle, and that ha IS sending out scouts to watch the British movements. These scouts are supposed to be in the neighbourhood of Handouk, but the British force that has been sent there will, no doubt, take precautiops to guard against any sudden advance of Osman Digna's new followers. Early yesterday morning General Stewart, with mounted Infantry and two squadrons of Hussars, advanced beyond Handouk to Otao, a place eight miles westwards, and 20 miles from Suakim. As on the previous day, no Arabs were encountered, but at Otao a sheikh—Hadar Abdullah—put iQ an appearance, and promised to visit the camp at Han- donk to-day with 100 men. He reported that Osman Digna ie atilt in the Tainanbid Valley, and it is generally under- stood that he has with him about 2,000 fighting men, in addition to a large number of wounded. A reconnaissance Was made in this direction by Major Ford, with a squadron gHussars, but an advance of five miles failed to discover e presence of the enemy. It seems, however, to be gener- ally believed that Osman will risk another battle. There is still no news from General Gordon telegraphic ci?inenunication with Khartoum not yet having been restored. The interruption of intercourse gives rise to alarming _ro.,inours, and there seems to be no doubt that some of the ,"lbee between Berber and Khartoum have, as General Gordon expected, declared for the Mandi. It appears now to be accepted as a fact that Zebehr Pasha is not to be sent „ Khartoum, and while uncertainty prevails as to the 'abus Governor of that place, the sheikhs who are disposed to be friendly towards General Gordon are afraid to corn- Mit themselves lest they should subsequently be attacked by the followers of the Mandi. The reports from Suakim are conflicting with regard to _ Position and intentions of Osman Digma. General ISrahani appears to be of opinion that his brave adversary IS about to be deserted by the sheikhs who had gathered .!°und him; and another report states that Osman has fled into the interior. A third version represents Osman as !gain ready for battle. The proclamation against him has been withdrawn, and the Arabs have -been informed that no riloy reward will be paid for his capture. general ewart continues to move his detachment about, bat at present there seems to have been no advance beyond nandoob. At Cairo great anxiety is felt in cosequenee ,*( the continued interruption of communication with Khartoum.

Osman Digna's village, with its stores of ammunition, has been destroyed. General Graham reports to the War Office that Osman %tut has fled to the bills, and that appearances are favour- able to the Berber road being shortly opened. _Several correspondents agree in stating that the rank and we of the expeditionary force are extremely dissatisfied with the prospect of a march into the desert. The men of the Second Brigade, who have been "interviewed" by correspon- dents, indulge in unsoldierlike reflections on their officers, Whom they accuse of unskilfulness. The Black Watch say that the Arabs did not actually "break" the square, but Rtreanted in through the gap which was loft when they (the Highlanders) were ordered to charge the enemy in front, thus breaking up the formation.

FRANCE AND TONQUIN. With the French in possession of Bacninh, and the Ton- quin question still unsettled, it is highly improbable that the Chinese should now be seeking to embroil themselves with Russia. A rumour to this effect, howeyer, is forwarded from St. Petersburg, where it is asserted that Chinese in- stigators are now in the Corea disturbing the friendly rela- tions that exist between the Corea and Russia, and endea- vouring to stimulate the native antipathy towards foreigners, so that the foreign trade of the country will destroyed. The Chinese, undoubtedly, will do what they eau to keep foreigners out of the Cores; but this Russian rumour will need confirmation before any importance can be attached to it. A Shanghai correspondent gives what appears to be a ear- correct account of public feeling in China on the Ton- rill question. He states that the Chinese Foreign Office is IStraCted by conflicting opinions; that the Government is Willing to relinquish the sovereignty of Armin and to give !P the whole peninsula to any European Power that will Ned the French; and that, so strong is the feeling against 11.ance, that even if the Chinese Government were willing !.? agree to extravagant demands on the port of the French, !lie country would probably not allow them to do so. In a litlle time this excited condition of public feeling in China will no doubt again subside, but in the meantime it would tPear that the statements coming from Paris, to the effect at.the Chinese have already sought the intervention of 'agland and America are at least premature.

HOUSE OF COMMONS, SAIIIRDAY.

ANOTHER ATTEMPT 10 CENSURE THE GOVERNMENT FOIL/M.—The House held the first morning sitting of the session oin Saturday, and by a combination of unexpected debates End Irish obstruction the sitting was prolonged until a quarter to six o'clock on Sunday morning. Mr. Gladstone did not attend, but the House was informed that a Catofnet Council had been summoned on Saturday forenoon. Lord Hartington was severely cross-questioned in regard to affairs in the Soudan, but could give no information beyond what had already been made public.—After considerable discussion, Mr. LAROUCF/ERE moved a resolution d-claring that no necessity had been shown for the recent sacrifice of life at Teb and Tamanieb.—Mr. HENRY RICHARD seconded the resolution as a protest against these operations, which constituted "a crime and a curse."—ln the subsequent debate much capital was made by Conservative speakers out Q 1 a general absence of Ministers, who were in Council, and a complaint came from the Opposition that this absence was intentional, it being clearly under- stood that this discussion had been fixed for that time.—Sir C Dilke, Mr. Childers, and Lord Elartmgton positively affir- med that no such arrangement had been made, and the noble lord, in replying on the motion, "distinctly declined" to be led by any violent demands into explanations and statements of policy which he considered injudicious in view of operations in Egypt.—Eventually the motion was rejected by 111 votes to 94.—The Home Secretary, when the numbers were announced, was overheard to remark that "that dirty trick has not succeeded," and the Speaker's opinion was sought as to the propriety of the observation.— Sir WILLIAM RAROOURT assured the House that he had in- tended no personal offence, and withdrew the words. The House went into Committee of Supply at half-past .ten o'clock, and disposed of a large number of votes. At three o'clock on Sunday morning the last supplementary vote—of £l,OOO for county court officers in Ireland—was reached, and gave rise to an animated debate. Mr. Healy and other Irish members resisted the vote by successive motions to report progress, and questions on points of order which arose from excilfed remarks by members. Mr. Lyulph Stanley was accused of using words imputing that the Irish members entertained murderous feelinas towards landlords, and after stating that his remark applied to their consti- tuents, the hon. member unconditionally retrac ed his ob- servation: Mr. Healy was sharply called* to order by the Chairman for observations ,respecting his ruling, but pro- mised to ask the Speaker's opinion to•day.—Ultimately the vote was carried by 59 votes to 7, anti the douse was re- leased, as stated, shortly before six o'clock. _

div.head: HaUSE OF LORDS.-MONDAY.
div.p: HaUSE OF LORDS.-MONDAY.

Tu TRANSVAAL —The main business bature the House was a discussion on the Transvaal Convention of three years ago, which was introduced by Earl Cadogan. His lordship, holding that the covention had been inoperative, thought it Should be superseded by the new agreement, in case the latter was ratified by the Volksraad. After a de- claration by Lord Derby to the effect that our suzerainty had not been abandoned, the Marquis of Salisbury thought a ratification by Parliament of the new treaty might have been insisted upon as one of the conditions of signature. The treaty was one of retrocession, and afforded no security for the proper treatment of natives within the Transvaal Republic. The Earl of Kimberley drew attention to consti- tutional usage in the ratification of treaties, and deprecated farther discussion at the moment. The 'matter was then allowed to drop. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MoNnev.

THE BUDGET.—The CHANCELLOR Of the EXCHEQUER, answering Sir S. Northcote, said he hoped to Introduce the Budget before Easter, probably on Monday, April 8, pro- vided the Franchise Bill had been read a second time. _

KHARTOUM.—Mr. A. Bartlett having asked foe informa- tion of the intentions of the Government hare mrd to affairs at Khartoum, Lord HARTINGTON said the Government would make a statement as soon as possible, but it was not desirable in the interest of the public service that it should be made until it could be complete. His Lordship further stated that a telegram bad been sent to Admiral Hewett pointing out that such a proclamation as he was alleged to have issued fot the capture of Osman Digma ought not to be put forward without communication with Sir E. Bar- ing. THE ABMY.—On the motion to go into committee on the Army Estimates several discussions on matters of army ad- ministration were raised.—Colonel TOTTENHAM characterised our army as a gigantic sham, and said we were living in a fool's paradise, and nothing would disturb us but such a storm as burst over our neighbours across the Channel. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TIIESDAY..

On the motion of the Marquis of SALISBURY, it was agreed that all private bills which proposed to clear away dwell- ings of the poor should be circulated in the same manner as public bills. His lordship thought that the over-crowd- ing of the poor had been increased and intensified by private bill legislation as conducted heretofore. HOUSE OF COMMONS—TUESDAY. Tim CONGO TREATY.—Mr. Jame BRIGHT mentioned the Congo Treaty, and asked if an opportunity would be afforded for an expression of opinion before it was ratified.— Lord HARTINGTON replied that the treaty would not be rati- fied with any. undue haste, and asked the hon. member for Manchester to postpone farther inquiry upon the subject until the return of the Premier, or at least until Thursday. ADMIRAL HEWETT'S PROCLAMATION.—The Government was questioned as to the proclamation offering a reward for the capture of Osman Digna, and the Sacarreux for WAR stated that the terms of the document were such as the Government could not approve, and consequently a telegram had been sent to Sir W. Hewitt directing that the offer of a reward for the capture of Osman must be withdrawn in the manner which might be considered most jodicious.—Lord E. FITZMAURICE stated that no despatch had been received from General Gordon for a week, and that the wire was not now working between Shendy and Berber. Tax CATTLE DISEASHS SILL.—T4e second reading of the Cattle Diseases Bill was moved by Mr. DODSON, who ex- plained that the measure was intended to hit the happy points which would give the maximum of reasonable security to the stockholders without hampering trade or raising the price of meat.—Mr. A. ARNOLD thought the measure was not needed, and that it afforded means whereby a good deal of unnecessary restriction might be placed on the food supply of the people, to the detriment of a large number of consumers throughout the kingdom. He should not propose the amendment he had placed upon the paper, but reserve his right to oppose the measure, should he think it necessary, during its progress through the House. —Mr. J. HOWARD thought the speech of the hon. member for Salford was one-sided, and urged that if cotton or wool imported from any particular country was infested with a particular parasite which upon intro- duction into this country had power to multiply itself almost indefinitely, the cotton spinners of Lancashire and the wool manufacturers of Bradford would not insist that the doctrine of free trade must be upheld in that respect.—Mr. C. S. READ, in supporting the bill, urged that Elie butchers were largely to blame for maintaining the price of meat. He also urged that the use of milk from diseased animals was the cause of a good deal of disease among human beings.—Mr. W. E. Forster, Mr. Chaplin, Mr. Barclay, Mr. Ha.stings, Mr. Ackland, and Mr. Bryce took part in the debate, and an Irish member was speaking in opposition to the bill when according to the rules the debate stood adjourned.—When the Honse'resumed al nine o'clock it was: immediately counted Ott. THE ass- in-ormmits BILL—The afternoon was devoted to the discuesion of the Leaseholders (Facilities of Purchase of Fee Simple) Bill, the object of which is to enable the holder of any lease of a house, cottage, or chapel that has twenty years or more to run, to purchase the fee simple through the medium of the county court.—The second reading was moved by Mr. BROADHURST, who argued that the wretched invention of leasing land for building purposes had degraded and almost ruined house building throughout the coantiy. , Having tiointed out the viciousness of the life lease system, the hon. member contended that it would be wisdom to pass a moderate measure of enfranchisement which would give to every landlord his just dues, rather than delay legislation until it became impossible to resist some more far-reaching scherne.—Mr. GREGORY moved the ' rejection of the bill, and Mr. ALCIERNON EunaTore objected to it because it would interfere with freedom of contract, and create nothing but confusion and disturbance.—The ATLORNEY-GENERAL thought the bill would be unworkable; it would not do any gp?d, but would play into the hands of land jobbers and specubitori; and therefore he could not give it his support.—The debate was continued by Lord R. Churchill, Sir IL Oiffard, and other hon. mem- bers, and ultimately upon a division the bill was rejected by 168 to 104. HOUSE OF LORDS.—THIIRSDAT.

div.head: IRELANP.
div.p: IRELANP.

COLLISION AT SEA AND Loss OF Srx LIVES —lntelli- gesce reached Cork on Tuesday that the German barque Lucca and the American barque Annie Johnson came into collision on Sunday morning. The German vessel was sunk, and six of the crew were drowned. The Annie John- son ran into the Lueca. The Irish Master of the Rolls on Tuesday refused to grant a special subpcena to compel Mr. Perna', M.P., to attend as a witness in an action in which he sued one of his tenants for three years' arrears of rent on lands in Wick- low. The defence is that Mr. Parnell had assented to as- signments on defendant's interests to another person whom Mr. Parnell stated he would hold accountable.

While divine service was proceeding in High-street Roman C Itholic Church, Dublin, on Sunday, Joseph Enly. a pri- vate in the Scots Guards, rose from his seat, and, addressing the preacher, Rev. Mr. O'Connor, made use of filthy and profane language. The congregation loudly expressed their indignation, and beer ming excited ejected the soldier, using considerable violence. On Monday, at the Dublin Police Court. the soldier was fined 403., or one month's imprison- ment. SERIOUS AFFILAY.---A Monaghan Correspondent telegraphs I that a shocking tragedy took place on Monday evening, at I Killycooley, arising out of a quarrel about a right of way, ' between a family named Kelly and their neighbours. One man, named M'Gale, had his skull cloven through with a hatchet, death being almost instantaneous. Another, named Brien, was so badly injured that his life is despaired of. A third man was dangerously wounded, and lies in a critical condition. The police arrested two brothers and two sisters of the Kelly. They were removed to Monaghan and lodged in jail. The "vitriol throwing case" in Arklow has excited an " intense sensation." The victim was a solicitor, named Toomey, and his alleged assailant a young lady, named Tyndall. The circumstances of the case are mysterious, and a good deal of recrimination has taken place ;but the affair has been further complicated by the marriage of Miss Tyndall to a person named Gyll. It is new said that Gyll purchased the vitriol which his wife threw over Mr. Toomey, and told her to use it. If this be so, the young lady's ac- count of the transaction—namely, that she only threw the vitriol as a last resort to protect herself against Toomey— becomes, to say the least of it, somewhat doubtful. Mr. Parnell, speaking at a St. Patrick's-day banquet on Monday evening in London, said that in order to work out Ireland's future and regeneration they must rely only on the exertions of Irishman at home and abroad, for he did not depend upon any English party. He was confident that the future was never more promising, for a spirit had been infused into the Irish people which would never die, and they thoroughly understood the weak points in their ene- mies' armour. He felt confident that the time was very near when Irishmen of all sections and religions would meet on Irish soil and celebrate St. Patrick's-day ueder the protec- tion of an Irish Parliament. Then they could seed that message of peace to England which could never be sent from Ireland save by a self-governed intim,. Mr. A. M. Sullivan also addressed the gathering. ETIC'ING A DYING MAN —Early on Wednesday morning, a constable, while on duty in Werburgh-street, Dublin, observed two men carrying the body of a man out of one of the houses there, and placing him in a sitting position on the footpath. On examining the body the officer found that life was extinct, and thereupon he entered the house and arrested the occupants. who gave their names as Jos. Lynch (framer), James Coleman (plasterer), and Anne Robinson, a widow. The body was conveyed to the hospital, where it was identified as that of John Frere, aged 50, a lodger in the house. No marks of violence were found on it. From later inquiries it appears that the deceased was dying from bronchitis, and Robinson, the owner of the place, demanded from him some gent he owed her. He had no money, so she, assisted by the other two prisoners, carried him into the street when in the act of expiring. Mr. Tuke has published an account of the operations of the Emigration Committee in the congested districts of Connemara. A considerable amount of money has been remitted to Ireland in the tete) past years by emigrants who have gone from Galway and Mayo. As to the "robbing of the shopkeeper" by sending away the people, Mr. Take bears testimony to the highly honourable way in which the emigrants have discharged their old debts. tie mentions the case of a very small shopkeeper in a remohacorner of Gal- way who had received £BO of old debts in this way from remittances sent home by emigrants, and another instance of a larger shopkeeper, who was originally much opposed to the work, and who has written to say that considerable slims have been sent to him, and that more has been done by emigration to relieve the district than by any other previous form of relief. As regards another use which is made of the remittances, it is notorious, he says, that a very large amount has been de- voted to the payment of rent—indeed, it is stated that many evictions have been prevented by the "American money," just as in Swineford or other portions of Ireland the rents are paid from the earnings received for work done in England or Scotland. The hishman takes, of course, a different view. It trots out the old imposture about the Irish battalions at Fontenoy," and warns us that in Eng- land, in Canada, Australia, and the States, 'the fierce love of fatherland" and the "grim bate," .ke., is preparing avenging hosts who will be ready to avail themselves of England's difficulties. Meanwhile it is to be observed the said hosts are living peaceably and "doing well," and know that they will have a share in any measure of prosperity that falls to us. They will be amazed to learn, on the authority of Mr. Parnell's jonrnal, that "to seek for any remote analogy for the atrocious action of England towards Ireland we must go back to the days of Atilla, the scourge of God,' or contemplate the skull-pyramid con- quests of Tamerlane."

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL
div.p: THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL
BILL.

The Lords' Committee on the Ship Canal Bill resumed the inquiry on Monday. Mr. S. Andrew, secretary of the Oldham Cotton Spinners' Association, referred to the man- ner in which bales of cotton were left or the quays at Liver- pool, exposed to damage from weather, and said such neglect would not occur at Manchester. He believed the cotton market would be removed to Manchester if the canal Was made. Mr. D. Adamson was cross-examined on certain points of his former evidence. Testimony was given as to the probable saving of cost to Bolton spinners and manu- facturers by Mr. Barlow, managing director of a large con- cern in that town. Mr. Alderman Hopkinson, ex-mayor of Manchester, gave e7idence as representing the Corporation. He believed the judgment of the citizens had been taken in every possible way, and that the whole population was unanimous in demanding additional facilities for transport- ing goods between Manchester and the sea. He antici- .pated that the scheme would be of immense advantage to the district. On Tuesday Sir Joseph Heron, Town Clerk of Manches- ter, was examined. He said the City Council were strongly in favour of the scheme. Liverpool charges must continue to be high, seeing that the debt of the Dock Board was now £18,000,060, as against £B,OOO 000 in 1857. There was a large amount of capital awaiting investment, and he had no doubt that £10,000,000 could be and would be subscribed for the Ship Canal scheme In Manehester and the district aloe. 'llr Alderman Bennett also gave evidence in sup- port of the,hill, and declared his belief that the necessary capitafWonld be forthcoming. The Mayor of Salford (Mr. C. Makinson) and Mr. Alderman Thompson (Manchester) were amowthe, other witnesses called by the promoters. The list-named ,gentlipnan said the passing of this bill Wtrdld'nolderibt entAlli hpon Manchester a new and large drainage admit.. On Wednesday thkeyiflence was mainly that of Manches- ter merehand in ifs4ftri bt cheaper transit between the city and foreign market Mr. Sam Mendel said that at one time he exported four, inandred tons of goods per week, and if the Canal had existed during the time of his commercial activity he would have,relved Sfe.ooo. per annum in transit charges.—Sir J. C. Lee thought a reduction of the present heavy rates of freight was of Vital importance to the suffer- ing trade of Manchester andY Lancashire generally. He expected that such Altiltioit Would come Irons the Construc- tion of the Canal.—Mr. Pope, Q-C, who represents oppos- ing railwarinterests, did not dispute the assertion that Mattchieeter mattbante ^would derive substaatial benefits frpnadowerecl rates folls,owing upon a completion of the tindertaking.--Evidence was given to show the injurious effenroroPPressive tales of transit upon the heavy iron trade ! of Manchester, as exemplified by the Ashbury Waggon Corn-

pan?. Mr. George Woods, examined by Mr. Balfour Browne, said he was secretary to the Longford Wire, Iron, and Steel Company, Limited, Warrington, which was the seat of the iron wire trade. div.head: TARBOCK.
div.p: TARBOCK.

ALLEGED ASSAULT BY A FARMER. At the Prescot Police Court, on Tuesday, John Taylor, farmer, Tarhock, was charged with having assaulted Thomas Penney, a farm labaurer. The cornplainant, it seemed, is employed by Mr. Richardson, a farmer, and a neighbour of the defendant. On Sunday, the fhli inst., he was going past the defendant's house on a footpath.when, he alleged, the defendant struck him and knocked him into a hedge, and also tore his coat. In defence several witnesses were called, who stated that the complainant was in the habit of going and‘mmoying the defendant, and who denied positively that any assault had been committed. A fine of 2s. 6d. and costs was im- posed.

div.head: SALE.
div.p: SALE.

DEATH 7a.Obi HYDROPH—O—BI—A7LA dreadful case n 4 death from hytimphobia took place at Sale, near Manchestcr, on Sunday. On the 3tst of January, William Gray. coachman to Mr. Scott, Brooklands Hotel, found a small slate-colcured terrier dog near Brook Ian& Cemetery. It appeared hungry and starved; and deceased took it into the stable and led it. Subsequently he patted the dog, which flew at him and bit him on the chin. The dog was destroyed, and the wound was cauterised, and appeared to heal up. No unfavourable srmptons presented themselves until Friday last, when the deceased was seized with rabies. Dr. Renshaw and a doc- tor from Manchester Infirmary were called in, but, despite all efforts, he died a horrible death at one o'clock on Sunday. The deceased leaves a widow and two children. SANDBACH.

FEVER E.PinExtc. A special meeting of the Sandbank Local Board was held on Saturday (Rev. J. R. Armistead presiding) to consider a letter from the Local Government Board with reference to the water supply and sewerage ar- rangements. It was stated that there were newly 70 cases of fever in the district, and a sur:gestion to close the schools was discussed i It was decided to take steps to close the public schools in the township. The meeting was adjourned to enable Dr. Fox, the medical officer of health, to report as to the best means to be adapted. SO ITTEI WORTH - WITH-CROFT.

SCHOOL BOARD.—Tbe monthly meeting of the above Board was held in the Board School on Tuesday evening. Present—The Rev. T. P. Kirkman (chairman and clerk), and Messrs. James Hatton, Lewis Birchail, Richard Turner, and Alfred Dixon (attendance officer). Tho Attendance Officer submitted his report, which stated that he had visited the various schools in the Board's district during the past month, when he found that 37 children had been away from school sick during the month, and that several of them were away sick at the present time. He also reported that he had served one notice on a parent for a child to attend school in pursuance of the bye-laws and summoned four parents to appear before the Board, all of whom appeared, and were warned that unless their children attended school more regularly they would be summoned before the magi- strates. The report having been adopted the proceedings terminated, there being no other business. WINSFORD.

LIBERAL CLuis.—A lecture on the franchise was de- livered at the Liberal Club room on Tuesday night by Mr. John Buckley, F who gave a detailed account of the great constitutional changes which led to the growth of the franchise and those particular epochs of our history when the peoples rights have been most respected and the coun- try sived trout anarchy and ruin; when our glorious con- stitution has been consolidated and perfected, and the people rendered happier and more contented. The reform Bills of 1264, 1832, 1867, and the proposed one for 1884, were dwelt upon at large and the credit of the changes made, placed to their right accounts. In the unavoidable absence of Dr. H. Leake as chairman, the Rev. W. S. Symons pre- sided, and in a very suitable manner introduced the lec- turer. After the lecture, Mr. Hough sang a political song entitled " Fhe Franchise" in a very effective manner, elici- ting an encore. Mr. Bate proposed the best thanks of the audience to the lecturer and urged that such lectures should be oftener. Mr. Tolfree, the , secretary, seconded.— Mr. Buckley acknowledged the vote and proposed a simi- lar compliment to the chairman and Mr. Rough, which was passed unanimously. A vote of condolence with Mr. Gladstone in his present indisposition, and with her Majesty's Government, was proposed and unanimously carried, and will be sent by the secretary to its proper des- tination.

div.head: ITEMS OF CHESHIRE NEWS.
div.p: ITEMS OF CHESHIRE NEWS.

CATTLE DISE&SE IN CHESHIRE.—The weekly returns issued on Wednesday show that there is only one animal remaining under treatmant. for foot-and-canuth disease in the county, against nineteen last week. Eighteen animals have recovered, and there has been no fresh outbreak. The complete stamping out of the disease is now confidently anticipated. This is the most gratifying report for the past twelve months. . _ .

ENSILAGE IN CHESHIRE. - A meeting of tke tenants on the Peckforton estate was hell at Peckforton Castle on Mon- day, by invitation of Lord Tollemache, of lielmingham, to consider the question of ensilage. Lord Tollemache, in ad- dressing his tenants, said this was probably the first meeting hell with a view of extending to tenant farmers the advan- tages of making ensilage as fodder for stock. The offer he had to make was to construct silos on the tenants farms, on condition that if the making of the ensilage proved an ad- vantage the tenants should pay five per cent interest on the outlay; bat that if the reverse was the case, notwithstand- ing every care having been taken in the filling of the silos and weighting the ensilage properly, the tenants would have to pay nothing —(Loud applause.) lie made this offer for the purpose of encouraging a system which would, he was persuaded, benefit greatly those engaged in agriculture, not only in Cheshire, but throughout the kingdom.—(Applause.) —A discussion then took place among the farmers prEsent, and, as a result, Mr. Walley, of Tilston, moved that the hest thanks of the meeting be tendered to Lord Tollemache for his interest In the welfare of the tenants' and that the terms offered were the most liberal that could be conceived. This was seconded by Mr. Allwood, of Borland, and unanimously carried.

EAELLESTOWN CO-OPERATIVE SOCITTY.—In connection with this society a public entertainment was given in the Co-operative Hall, on Saturday evening last, when Bea Brierley's comic Lancashire sketch, entitled " Fratching- ton's of Fratchingthorpe," was cleverly given by Messrs. Butterworth and Travis. There was a large audience, who thoroughly appreciated the entertainment. Several songs were given daring the evening. rnESCOT HIGHWAY Boadan.—On Tuesday morning, meetieg of this Board was held at Prescot for the purpose of completing the business of the Board's financial year. The chair was occupied by Mr, W. L. Evans, and there were also present Messrs. T., Pilkington, M. Lowe, and John Leatherbarrow, together with Mr. Cross (clerk), and Mr. Golaworth (surveyor).—All the remaining accounts of the year having been submitted and passed, it Was reported that the township of Knowsley was still £l3O in arrear on its call. It was resolved that the overseers of that township should be written to and asked to pay this sum before the 25th lust —This was all the business. , HALF-HOLIDAY MOVEMENT AT ST. HELENS.—On Mon- day evening a meeting of tradesmen was held in the Fleece Hotel, Sc. Helens, to further consider the question of the Thursday half-holiday, the three months daring which it was agreed to close the shops having expired. The chair was occupied by Mr. Henry Martin, Chefroh-street. There was a good attendance. From the disetfetlitat'Which took place it appeared to be considered by most nf tlieles present that the halt-holiday was a very great boon not'enly to the assistants,but also to the tradesmen themselves. A deputa- tion wasnent from the meeting to wait upon Mr. Piton, draper,' Cbttrch-Hreet, who has hitherto ref used to join the movement, to see if he would now join, bat on returning the deputation reported that that gentleman still adhered to his resolution to keep his shop open. It was, however, agreed that the half-holiday should be continued for another three•montbe at least.
