GREAT LIBERAL DEMONSTRATION AT EARLESTOWN. The Liberals of Earlestown and district held a Meg en- thusiastic gatheeng in the Vieduct Institute. Eeriest Own, on Wednesday evening, Preceding this meeting the mem- bers of the Liberal Club held their annual meeting, and the business transacted is repootedin another column. At the public meeting the attendance was a very large one, and the stirring and eloquent addresses of the various gentlemen who expounded the principles of the Liberal party main- tabled an enthusiasm among the audience which fouod expression in repeated and hearty cheers. The chair was occupied by Colonel George McCorgoodale, if., of Newton- le-Willows, and he WAS supported on the platform by Chas. Pilkimgtotie Esq., J.P. (one of the vice-presidents of the flub), Committer Miles (Liverpool), A. Nilson, W. C. Raw- lins, G. H. Croxden Powell, Esqs. (of Liverpool), Messrs. Richards and Leach, of Manchester (representing the National Reform Union); the Rev. F. N. Shimmin (Earles- town), Dr. 7. E. Hayward ( Haydock), and Messrs. B. ; Walker, G. F. Aveline, P. Nall, and Jokn Bahl (of Hoke- town!, As the gentlemen. neede their appearance on the platform they were very warmly received. At the call of the Chairman' Mr. THOS. Howann (secre- tary) read letters af apology for non-attendance from the Rev. W. C. Tayler. Richard Pilkington, Esq., JO'. (St. Helens), W. W. Pilkington, Eye (St. Helens), and a tele- gram from A. C. ItecCorquodale, Esq., J.P., who WAS in London. The CHAIRMAN said that they were met that night to eonsider priecipelly the extension of the franchise. A bill had been introduced on the subject in the House of CMo- mons, and, however interesting that might be to the rest of the United Kingdom, it was particalarly so to the people MI thin country. It was further particularly of interest to theca residing in that locality. (Hear, hear.) It was not more than fifty years since the Zfancbester and Liverpool Rail- way, which passed the town, was constructed ; and at that time Manchester had not a representative in Parliament, whereas the little place of Newtown had two members re- turned by about nineteen electors. (Laughter.) The Re- form Big of 1882 had, changed all this. Mbochester had got its representatives, and they had been taken from Newtown. But Manchester bad grown, and the people bad had to go out of the town. A great number of works and mills had to be built outside the towns.- A great deal of the men employed at the large works in Earlestown had bees brought from Manchester. There went the Vulcan works, employing a great number of skilled men engaged in the making of hmornotives to a very large extent. Whilst in Manchester these men had a vote • but when they came to Eerlestown they were de- prived of it, simply by their removal sense sioteen miles, or an hour's journey from Manchester. One of the im- poses of the bill was to remedy this grievance and iniestice to working men, and he had no doubt that when the matter became thoroughly sifted in Parliament it would be put right. (Applause.) The measure centempla'ed the addition of 2,000,000 of voters to the' electoral roll. It was urged by the Conservatives that all , these fresh electors would turn over and join their side. I If that was so it was a very bad argument to use in opposing the bill; it should be rather something .t 0 make I them support it. (Heir, hear.) It should make no differ- ence in the course the Liberal party intended to pursue. Whatever might be the ultimate effect they had to do jus- tice to the people. A great change had taken place in the character and in the power of working men, and it WAS their dit y to give them the same privilege in the c nentry which would be enjoyed in the town. (Applause.) He would say frankly that if that bill passed and the working men choose to go round and become Conservatives by all means let them do so. Let each man act as he thought. right. (Applause.) Then they said the House of Lords had made up its mind that if the bill went there to throw it out; but the House of Lords must remember that they would have to obey the dictates of the country. He would be sorry to be one of those who wiled do away with the House of Lords, because they had in time past found great benefit from that house in checking hasty legislation, but that was not hasty legiela- tion. With regard to the Hones of Lords, he thought a change might be very advisable; it was not fair that when a member of the Upper House disgraced. himself and acted improperly, and showed himself to be an immoral man, that born legislator should still have the privilege of taking part in the legislation of the country, ((deer, hear.) He hoped that some of the younger men who were present would see in the future that the Sovereign of the land who, had the power of granting would also have the power of withholding the privilege of legislation, and even of a title for a time on the misconduct of any member of the House of Lords. The Commons were judged on that principle, and if they misbehaved themselves were no longer quelified to discharge the privileges which honest men enjoyed. Remarks were made at a recent meeting in that neighbmr- hood by one gentleman who said that he had entirely changed from a Liberal to a staunch Conservative. It was a pity he did not give his reasons for that change, because they might have been convinced also or have been able to bring forward counter arguments. That gentleman might have been able to tell them that the Liberal party had made mistakes in such measures as the repeal of the paper duty, that the poor man had no right to his halfpenny paper, by which he was kept too well-info med. He might have been able to show them that it was a mistake to inaugurate the system of free trade by which the food of the people had been increased in quantity, improved in quality, and reduced in price. (Hear, hear.) But he did not bring forward any such arguments, and that was a pity, because they would have been better able Co understand the position of that gentleman. He had heard it said by a young man that a large number of his friends were Conservative; and he (the speaker) believed that was so, because it was thought that Conservatism was the more fashionable creed—in fact, he had heard it said a Conserva- tive could be told by the faultless neatness of the polish of his boots. (Laughter.) Well, that might be so, for they could net all attain to such niceties; but the Liberals had at least this proud fact to boast of—that their party had done much to improve the position of the working man. The wee king men present would all jOn in that assertion, and not only so, but they would agree that the manners and morals of the people were also improving, crime and pauper- ism having largely decreased. The change which was now contemplated by the Government in the extension of the franchise to all who were able to think and act for themselves would, he believed, add strength to the consti- tution, and increase the happiness of that great empire. (Applause.) ( aear, bear.) With such principles and such leaders as the Li eerals had they need not be afraid of the appeal to the peopl.! with which Lord selik- bury seemed to threaten them. They had seen the mime of Liberalism steadily advancing in the past fifty veers,. tin?' they believed it would be BO in the future. Strong in Ad faith, they looked forward with undaunted c el-rage to She time when the rankanf battle should once more be formed, and when, as they helieved, the banner of victory woad float over the Liberal ranks, after what might not perhaps be an easy, but would- certainly be a decisive victory. (Rear, hear.) Mr. W. C. Itemizers{ Liverpool) propose 1 :—" That this meeting of the inhabitants of Eerlestown and district views with greet alarm the amendments proposed to the Govern- ment bill in the House of Lords retarding the importation of foreign live cattleinto the United Kingdom, and further- more, this meeting expresses an earnest hope that Her Majesty's Government and the House of Commons will re- fuse their consent to such amendments, which, if carried into effect, would limit the supply of meat to our working classes, thus effectually lowering the value of their wages in increasing the price of meat." He explained that the amendments of the House of Lords to the Goveenment bill affecting the importation of cattle would make a differeae of about 15 million tons. What would be the effect of stopping this meat be upon the working classes?' It would immediately raise the price, and consequeutly the value of their wages would be smaller, and the men would be poorer. The trade of the country would also be correspondingly affected The object of introducing the amendments was simply to get in the thin edge of the wedge of protection of landed interests. If they would carefully examine all Tory legislation from the . housing of the poor down to the meat supply they would find that it always went in the same direction of landed interest—to protect and increase the value of land, to raise the rents, and consequently to swell the pockets and purses of the great land-owners. R•O thought the present was the time when the Government needed all the support the country could afford them, for the amend- ments of the House of Lords were a retrograde movement. He asked them to stand shoulder te shoulder and show they were united as a Liberal party in supporting the Premier as the sun of his glory now sets in life, and so gild with yet brighter radiance that glorious monument which shall be raised to his memory, and which this country will give him, namely, the lasting veneration and love of the English people. (Loud applause.) Mr. RICHARDS (of Manchester) heartily seconded the resolution, and in doing so said he thought that in the amendments to the Cattle Importation Bill they had protec- tion showing itself once more. It was an attempt to throw a sop to the farmer by increasing the value of the produce of the farm, but it was a very mistaken one, and he thought it would result disastrously to the farmer as well as the consumer of mat. The action of the Tory party in that matter opened up the whole question of their food supply, and speaking to those whom he thought would stiortly be enfranchised he could call their sued it attention to it, because it was a matter they would have to deal with in the near future when considering the land laws in Eneland and their relation to the feed supply. They were told by the best authorities that it was possible to increase the food supply of this country by three million pounds per annum —between 50 and 100 per cent. They should remember that the amendments were cemiag from that class which had always opposed the improvement of the English people, and if they allowed legislation like the preseut Amendments to pass, thereby increasing the value of food, they were materially diminishing the value of their wages and earn- ings. He did not want to see any Improvement or reform of the Upper House ; they should either tolerate or abolish it. (Applause.)

Mr. P. HALL (Earlestown) supported the resolution," re- marking that though he would not go &Vat- as his friend who had just sat down, and say they ought to abolish the House of Lords, 'yet if that institution could not see to its beat interests in giving food to the people, be would almost go in for abolishing it. (Applause.) If they as Liberals allowed such things to be introduced into the proposals of the Government as the House of Lords had suggested, they would not be doing their duty. They should tool: at the matter not as a political question, but Liberals and Con- servatives should unite in supporting the Government against the restrictions which the House of Lords desired to put upon the cattle trade. (Applause.) This resolution was also enthusiastically calried.
On the motion of Mr. G. F. AVELINE, seconded liqr Dr. T. E. HaMann, of flaydock, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the speakers, on behalf of whom Mr. Itewuris responded._

M. G. H. C. Powett, of Liverpool, in moving a similar compliment to the Chairman, stated that Colonel McCor- quOdale was always active in the Liberal work of the dis- trict, always to the front, and always encouraging those about him. (Applause.) If they hsd more such men tpe he in South-West Lancashire they mirht rest assured that when the next election came they would have a greater success than they had on the last occasion. (Applause.) Mr. T. Hovraun heartily seconded the motion,which wee • accorded with much enthusiasm. Colonel McCourunonat.ii, On rising to respond, was I received with cheers. He thanked teem sincerely for the cOrdpllment, and went on to say that the meeting had been alitsrte'ptly unanimous and haOrnonioua one. The only dif- ference seemed td be with reference to the House of Lords. (Laughter.) For himself be thought the House of LordP, which was an old institution, would mend, and be a noble ' initftntlon torn long time to come. (Rear, hear.) I The meeting then concluded.

div.head: DIST RICT NEWS.
div.p: DIST RICT NEWS.

ALTRINCHA.N. THE ALTRINCHAM BUILDING bOCIETY.— A meeting of the shareholders of the Aitrinchaun Building Society was held at the offices of th • society on Tuesday, Mr. Ambler in the chair.—Mr. Fowden, solicitor, of Altrincharn, presented a report showing the position of the society.—Mr. Lindell (Nichols, Harris, and Lindsell) and Mr. Craven (Brett and Craven 't submitted a scheme for the dissolution of the so- ciety, the loanholders to be paid in full, and the remaining asses to be divided rateably between the shareholders. It was explained that if the scheme could be carried through, the expense of liquidation by the Court could be avoided. The amount owing to the loanholders is considerably less than two-thirds of the assets, so that the scheme would not involve any loss to the loanholders —A resolution was tin- anitnously passed in favour of the society being dissolved in accordance with the scheme submitted, and a committee was appointed to settle the details of the proposed deed of dis- solution and settlement. C A.DISHE A.D. The Wesleyan quarterly meeting of the Cadisbead circuit was held in the large ves,ry of Cadishead Chapel on Monday last at six o'clock in the evening. The members were generously entertained to tea at the house of the society steward, Mr. Johnson. At the close of the tea the friends adjourned to the chapel. We were favoured with the presence of the chairman of the district, the Rev. Dr. Pope, who addressed, the meeting on revivals and on different phase!, of preaching. The address was chaste and beautiful, wide in its range and forceful in its application. The re- portof the day and Sabbath schools in the circuit was satis- factory and encouraging. The spiritual condition of the circuit is very hopeful. The congregations generally goed and increasing. The Rev. It. Dillon was most cordially thanked for his services during the year, and was heartily and unanimously invited to remain a third year on the circuit, whioh he has consented to do. The meeting was brought to a close, big with hope for the future. DO WNA.LL GREEN CHURCH OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE SOCIETY.—A. meet- ing was held last week, .in the Ashton Rectory Schools, Downall Green, for the purpose of re-organising a branch of the above, vihicb, though having existed for some years, has from certain causes been in abeyance. Tne meeting, which was fairly attended, was presided over by the Rev. W. J. Melville, the reepected rector of the parish, who, in opening the proceedings, said he had a pleasing though solemn duty to perform. After saying hew pleased he was to see so many attending the meeting which he had called, he had, be said, ascertained that it was the wish of many of his parishioners that the branch be re-established. They.. must bear in mind, however, that having no curate, he had to perform his parochial duties single-handed, and he would, therefore, ask them to render him all the assistance they could. After adducing sound scriptural arguments in support of the temperance cause, the chairman introduced the Rev. .% Hirst, organising secretary for the diocese of Liverpool, who addressed the meeting and spoke in high terms of the good the society had already effected. He He gave statistics showing the amount of intemperance still existing, and instance' such places as Widnes, Peugeot, Whiston, St. Helens, where, he said, the branches were doing great good. In CODCIII9iOO, he earnestly urged every one present to join the society and to try and get others to join also.—A meeting of the Ashton Holy Trinity branch of the Church of England Temperance Society was held on Mon- day evening last, the rector presiding. This being the first meeting of the newly-formed branch society, the business was entirely formal. The respective officers appointed for I the working of the society are: President, the Rector; vice- president, Geerge James Robins, Esq. ; secretary, Mr. J. Riffles; treasurer, Mr. Joseph Robinson. The committee consists of twelve members, four of whom are ladies. TIATDOCS. -

Harnocx LOCAL BOARD—On Monday afternoon a special meeting of the Haydock LOCAI Board was held for the pur- pose of passing accounts so that they could be made up to March 25th, the end of the financial year. There were present :—Messrs. C. Pilkington, John Jackson, Wm. Alker, and Thomas Turnbull (clerk). The business was merely formal. The clerk submitted accounts amounting to £92 ss. (3d, which were examined and passed for p4yment. The meeting thei concluded. LOCAL BOARD ELECTION AT HAYDOCK. The annual election of three members of the liaydock Locil Board is at present creating some interest in the township. The re- tiring members are—Messrs. Joseph Evans, Thomas Jack- son, and William Alker, all of whom are eligible for re-elec- tion. There are rumours that at least one other candidate will be proposed. Nominations have to be seat in to the returning officer (Mr. W. Balharrv) on or before to-morrow (Saturday), and in Case of a contested election the voting papers will be seat out on the 25th inst., collected on the 29th and examined on the 31st inst.

div.p: HUYTON.

HUYTON CHURCH —A sermon was preached on Sunday morning in the above church on behalf of the Curates Augumentation Funds, by ths Rev. J. R. Humble (organis- ing secretary), who took for his text, " But the priests were toe few," IL Chronicles, 29th chapter, 34th verse. The col- lection amounted to £l7 18s. 5. . . .

FATAL ACCIDENT NEAR PRESCOT.—An inquest was held at the Hazels, the residence of Major W. W. Pilkington, IP., by Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, on the body of John Webb), butler, who was killed by falling over the balustrade to the hall beneath, whilst lighting a lamp. Evidence of identification was given by the widow and son, parlour-maid (Ross), who found deceased, and Dr. Hall, whose medical opinion was that concussion of the brain was the cause of death, and a verdict in accordance therewith was returned. Srzeurio HURDLES AT lIIIIITON.—A ragged young

fellow, named Bernard Carroll, was or Tuesday charged with having stolen three iron hurdles, the property of Mr. E. Lightfoot, farmer, Sandy-lane, Huyton. The hurdles had been missed between the 10. h inst. and the 12th inst., and it was afterwards ascertained that he had pawned them at a marine More dealer's short in PrescOt. The prisoner pleaded guilty. Superintendent Barker stated that Carroll was one of th worst characters in Prescot, and had been convicted many times.—He was sent to gaol for three months' bard labour. CHIIRCII OF EMMA/CD TEMPEROICE SOCIETY (HUTTON BEAECE).—The fortnightly meeting of the above was held ' in the infant school on Monday evening, Mr. E. B. Williams in the chair. Miss Newsy presided at the pianoforte, and played solos. Songs were contributed by Messrs. J. J. Daw- son, G. Jowett, and J. R. Webster; readings by the chairman and Messrs. J. Webster and J. Roberts. An address was given by Mr. R. W. Roulston, of Liverpool, dealing with the temperance question in a homely manner. He illus- trated his theme by anecdotes of domestic life in happy and squalid homes. The proceedings were of lively interest throughout, and closed in the usual manner. OVER. A grand entertainment was given in the Over Board Schools on 'Fund iy night in aid of the Chester-road Primi- tive Chapol by the choir of the Nantwich Primitive Methodist Chapel. The chair was ably tilled bv Mr. W. Lea; of Nantwich, and the following programme was rendered. Ae a choir they sang" Consider the lilies,"' The Lord is my Shepperd," "God our refuge," "The Mariners," "Come where my love lies dreaming," and "The itehgrove." , Miss Broomhall sang " Smiling faces," "The first cuckoo," and with Miss Williamson "When ellen we meet again." She also sang the A.B.C. duet with Mr. Walker Miss Williamson sang "Thy voice is near," and "A basket of loves." Messrs. Williamson, Walker, and Wood gave "A little farm well tilled." Mr. Hide recited "The bellmatl," and Mr. Cheetham gave a temperance address. Miss Cox recited well, and Mr. Walker sang "Old friend John." The Part song "The schoolmaster" was much appreciated. The funds will be greatly benefited as there was a good atten- dance. RLXTON,

_ HILTON WESLEYAN CHAESL.—A week of special religious Services was held in the Wesleyan Chapel, Riaton, which commenced on Sunday, March 9th, by Mr. Buchall preach- ing very impressive discottrses to large congregations. The aervice on Monday evening Was conducted by Mr. Hopewell, Tuesday, Mr. Jeckaott end- some friends from Warrington; Wednesday by Mr.-Williams ; Thursday by the minister of the Circuit; rriday by Mr. G. Whitdeld; Saturday by Mews. Vialton and Wright. These services have been -a great blessing to the people of Rixton and the nel4looThir hood—the chapel belog won tilled night after night. - DE4yLf BY DnOWNING.—A very sad occurrence has thrown quite a gloom over this place in the-death, by drown- ing.; of a Mr. Thom tson in the Irwell at Warn on Wednes- day. He was in the act of wheeling a barrow,from a barge aortas a plank to the' shore, when he- missed his footing and aventoYer WED the river. Ha rote to the surface once. The efforts made to save him were of no avail. He struggled for a time, but the current was too strong and he sank. The body was recovered the following day. The inquest has been held, verdict "Accidental death. Deceased has left a widow and ten children. He was present in the Wesleyan Chapel,,Rizton, on Monday and Tuesday.

SATURDAY,

, i AT a late hour the other morning there took place in the House of Commons one of those discussions which in the interest of the British taxpayer is dc-seiving of more atten • tion than it has received. It affords a striking illustration of the • extravaka.nt manner in 1 which the,taxpayers'.innney is squandered by royal personages; and but for the opposition offered by a small though compact band of i honest Radicals, we have no doubt that the !Tories and—we regret-to say it -7-Liberals as I well weuld have sanc:ioned. without even a I protest, the unixecessary.eipenditure to which 'we propose to draw attention.. ' The discus- sion, we think, alsO shows that the day will ,come, .and probably with a reformed House of Commons it is not tar distant, when the - encroachments of royalty,upon the estimates will have to be considerably, if not entirely, - checked. Each ineMber of the Royal Familf is allowed a hanri:ome ritorint yearly for his or her maintenance from the Exchequer,—a sum it is admitted mire than sufficient for 1 their wants, and it is not too ninth to expect that if they will accept Garters, and- indulge lin luxuries in the shape, of special packets to i convey them across th,, Ct,..-;titrel, they should at least have the d ,c, -,cy t 3 pay for-them out lof their own ' parse,. and thus show a little i more consideration for the poor 'taxpayers, i who have already quitxt sufficient to bear. It is pretty well 1t.11.,),Ni• •'''' : •dest son of the PRINCE of WALES has been given a Garter; but We question if th, fact is quite as well established that bec,use such a decoration has been conferred u, on this young gentle- man we have had to. .y fees amounting 10 no less than £548 y • oi It may not -be uninteresting to 1, . -.; that of this sum the 1 DEAN Of WINDSO - -*. ' -pectable fee, llv is paid to Si,. istrar, £9O to the IGarter King, and ft .d comes in for : Zzo ; whilst the , ~Liimer and the i singing boys. rer, . :,-, ,i round sun' pre- amongst them for' - Vi -eS at, -we
I
, I
s•
th cil th
CU CI PE
will use the Ltes elvily his —a for pect lge S to uld out :tie It

sume, the investiture. We may take it that in the last case the fees are fairly earned. This sum of £54.8 9s. 4.d., together with another item of £920 in respect of special packets for the conveyance of distinguished person: between Dover and Calais, is, it ap- pears, included in a vote of £7,020 for repay- ment to the Civil Contingencies Fund, and this vote was submitted to the House of Com- mons for approval on Friday. Mr. LAROU- CHERE moved that the vote should be re- duced by £1,548 95. 4.d., the amount of the Garter fees and the cost of the special packets. This the hon. member did on the substantial ground that the recipient of the Garter, even though the son of the PRINCE of WALES, should pay for the honour, and that the royal personages who use the Special packets should also pay for them. With respect to these packets it may be in- formation to many readers if we repeat what Mr. LABOUCHERE pointed out to the Committee of the House of Commons that when the PRINCE of WALES crosses to the Continent for his own amusernent it costs the country Lzoo ; the DUKE and DUCHESS of EDINBURGH are, however, conveyed for £.l6e; the DUKE and DUCHESS Of CONNAUGHT for , Ziao ; the DUKE and DUCHESS of MECKLEN- EITRG also for Liz° ; for the CROWN PRINCESS of Germany there is a charge of £Bo ; and for the DUCHESS of TECK, the DUKE of CAMBRIDGE, and other lesser personages £4O. According, therefore, to the merits or demerits, the importance or insignificance, of these royal personages, the cost to convey them across the channel ascends or descends. But the most aggrava- ting point in connection with this expenditure is that not only do we thus pay for the con- veyance of our own Royalties, but it seems that for every one connected wi.h Royalty on the Continent who comes here a packet has positively to be taken at the price of 24.0 to bring them over and another to take them back," This, to us, is carrying the matter too far; even if we are compelled to pay for the conveyance of our own Royal Family, surely we ought not to pay the travelling ex- penses of their foreign friends and relations. It cannot be urged that the members of the QUEEN'S Family are not able to pay for these Packets themselves. The PRINCE of WALES, for instance, receives something over £120,000 a year from the public Exchequer. The payments to the DUKE of EDINBURGH reach £27, 000 yearly ; but a better idea of the Duxes wealth may be gathered from the fact that his wife on her marriage brought him a privwe fortune of £90,000, a marriage Portion of £300,000, and her life annuity of £11,250 a year. The DUKE of CONNAUGHT is scarcely so fortunate, but the total annual payments to him from the public purse amounts to over £26,000 yearly • and the DUCHESS brought him a dowry of £15,000. And the DUKE of CAMBRIDGE cannot be said to be a beggar, for he enjoys a yearly income of £22,000 odd from the nation, In this way we could go on showing the very handsome annual income provided for each MeMber of the Royal Family to whom Mr LABOUCH ERE referred. But apart from the question of the yearly income, it should not be forgotten that four yachts are maintained by the country for the use of the Royal Family at an average annual cost of £34,656, the original cost of these vessels being £275,528 It will occur to most people that these yachts ought to be used for the con- veyance of Royal personages across the chart nel, but for some reason or another 'not quite apparent they are not. Special Packets have, thefefore, to be chartered tf? suit the Royal wishes. A charge is thus thrown upon the people which ought not to be borne by them, and it is, we think, to be regretted that the vote has not been more resolutely resisted by both Tories and Liberals, as well as by Radicals. We ought, at least, to be consistent, and if we will go on paying for special packets, we should also pay or special trains; yet, as a matter of fact, members of the Royal Family when they are conveyed anywhere by special train pay for the luxury out of their own pockets, and so, a.:B Mr. LA.BoucHERE puts it, should they pay for their .special packets. If they are too niggardly to do this, ar.d the royal yachts are not to be used for their accommodation, then they ought to be content with the ordinary Packets. We need , scarcely say that the sround9 upon which the Radical Secretary for the Treasury (Mr. COURTNEY) defended these charges were of the lamest possible character In the one case, the payment of the Garter fees, " custom " was the only ex- cuse he could urge in justification of the charge; the other, the payment of the Packets, was defended on the ground that an ,ancient prescriptive right" existed whereby la? MAJESTY and the children of HER MAJESTY were entitled to use one of the ships of the navy. To use them, however, would -be extremy inconvenient and mach more ex- pensive to the Admiralty, and it was really a cheap commutation to have a packet carrying Royal Personages across for £-4o instead of a .the being ordered round." In our opinion soonerthese "ancient prescriptive rights" and "customs," ?like expensive and un- necessary, are al)olisheod, the better it will be for all concerned. It would be well if Royal Personages themselves saw the propriety of Withdrawing these charges so that thc House of Commons should not be troubled with the discussion of questions so distasteful:; if they are not withdrawn, we may rest as9ured that the opposition to such encroachments will gather strength year by year until the House will at length refuse to grant the money. It would also be well, we think, if debates of this character cannot be avoided, that they should take place at an early hour in the evening instead of a late hour in the morning, so that snore pro- minence could be given to them, and the ex- travagance a5..3 injustice of the charges exposed.

BLUE RIBBON GOSPEL Amor, WIDENS—In connection with the departure of Staff Captain Blmes to the North of Scotland from the Widnes branch of the Blue Ribbon Gospel Army, several meetings were held on Saturday, Sunday, and Monday, and Captain and Mrs. Elines de- livered farewell addresses. On Monday evening a crowded meetieg was held in the Public Hall, Mr. Hudson presiding The Chairman on behalf of the members presented Staff Captain Elmo and Mrs. Elmes with a nurse of gold, a workbox, and several other articles as a mark of esteem and

respect. UNPROTOHED ASSAULT AT WIDNES.-At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Michael Redmond, a young man, was charged with assaulting another young man named Thomas Chantler.—At four o'clock on Saturday afternoon Redmond was standing near the gate of Messrs. Hutchin- son's works, when the defendant walked across the street to him, and struck him on the face. Redmond said, "That will do, Mick." Defendant then struck him twice again, and cut his left eye brow.—Tbe Bench characterised the assault as a most unprovoked one, and fined the defendant, who pleaded guilty, 20s and costs, Ss 6d. " How A HALEWOOD BOY ACQUIRED LlVii STOOL— On Monday, at Widnes Police Court, William Houghton, 15 years of age, living at Halewood, was charged with steal- iv, between Saturday night and Sunday morning, a tame rabbit, worth 2s, the property of William Leather, son of John Leather, labourer, Poller's-lane, Halewood. He was also charged with stealing three pigeons, worth 7s 61, the property of John Wilkinson, labourer, Ditton. The rabbit and birds were found in the prisoner's cote on Sunday by P.C. Worthingten, and evidence having been given, prisoner was sentenoed to two months' hard labour. ALLEGED UNLAWFUL WOUNDING AT WIDNES. - At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, John Mallett, labourer, was charged with unlawfully wounding Patrick Brophy, another labourer, at Ditton.—From the statement Of Superintendent Barker and the evidence of Emma Wood it appOared that on the previous afternoon the two men in Wood's house become involved in an exciting discussion. They retired behL.'d Wood's house, and the prisoner ran at the prosecutor with aid intention of kicking him in the stomach. He failed to do so, and struck Mallett's mother with his fist. He afterwards kii,Yed the prosecutor twice in the lower part of the stomach, initu:ng him so severely that he was un.onble to appear at the court.--The prisoner was

- remanded. - MILE ADULTERATION AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Patty Sessions, on Wednesday, Mary Murphy, milk dealer, Widnes- road, Widnes, was summoned to answer a charge of selling milk which was not of the quality and substance demanded. —Oa the 27th February Inspector Wood purchased a pink of new milk, for which he paid 2d, at the defendant's shop. He divided it into three parts. One part was left with the defendant, one was retained by the police aqthorities, and g third was forwarded to the County analyst by Superinten- dent Barker, The County analyst certified that taking as the standard the poorest quality of milk, the (-ample contained 20 parts of added water to every hundred parts of milk.— The defendant denied that she had adulterated the milk in any way whatever. She knew that it was of very poor quality, and about six weeks ago she asked Mr. Dixon, the farmer who supplied her, to have it analysed.—Mr. Gaskell, Jun., said the Bench considered the case a very bad one in- deed. She had been selling for six weeks milk which she knew was bad, and she would be fined 20i and costa,

61 78 ad. A FOWL STEALER TRAPPED AT WIDNES—John Ireland was brought before the Widnes m agistrates on Monday charged with stealing ten fowls, value 305, the property of James Marsh, boiler maker, Lugsdale-lane, Widnes.—From the statement of Inspector Wood it appeared that Mrs. Marsh saw the hens safe in the cote at half-past seven on Friday night. Next morning nine hens and a cick were missing, and information was given to the police. who as- certained that five of the stolen birds were in an empty house in Oxford-street. Constables Tiinparley and Dowlson, dressed in plain clothes, watched the prernieea Until tea &click on Sunday night, when the prisoner entered and went straight to the pantry where the birds were concealed. As he was leaving the house five minutes later he was seized by the officers, who found one of the fowls in his pocket.—Doudson remarked, "You have done this very clumsily," and prisoner replied that he did not steal them very clumsily, and he was willing to serve six months what be had done. He now denied stealing the landlady had told him that she had in. ',ased one of her fowls, and having "en some f'.:-.fiers near the house in Oxford-street he went tiler. end A$ taking one of the fowls to see if it was landlady's when the police caught him.—The Bench sentenced him to two months' hard labour; _

A VIOLIAT FElai.LB AT WARRINCITott.—Oa Tuesday, at the Warrington Borough Court, Bodelia Knockton (18), an old offender, was charged before Major Cartwright and Alderman Holmes, with committing an unprovoked assault on Sarah Daniels and Sarah Jane Platt on the previous evening.—Complainant Daniels said that she was going home with an old lady friend and the other complainant, when the prisoner, who was in company with two other girls, came past and attempted to push the old woman down. Complainant remonstrated with her, and prisoner then struck her on the face.—Complainant Platt said that at the time in question she was wearing he "salvation bonnet," and Ike prisoner came up and said semething about pulling her " ballelugh bonnet" off. Prisoner then hit witness's grand- mother, and afterwards hit her, when she went for a police- man.—P.C. 38 spoke to being called to take prisoner into custody, and gave corroborative testimony as to her vielenae; the prisoner told him that if there were no other officers about he should have semething for his trouble. (Laughter.) —The chief constahte (Mr. Hunt) said that the prisoner made her first appearance in court in 1882. when she was 16 years of age. Since then she had been brought up tea times, and had been committed to goal eight times, and dis- charged twice. She could not let anyone alone—Prisoner was sent to the House of Correction for two months' with hard labour, and informed that at the expiration of that time she would have to be bound, herself in £lO and two 'sureties in Sle'each, to keep the peace for six months.—On leaving the court she used violent language, and made an attempt to assault the complainant Platt. Mutate/ca.:WS ASSAULT AT WIDNDS. Before Mr. Hol- brook Gasket:, senior, and Mr. John Brock, at Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Michael Reddingtcn, a powerful looking chemical labourer living in Lngsdale-road, was brought up on a chargo of unlawfully weanding Henry Gorman, also a labourer, of Grenville-street. About half-past nine, on Saturday aight, Gorman was walking along Legsdalf-road. in company with Sarah Agnes Devereux and Annie Gal- lagher, respectably-dressed girls, who appeared in court. The prisoner rushed eat from a place wh:re he bed ap- parently been concealed, and knocked Gorman's pipe out of his mouth without saying a word. " Mate," said Gorman, I what did you do that for? 1 will see your betters about IL'' No sooner had he uttered these words than the prisoner, who had something in his baud, knocked bun down. He lay. nt2 the ground tanconscious,/and when he regained son- sibilitv he was at home.—Mics Deverenx, who stated she I was 14. years of age, and lived in Victoria-road, deposed that the ?rummer appeared to be vexed at Miss Gallagher saying to him" Do you want any lodgings," in fun. He told wit- nese that he was not going to touch her but if he could get hold of Gallagher he would "swing for her." An attempt is being made to establish in London a branch of the German Society for the worship of Wagner. Its object is, primarily, to provide funds to defray the ex- penses of the Bayreuth Festivals whereat Wagner's colossal and incomprehensible "music dramas" are played to audiences which, unfortunately, do not pay. The sub- scription of membership is 103 a year, payment of which secures certain advantages net forth with ponderous humour truly German. In the first place subscribers may have the privilege of going over to Germany and voting at the general meeting of the United Wagner Society; secondly, they will be permitted to swell the subscription list of the Bayreuther Blatter on a further payment of Is a year; and, finally, "should the societies' funds permit they will be offered tickets of admission for prospective performances at Bayreuth at reduced rates. Lord Dysart is the president of the promising society, which to the ordinary mind is as attractive as an hour or two of Wagner's music. Sir Moses Montefiore has recovered from his atteck of bronchitis, and is still going steadily on for his hundredth year. The old baronet is still vigorous in mind and quite as strong as could be expected in body. lie eleepa a good deal, takes much carriage exercise, and feeds regularly. Against Weston's walk on temperance principles may be backed Sir Moses Montefiore's prolonged life on a generous wine diet. For many ye3ra longer than ordinary people live Sir Moses was accustomed to take his bottle of port daily. He now lives chiefly on a diet composed of port wine and milk. If Fir Moses should see his centenary, the circumstance will, I know, be open to the question of "how much longer he would have lived if he had not taken his daily bottle of port, and in these latter days dispensed with wine in his milk ?"

The lynx eyes of the lady who was talking to me a fort- night ago on the subject of the strength of the Woman's Suffrage Party in the House of Commons has fallen upon the paragraph in your London Letter, wherein the matter was discussed. I mentioned her statement that the opinion of 500 monikers of the House hal bean definitely ascer- tained, with the result that 240 bad declared themselves in favour of Woman's Suffrage. I did not presume to make any comment, but mentioned that I had repeated the fact to a member of the House, himself a leader of the Female Suffrage Party, and he had been agreeably surprised. My instructress sends me a copy of the Woman's Sitfrage Journal, in which it is stated that the opinions of 485 members of the present House have been ascertained, and that 24t are in favour of Woman's Suffrage, and 236 against —figures which amply justify the statement made by the lady. There still remains the remarkable fact that with parties so evenly balanced in the House of Commons, the question of Viroinan's Suffrage has hitherto been regarded as outside practical politics, and whenever a division has taken place its supporters have been sorely worsted. It would be hatereeting to note what becomes of the 249 in the division on,Mr. Worrall's resalutioa. Mr. B. W. Leader, A.R.A., Will be represented at the Academy by three pictures; one is called When day is done," and illustrates the line in Gray's Elegy, "The ploughman homeward plods his weary way." Along a clay read whose ruts, filled by recent rain, reflect ,the evening sky as the sun is setting behind the village church and farm houses, a ploughman with his team of three horses is returning to the homestead, and on the left of the picture a woman is driving home a dock of geese across the common. The scene is taken directly from nature near the village of Whittington,.clese to the artist's residence. The second work is a riverside village on the Welsh borders. The sun is rising behind the distant hills, and the morning mist is clearing off. In the mid—distance is a foot—bridge, and by the riverside road a boy drives a flock of sheep. The third picture, entitled, "Flow down Soli rivulet, to the sea.

SEATER ACCIDENT AT WIDNES. NARROW ESCAPE OF FOUR MEN. At the sewerage works of the Widnes Local Board, on the West Bank Marsh, four men, named James Bartlett, James Larvin, Edward Gwine and Thomas Cummersley had a narrow escape from suEfocation on Wednesday morning. The main Bawer, it appears, is being constructed parallel with the Marsh brook sewer, into which is drained the deadly was“a liquors of the various alkali works; and under the direction of Mr. Matthews, contractor, a trench is being made there. At six o'clock two men descended the trench, and discovered that it was filled with sulphuretted hydrogen, a gas of very poisonous qualities. They were just able to signal this fact te their fellow-workmen on the brink, when they became insensible. Two men immediately volunteered to attempt a rescue, but on being lowered into the sewer, which is 21 feet deep, they, too, were overcome, and one fell senseless to the bottom. The ether clung to the chain, and was drawn up in a semi-conscious state. The railway crosses the sewer at this spot, and several waggons at the time stood over it. These were removed to allow a free passage of air inte the sewer, and the escape of the gas. The work of rescuing the three men was thus rendered less hazardous ; and in lees than ten minutes after the first two men descended the three unconscious workmm were brought to the surface. In the meantime Dr. O'Keeffe had been sent for, and that gentleman on his arrival used every effort to restore the men, and with success. They were subse- quently conveyed to their homes. Larvin lies in a dan- gerous condition, but the other men are gradually re- covering.

THE BONA-FIDE TRAVELLER QUESTION. At Runcorn Police Court, on Monday, before Mr. C. Reynolds, John Kennedy and James Beattie, of Widnes, were summoned to answer a charge of having, on the 9th Inst., at Wilson's Hotel, Runcorn, unlawfully and falsely represented themselves to be travellers, thereby obtaining intoxicating liquors from Henry Jackson, the landlord—Mr. J. W. lin i•• lee, of Widnes, defended Kennedy.—Mr. Jackson said on the 9th inst., at about a quarter p tst eleven, the defendants entered the house and went into the smokeroom. They ststed they were travellers, and were each supplied with a glass of beer.—ln cross-examination by Mr. Knowles, the witness said it Was a custom to supply people with liquor who presented a bridge ticket and came "far enough." —Mae Annie Harrison, the waitress at the hotel, said the door of the house was unfastened on the morning in ques- tion. When the defendants walked into the smokeroom she asked them if they were travellers. They replied "Yes, from Widnes." She did not question them further, but sup- plied them with liquor.—ln reply to Mr. Knowles, the wit- ness said it was a custom to sapply men if they produced a bridge ticket. She had supplied men on a Sunday before on producing a bridge ticket. She thought she was doing right. Mr. Knowles, address- ing the Bench, observed that the case was one that needed little defence indeed. That morning he had asked the police .at Widnes if they had summoned any Runcorn people at Widnes for an offence of this description. A person walking from Widnes to Run- corn was a traveller according to the Licensing Act. The proper road from Widnes to Runcorn was through Warring- ton, a distance of 12 miles. The bridge was a private road, for which a fare was demanded, and if be (Mr. Knowles) Insisted upon going across without paying that fare he would be given into the custody of the police. He referred to the evidence that it was a custom to supply people on presenting a bridge ticket, and he sub- mitted that if the Bench considered an offence ' had Iven eommittpd it was not P. case in whiCh they ought to inflict a„penalty, but let it go forth to the public through the Press that the practice was wrong.—On two informations laid by the police the defendants were then charged with being found on the licensed premises of Relay Jackson duriug part of the period they should have been closed, and with giving false addresses.—P.S. McMichael deposed that at 20 minutes past 11 on Sunday morning, the Oth inst., he visited WilAtill'S Hotel in company with P.C. Sullivan. In the bar parlour he found live men sitting down, each with a glass of beer before him. The defendants were present. Lie asked Kennedy where they cune from, and he replied, " [came from Dittou," and Beattie made a similar reply. In reply to a farther question, Kennedy said he had lived at St. Helena, but now lived beyond the market at Widnes, but did not know the name of the street, while Beattie said he lived in Margaret- so at, Luodale; with A man, named Patrick Grady. From Inquiries since made witness discovered that there was o 1. Margaret-street in . n tivid tie ; end that Beattie lived at 21, and Kennedy at 69, Gerrerd-street. West Bank, Widnes. This place WAS not two miles distant from Wilson's Hotel.— PASulliyan corroborated.—Mr. Knowles said if there was no conviction in the first case the others would naturally fall through, aid he suggested that it should go forth to the publie through the Press, that persons walking across Runcorn Bridge Could not be euplietl with liquor in Raecorn during prohibited hours, if such was the opinion of their worships.—Mr. Reynolds said the Bench considered that the defendant, had pot mule a false representation as to their being traveling, Ite they stated they came from Widnes, and the case woula. be dismissed. A conviction would be reoordeil in each of the other CAS'S. The landlord had evidently been careless iii the management of his house as regarded Sunday closing, and the Bench advised nine to , act with more eiscretion in attending to people on firinday lenorniugs i.p the future. The defendant! wore each fined 100 and Costs 12e. 83., in two cat" total 22 fte. each; or, in default, 14 Jaye hard hiboar.

The annual premium in- come at the end .of the year was 1,200,790, being an increase of £35.841 over the year 1882; , and the rate of expenditure in this branch slightly exceeded ten per cent on the premium income. in the industrial branch the premiums actually received during the year amounted to £2 504 307 14s 2d, as corn- p claims corn- pared withot ttf2e ,y1e2a6r,022w 0.3 e instro 33t, the total he previous year. The eXpenees.of the branch, as eompared with those of 1882, showing a reduc- tion in the rate ef expenditure of 2i per cent on the pre- mium income. The development of the business in the in- dustrial branch the chairman referred to int wonderful, and remarked that-there really appeared to be no limit to the amount of business which inight•be done by this branch. The company-have latterly afforded every facility to these who suffered their policies to lapse to come back if they could, and as showing the magnitude of the undertaking we may mention that the postage of these letters alone last year amounted to £6,000. Owing to the exteneive opera- , time of the society the hoard of directors are naturally us- able to keep a strict watch upon the action and conduct of every individual agent and representative. but-it is satisfac- tory to learn that the Prudential'Vve adapted a system by which any agent who through undue ia1,111,11 the risk of compromising the reputation of the cantuany in addition to his own prospect!' of advancement, will inevitably be brougbt to book. It is also, we may add, the aim of the Board to that nothing hut good and safe insurancas are effee. ted. and with such an aim before them there is every reason to belieye the success of the Company will be no JIM . remarkable in the future than it has been in the past.
ST. PATRICK'S DAY.
WIDNES.

The Irish population of Widnes, both old and young, celebrated St. Patrick's Day in characteristic fashion. Dur- ing Monday afternoon the streets wore an animated appear- ance. Constant streams of people were moving along the main thoroagbfares decorated with the green emblem, men and boys wearing it in their hats and caps, and women and girls in their hair, while more than one pereen of the femi- nine gender passed along attired in a gorgeous green gown, ' and adorned with a head-dress trimmed te correspond. As usual on such associations, Bacchus had a numerous follow- ing, and a considerable number of men elevated if not with the good Rhine wine, at least with a liquor quite as potent, were to be seen at intervals wearing a happy smile, and in no way obstreperous. Certainly several disturbances oc- curred in various parts of the town, but they were of so trivial a nature as not to demand the interference of the police. _

div.head: IRISH NATIONAL FORESTERS.
div.p: IRISH NATIONAL FORESTERS.

Taking advantage of their half-holiday on Saturday th, members of the Pride of Erin Branch of the Irish National Foresters celebrated the anniversary of Ireland's Patron I Saint on that day by a procession. They were joined by a numerous contingent from the Wolfe Tone Branch at Run- corn, and the body numbered altogether nearly five hundred members. Starting from the Lodge-room in Wellington- street at three o'clock, the procession accompanied by the brass band of the Order, conducted by Mr. Beasley. paraded West-bank, Newtown, Lugsdale, and Bimm's-cross, the dis- play being observed by a large number of people, who maintained the greatest order. The chief officers in the pro- cession were Messrs. M. Babbitt, W. Horan, J. Duffey, J. Doyle, Edward Hill, T. Williamson, and J. Coleman. In tbe evening the members of the band were entertained te tea M the &Mania Hotel. T. MARY'S YOUNG MEN'S SOCIETY'. _ _

On Monday afternoon the members of St. Mary's•Youog Men's Society held a demonstration. About 250 met at the school and formed into processional order; and preceded by St. Mary's brass band and a beautiful new banner, paraded the chief thoroughfares in the town. The banner which I had been purchased by St. Mary's Total Abstinence League, bore on one side a representation of St. Patrick on a green I ground, and beneath was a scroll having the words "Pray I for us," and another in gold letters the title, "St. Mary's Total Abstinence Leage, Widnes." On the reverse was a representation of the Blessed Virgin, and the supplication " Mary saved without original sin, pray for us." The majority of the persons who took part in the demonstration wore the regalia of the society, while the members of the ' band were attired in bright green uniform, and a large crowd, attracted by the picturesque, accompanied the pro- I cession through the thoroughfares. On the whole excellent order was maintained, but in Mersey-road, a woman who stood in a doorway waved a yellow cap over her head and shouted "That'e the colour." This instantly sent the crowd Into a state of excitement and stones were thrown at the door by a number of persons and a scrimmage ensued. It subsided, however, as quickiy ash t arose, and when Sergeant Clarkson and Constables Bowerbank and Heaton, who had heard of the disturbance, arrived on the spot everything was quiet. The procession, in the meantime orderly, wended its way to West Bank and then returncd to St. Mary's, where the members dispersed. In the evening a miscellaneous entertainment, under the auspices of the Young Men's Society, was held in the volunteer Hall, which was wall filled. The programme opened with the performance of the drama, " Rosaleen Chu, or the twelve pins of Bin-a-Bola," which was admirably staged under the management of Mr. S. Quinn. The various parts were capitally filled by the St. Patrick's Amateurs, and the excit- isg episodes in the piece were effectively pourtrayed. The characters were sustained by Misses M. Muldoon, E. Far- rell, L. Jameson, and Mrs. Halt; Messrs. T. Mulvaney, J. Carroll, S. Quinn, J. Gordon, J. Quinn, 3. Wilkinson, H. Gorman, E. Tallon, M. Whelan, and P. Byrnes. In the second part of the programme songs were given by Misses Jameson and Hewitt, while Paddy Watson, the Irish singing clown from Manchester, and Mr. Fred O'Reilley, the Irish comedian, vocalist, and dancer from the same city, tho- roughly amused the audience during their cotnicalities. The St. Mary's brass band played several pieces of music under the conductorship of Mr: Farrell, of Warrington. ST. BED'S YOUNG MEN'S SOCIETY, APPLETON. ' '

- . On Monday night a concert took place in connection with the Young Men's Society, in St. Bede's School, Appleton, the room being crowded. The gathering was presided over by the Rev. T. Finegan. The Chairman explained that the concert had been arranged by the choir' who had obtained the assistance of Miss Kate Nono, of Liverpool, and Mies Johnson. The programme mainly embraced Irish music, which met with the full appeciation of the audience. TFle first item was a glee by the choir, which was rendered in good style. Mies Nono sang "The last rose of stammer," the artistic performance being warmly encored, and she sang in response "1 breath once more my native air." Mr. Han- lon next sang in a tasteful mariner "Eileen Alanna," which was well received. Next came a duet, entitled, "The noble hearts of Ireland," by Miss Brown and Miss Wright, the ladies in response to the applause of the audience being obliged to return to the platform, and sing the latter portion of the piece. Miss Leatberbarrow was very auccessful in the long, " Erin,my country," and in response to an encore sung the last verse of the sang. Miss Nono won well ' deserved applause in the humorous song, " Katey's letter," and her presence on the platform again was enthusiastically demanded. In reply, she sang with pleasing effect, "Racy I (=More," accompanying the latter piece on the pianoforte herself. Miss Johnson showed considerable skill in the pianoforte solo, "Killarney." Miss Brown secured an encore in the song, Dear little shamrock," and repeated the last verse. The next item on the programme was a /meg and chorus, "God bless you and Ireland," which was given by nye boys and the same number of girls, the soloists being Masters F. Leatherbarrow, J. Callaghan, and J. Walsh. The young male vocalists wore green ties and rose- tte* of the earns colour, whilst a sprig of shamrock occupied its place on each, the girls presenting a rather pleasing ap- pearance by the wearing of green sashes, and iaair ribbon of the much loved colour. In response to a well-merited so. core, the latter portion of the peace was given. Miss L. Leatherbarrow secured an Encore for her rendering of the song" Leshia bath a beaming eye," and in reply sang "The Rakes of Mallow." Mr. Hanlon was again successful in "The wearing of the green," and sang in response " Norala! The pride of Kildare." The glee "Let Erin remember the days of old," was a'so given. The accompanists were Miss J. Johnson and Mr. J. Caldwell, wbo performed their parts in a most satisfactory manner.—Before the conclusion of the meeting Father Finegan addressed tboso present, and said he was greatly pleased to see such a respectable audience. Of all the 15 years of his life in England he had not seen a more well-conducted and respectable audience than the , one before him. He was glad that so many Catholics could ' celebrate the day of their patron saint without the depres- sing influences of intoxicating drinks. He was only sorry I to see that some of his countrymen en that day were given to excess, but he was assured that his congregation were a sober, industrious, and respectable class. There might, he said, be larger audiences than the present, hut none more in love with the object of the meetings than the oneover whom he presided. He urged them to be sober men, and after eslogising upon the work of the Apostle and Saint Patrick, who, he said, brought the light of Christianity to their be- loved country, he asked those present to show their thanks to those who had entertained them by a hearty round of ap- plause., a request which was warmly complied with.

div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD ELECTION.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD ELECTION.

• THE RATEPAYERS' ASSOCIATION. An adjourned meeting of the Widnes Ratepayers' Associa- tion was held in the Simms Cross Hotel, on Monday even• log, under the presidency of Mr. D. Wright. There weris: present Messrs. S. Sadler, J. Midwood, U. Dutton, E. Mart. Icy, R. Webster, J. Deakin, S. White. W. Streets, J. Beech, , • S. palin J. Brigg, T. Sadler, G. Chrimes, W. Sadlrr, W. H. ' Nuttall,'T. Albistort, J. Heath, T. Tanner, G. Albiston, T. , Lewis, T. Smith, E. Knowies, Natal], and S. Owens , (secretary). ' Mr. Ovriers said be had received a letter from Mr. Gas- ' kell, secretary to the Owners and Occupiers' Association, I stating that association had decidel to nominate only four candidates at the forthcoming election, and to facilitate Mr. j Sadier's re-election. There was, however, a strong feeling In the town against a combination of the two associations ; against outside candidates. It was therefore thought better ! that each :assoc:ation ehould act independently. Mr. Owens j replied that as this decition was not in harmony With the Ratepayers' Association's proposal, he felt bound to Day that this association would reserve to itself the right to take any departure they might think fit—tie CHAIRMAN thought the action of die Owners and,Occupiers' Association ; unfair in placing four candidates on their ;list, and asking the Ratepayers' Association to support one isolated candi- date. (Hear, bear.)—Mr, BRIGHS, although in favour of a compromise, acknowledged that their only course now WAS ' to fight, and fight manfully. He would rather lose all the ' men they had on the Board than that Mr. Sadler's name should be an isolated one. (Hear, bear.) Mr. SEWS I moved that the decisions of the previous meetings in regard ' to the election be rescinded. He regretted to take this course, because he believed the principal men of the other association were anxious to meet them in a friendly spirit. —Mr. Drrrrow aeconded the motion, which was carried un- animonsly.—Mr. Law's then proposed that the association j should Rominateand support three cendidates.—Mr. Samos seoonded.—Mr. SADLEIB moved an amendment, that four candidates be nominated, and the other association not re- ' oognised at all.—Mr fErrowr.ss seconded —Mr. WESSTEir inquired if they had four candidates to pet in the field, and the Caarnaterr replied four good men.—Mr. Wenn= ex- pressed his gratifiettion at this state of things, and observed that the other aseeciatina had treated them anything but like gentlemen. They first sounded the Ratepayers' AM- ciation and then turned their backs upon them, but the were quite qualified to fight, and this fact ought to be madey known to the public—The amendment was carried by 18 votes to three.—Mr. BRIGGS proposed tbat the toll gentlemen be nominated and Supportedßeecb_ by the aseeeirtienng: —Messrs. S. Sadler, S. White, J. , and W. Sadler.— The motion was seconded by Mr. Halaw, and carried tin- animously.—The meeting then considered rganisation. various plans of o

The Sub-Commitutioners at Limerick under the Land Act gave judgment cn Thursday on a large number cf jpplica- Lions from tenanta to have judicial rents fixed. Some Auctions were made on the Marquis of Landsdowne's pro- perty. A rental of about £2,400 per annum was reduced to £l,BOO. The reduction on an average ranged from 23 to 40 per cent, and a• clrrespondent says the tenants and they solicitors were extremely pleased with the deciaions.

div.head: EXTRAORDINARY DEATH OF A GIRL AT WIDNES.
div.p: EXTRAORDINARY DEATH OF A GIRL AT WIDNES.
OVERPRESSURE IN BOARD SCHOOLS.

The deputy coroner, Mr. W. T. Husband, held an inquiry on Wednesday, at the Angel and Elephant Hotel, Appleton, touching the death of a girl, aged 11, named Annie Dennett, who died on Monday. it is supposed, from injuries received on Tuesday, the 4th inst., at the Slinms' Cross Board Schools. Mr. Thomas Sadler was the foreman of the jury. Mr. G. H. Danby was present on behalf of the School Board; Mr. T. Showan being also present. . Mary Dennett, wife of George Dennett, living in Appia— ton village, said the body seen by the jury was that of but daughter, who attended Simms' Cross School. Het daughter had her dinner at her sister's, at t•iiams' Crow, on Tuesday, the 4th inst., at which time some blood was noticed upon her apron. When the deceas,d came home in the evening she complained that her head ached. Oa Mon- day morning, the 10th inst., she said she did not want to go to school, as her head was bad. She, hcirrever, went to school, and when she returned in the evening she again complained of her head, and in consequence of that she took her to Dr. Booth's surgery. Witness asked her daugh- ter where she had been hurt, and she replied." Here, on arty head." She mentioned the names of two girls she was playing with, and said that when she got to the b-p of the steps at school the girls pushed her downstairs. She alighted on her forehead, and her nose bled; but she was able to go to her class.

Annie Bennett, ten years of .age, daughter of Jelin Bennc.tt, rent collector, at 23, Frederick-street, slid she attended m Si,ns' Cross Board School, and was in the fourth standard, the deceased being in the fifth. When the accident hap- pened to Ann Dennett, witness, with Sarah Ellen Booth, Louisa Carr, Ellen Forrester, and about a dozen others were playing on the first lot of stone stairs leading into the girls' school. They were pushing each other through the door and shutting them up. The deceased had been playing about five minutes, when Sarah Ellen Booth got hold of her sleeve. When she loosed it witness gave the deceased a push into the room just as Louisa Carr had partly closed the door. Annie Dennett fell with her face on some wood and cut her nos, and she was taken away by the other ctuldren.—By a juror: The deceased did not fall down the steps. They were on the landing. Sarah Ellen Booth, aged 12, daughter ot Williert Booth, 6, Catlton-street, gave evidence to the effect that when Annie Bennett pushed the deceased into the room the doer was closed by some of the other girls, and she remained in- side for about live minutes. Witness then went into the room and found the deceased lyin; on the flpor. She p'cked her up, and did not notice that her nose was bleed- ing. _ _

Dr. Booth said be had known the deceased for seven or eight years, but had not had occasion to attead her profes- sionally. The deceased was not what be should call a strong girl. On the evening of March 10th Mrs.,Dennett brought the deceased to his surgery at Farnworth. She was complaining of persistent pains in the head and vomit- ing. He suspected brain mischief, and asked her if she hat had any blow on the head, and she told him that about a week previously one of the children at school had pushed her, in fun, and that she lost her bilance and fell against a door. On Tuesday the symptoms of brain mischief were much more pronounced. On Wednesday stupor had set in, dullaks of vision and hearing presented themselves, and on Friday she became comatose, and died on Monday, never having regained consciousness. He believed at the time of the fall the deceased was tuffeting from tubercular mischief, and that the fall was the exciting cause of men- ingitis. He had had a conversation with Zs. Showau, who told him that the child was very bright and intelligent, and the difficulty was not how to give her learning, but how to keep her back. By the Foreman: Mental exciternant or over study wonitl cause meningitis, and in course of time the disease might have been developed without any accident. A box on the ears would sometimes have the same cffect. Mr. Beech said he had children who attended the Simm.s' Cross School, and he should like to ask Mr. Dinky whether it was not the duty of the caretaker to keep an eye over the children between the time the first and second hell rang. If not, then he should consider the question whether the chil- dren should net he kept at home. The Deputy-Coroner said he had no doubt Mr. Denby would answer the question, and he should be pleased to give him an opportunity of doing so. It mast be remembered, how- ever, that the children, would have to go to some school, and althou.-sh they were not there to prevent accidents to children, he had no doubt the Widnes School Board would take every means to prevent such an accident as that hap- pening again. It might be a satisfaction to Mr. Beech to have Mr. Danby's word that no room such as the one referred to eshou'd be left open during play hours, and that a person should be there during play hours. Mr. Danby remarked that Mr. Showan would he able to give the jury the duties of the caretaker more particularly than he could himself. As st ited by one of the witnesses, the caretaker at the time of the accident was ringing the bell, and he could not possibly b 3 looking after the children. It was his duty while the teachers were away to see that no harm came to the children, and he was generally walkin,.; about for that purpote So far as k e (Mr. Denby) coalti understand, the Choral Society hat the use of the room on the steps, and on the day of the accident it was, unfortu- nately, not locked, and the children finding the door open began playing there. All the doors were, however, kept locked by instructions of the head master.

Mr. Beech: Thank you. Mr. Sadler observed that a large number of caretakers would be required to look after the whole of the children. Mr. Moffatt (a juror) said he thought the home lessor-a given to children were a greater trouble to the children than any bangs on the nose they might get. They tried the brain for meningitis more than the knocks they got. The Foreman: That question is being taken up in Par- liament.

Mr. Moffat : I an glad it is. Mr. Danby : You are one of those who think that over- pressure is brought to bear on the children? • Mr. Mara : I am. I have three children and lam quits Bare that one is suffering from it. Mr. Danby: Where you find that, I don't think you should, as a parent, allow it. _ - . " '

_ Mr. Moffat: I don't to a great extent. Mr. Danbv : It is said that children are now doing a year and a half's work in twelve months. Mr. Showan observed that from what took ploo3 In the school in the morning, the assumption of Dr. Booth was quite correct. During the morning, and before the accident happened, ths teacher allowed the deceased to go out of school, because she complained of her bead. There was thus an evident desire on the part of the teacher to humour the child and to be concerned about her health. The jury returned a verdict to the effect that death was due to inflammation of the membranes of the brain, super- induced or accelerated by the fall on the 4th instant, and attributing no blame to any one.
