div.head: DISESTABLISHMENT,
div.p: DISESTABLISHMENT,

_ Sir,--I have been muctr amused at the treatment this question has received from some of your correspondents. 'Boob and every one of them is content to ignore the main and central ques ion of right and justice, for which alone I bare been contending, and fritter away their time, thsir stationary and your valuable space in learned disquisitions • Oaths antiquity of this blundering old iniquity! The ilea! As though it was any consolation to the afflicted to be told that this malady was of old standing. Would Sindbad have better appreciated the old man of the sea, whom he bore so dissentingly, had this antiquated Incubus favoured him with long-winded tales of his genealogy, and enlarged upon the advantages of being ridden by the last of a long line of apes? Now, sir, I confess myself to be more conversant and more nearly interested in the modern anomalies and injustice of the Establishment than its ancient history I To be told tnat Job had boils in no way lessens the sting of these inflictions. Such of your corres- pondents who have taken up the gauntlet in defence of the Establishment have been peddling around and attacking small and unimportant aide issues whilst leaving the central questions untouched. Am I to infer from this that they are impregnable, and that these champions of Church abuses Aare not touch them? To enable some bolder spirit to do this I will again ask an answer to these questions. 1. Should people outside the pale and communion of the Church of Eagl ind be compelled to contribute in money or kind towards her support? 2. should the land, and through the land the tillers thereof, b 3 burdened by these imposts called tithes? 3 Could not a secular Parlia- ment be better employed than attempting to regulate the internal affaire of the Church? In reply to "A Church- rats," I hope he will excuse me if I say that his letter is a tangle of unwarranted assumptions. 1. Ile assumes he has 'pointed out the analogy" between the "trust funds" of dissent which are raised by voluntary contributions from the piera berg of the particular body or by equally voluntary gifts from without, and the compulsory levies called tithes. The " analogy "is very faint. The one is neither more nor leae a legalized robbery when exacted from non-mem- bers of the Char ch ef England; the other an entirely optional offering t o the denomination you prefer or admire. 2. Becaaae I ask for bare justice for Dissenters he jumps at o ce tr the conclusion that I am a Dissenter, belong to a religious body. and have a chapel. An accusation as un- founded as the baseless fabric of a dream. Then comes his 3rd and crowning absurdity when he talks of the manufac- ture of bishoprics, for which he said £500,000 had to be raised, and unblushingly accuses me and other Dissenters of being wishful to appropriate this money ! Truly this is an example of a robber accusing his victim of theft ! I, and I suppose the Dissenters with whom he classes me, have no objection to Churchmen and Churchwomen pileing bishop upon bishop, Liverpool upon Truro, if they think St. and raising the money amongst themselves and friends. We gladly concede the undoubted right of Church folk to enjoy their own, asking only as much for ourselves. In fact we object to being the victims of a defunct bigotry. I have no doubt the framers of the tithe laws sincerely be- lieved they were doing a good and a wise thing in thus compelling men to religious observances. Men in those days thought it a right and proper thing to meddle with the consciences of their fellows. It accorded with the opinions of the times. Dissent was then young and not merely dis- allowed, but absolutely prohibited. Tithes and compulsory religion WB3 floe natural, if not the logical, outcome of such opinions. But with altered circumstances must come , :altered leas. Dissent is now not meekly tolerated, but to :some extent encouraged and protected, whilst the Church herself has dwindled and become merely a sect among sects. —A am, As . JOHN PEERS. Penketh, March 18, 1884.

illir,-Want of time must be myexcnsefornotreplying sooner to the remarks of Mr. John Peers on this subject in the Examiner of the Stn inst. The only statements worthy of note or wanting any reply are these :-1. That the Church of England was estab!ished by Act of Parliament in the reign of Henry VIII , when that monarch was constituted its head. Prior to Ibis we bad only a branch of the Church of Rome." The words enclosed in inverted comas are Mr. Peers' own. And (2) his statements with respect to tithes, he says, It is held now that taxation without represeata- ?ion is an injustice. Is not this principle applicable to tithes? The layman, after paying the impost, has no con- trol over its disbursement. This latter and more pleasant duty being monopolised by bis clerical taskmasters. Thus, in effect, the husbandman is coMpelled to 'Work a certain number of days in the year for the benefit of dogmas and dogmatists with whichand with whom he is utterly unsym- pathetic. Wets it not that we know Britons never, never will be slaves,' I should be inclined to regard this as a species of white slavery. Again, tithes are, to Dissenters, a tax on conscience. Suppose a case. A farmer pays £lO a year off his farm as tithes. If he happens to be a Churchman it may be supposed to be his contribution to the church of his choice; but if a Dissenter, lie is compelled by law to pay tithes, and by conscience to contribute towards the support of his own creed. In this way the Dis- senter is handicapped in comparison with the Churchman." Now, with.respect to his first statement, I deny it flatly and an historical knowledge of English Church history o the most elementary kind would support me. However, is his letter Mr. Peers (as though he could scarcely rely on his statement:. asks me to point out how the Church of England was establisheri, if it were not ache says. With your sanc- tion, Mr. Editor, I will endeavour to comply with his re- quest, and I send you herewith a short sketch of Church history which I have divided, and which I will, with your permission, continue in next week's Examiner. And now with respect to Mr. Peers' second statement as to tithes. I must say that to discuss that qurstion alone I should take up more apace perhaps than you would feel justified in al- lotting to me, and having no time to enter into the question folly, must content myself with observing, en pas- sant, In reply to Mr. Peers' query, viz., as to whether the principle that taxation without representation is applicable to tithes—that it is not ap- plicable, inasmuch as tithes are not taxes. They are neither levied, nor collected, nor appropriated, as are taxes. As to representation, I do not quite see what Mr. Peers means. Lie is certainly represented in Parliament, and if he has no representation in the Chutce it is because he decline's It. Mr. Peers says "tithes - are to Dissenters a tax on con- science," and he supposes a case which I have quoted above. In reply, I say that every tithepayer pays his tithe as; legal charge on the land, quite irrespective of the object to which it is devoted, and if the Church were robbed of the tithes to-morrow, and they were confiscated to the State for generel national purposes, he %mild still htidetlie pay them,'lnd, perhaps, for the support of an Object tbac' be Might be as little in sympathy with as the °Support of the National Church, and even to hie mind tar less deserving. For instance, a peace-at-any-price' marl snight have to pay tithes tor the supportof war, just as now he haa sometimes to pay his taxes for the same bbject, and has always to pay them to keep up a standing fleet and army. A teetotaler Melt-NW to pay them for keeping up a machinery to license, inspect, and superintend public- house, and to support men and women as criminals and paupers who had brought their misery on therneelves through drink; and an anti-vaccinationist might have to pay them for the support ot vaccination and vaccinators. A tithe is, of course, a tenth chargenpon the value of land, and it makes no matter to the man erYso pays the rent, whether he pays part to the landlord, part to someone else, or the whole to the landlord. When a person paya a tithe it is not to the Charch. It lea gift pure and simple from the land. And as to it going against the conscience of a Dissenter to have to pay something towards the support of the Church of England, it does nothing of the kind. It is no businessof ours whatever to whom the rent goes. The total amount a men will Ilafasto-pArictlic-ad by other laws, and it is no use in bringing conscience in whatever—whether it goes to three people, ten people, or one person. A man is bound to pay On common busines.s principles that which the land fetches, and if he pay tithe he pays so much ess rent. Thanking you for your valuable space, of which I (E. have taken so much, I am, yours, cite, Warrington, March 20, 1884. CHURCH. HISTORY: A. SKETCH. The Church of England of the present day is a continua- tion of the Church of the earliest ages in this country. She is the same old Church of the land, founded bete in early times before our Saxon forefathers came t„.) England. The Church was never established by tbo State or by Parliament or by any King of England. She established herself long ages

CHESHIRE FARMERS AND EVASIONS OF THE HOLDINGS ACT. One of the largest and most prolonged meetings of the Chester Farmers' Club since its establishment was held on Saturday, at the Blossoms Hotel, Chester, Mr. John Roberts, of Well House Farm, Saltney, presiding. The special business of the meeting was to hear a paper read by Mr. Henry Davies, of Wervin, giving the version of the trustees of the Ashton estate, with reference to the case of Mr. Samuel Denson, of Picton, who received notice to quit because he refused to sign an agreement by which he would have been deprived of his privileges under the Agricultural Holdings Act. In the first place, however, the meeting rescinded a former resolution in order to have a full discus- sion on both sides of the question. Mr. Davies read his paper, the principal points in which, as against Mr. Denson, were that the latter wanted from the agent of the Ashton estate a certificate which would enable him to get compensation from the incoming tenant for improve- ments effected during the past six years; and that Mr. Denson wanted to plough up a field, while he would not consent to the condition that upon leaving he should leave it as he found it, and not claim compensatien.—On the other side, Mr. Mounfield urged that at the November rent audit the agent of the/estate submitted to his tenants a pro- position that six months' notice should be °neigh instead of twelve (as allowed under the new Act), and that in case draiaage was required the estate should find pipes, and the tenant do the work, and "do away with all question sr talk of compensation." Mr. Denson, however, said the new Holdings Act allowed twelve months' notice, and he woeld abide by that law. As to the second proposition, he said that was all right if the landlord agreed to give the tenant, if, in unfortunate circumstances, he had to leave the farm, the value of his unearned compensation for the work that he did. For these reasons he refused to sign an agreement to the contrary, and received notice to quit—After a warm discussion, Mr. Baxter proposed : " That the members of the Cheshire Farmers' Club fatly tympathise with Ur. Denson for the action he has taken in Aefending his rights to compensation for improvaments, and condemn any action that may be taken by agents or land- lords to evade their responsibility to their tenants under the Tenants' Compensation it'Charraley seconded: Mr. T. J. Dutton moved as an amendment --" That both sides of the question having been heaed, the club should takii no further notice of the natter."—On being pat to the vote. 23 voted on each side, bat the amendment of ' Mr. Dutton was carried by the casting vote of the chairman.—Mr. Den- son was absent thrtsuglifillnese.

before there was a State in the sense that we undertand the word now—long ages before there was a Parliament, and before there was an English nation capable of any such a national act. We cannot tell with absolute certainty when the light of Christian truth first flashed upon Pagan dark- ness in Britain, but we do know from the earliest of our ecclesiastical historians that the name of Christ was men- tioned in England before the time of the revolt of the British forces under Boadicea, and this carries us to an event which took place in the year 61, so that we are sans- ' lied that Cbristrian truth had been brought within the borders of our country during the lifetime of men in whose memory the great tragedy enacted on Calvary was still fresh. Various writers give different authors who brought first the Truth to tie. At that time England was a dependency of Rome. There was a trade carried on with Britain, and people came from every country and clime in the civilised world, attracted by the mineral wealth of the district, and therefore it was not unlikely there was a con- nection with Rome at the time St. Paul was a prisoner there, when the new doctrine was brought to us. We know that the wife of Aulus Plantius, the Roman pre-prmter, was an English woman, and became a convert to Christianity. We also krrow that Claudia, the wife of Padens, mentioned by St. Paul, in his Second Epistle to Timothy, who was also a convert, was an English woman, the daughter of an English prince. What was therefore more natural when they came back to their own country, than that they should hays brought the glad tidings with them. Coming down to a later period, we know there was a Christian Church established in this country, teaching the truths of the Gospel as we know them now; a Church that was Episcopal in its character; it had its bishops because we frequently found them taking part in councils concern- ing the affairs of the Church. The third century was an important period in the history of the Church; it was the time of the persecution of the Emperor Diocletian, and England suffered equally with other countries—it was be- cause the truth was widespread at that time, because there were many churches in the country, many bishops and seminaries, that the wrath of Diocletian was raised, and England was subjected to persecutions like other parts of the civilised world. The town of 'at. Albans, known at that period as the City of Verulum, commemorates the martyrdom of St. Alban, in 303, in its abbey, recently raised to the position of the cathedral church of the diocese. In the same manner similar events were commemorated in the name of Lich- field, the meaning of which was" the corpse-field ;" and the city arms represented a field with a number of persons slain, who bad died for tile truth. In 314 there was a council held at Arles, a town in the south of France, and at that assembly there were three bishops of the British Church present—the Bishops of London, York, and Caerleon-upon- Uske. There can be no doubt, therefore, that a branch of the Christian Church existed in Britain some time before this occurrence, and the knowledge of this fact becomes very im- portant when we consider the claim sometimes advanced by Rome that it was to the Roman monk Augustine (597 An.) that England really owes its Chris- tianity. Again, in 347, at Sardice, and in 359, at Arimi- nuoa, there were councils of the Church, at which British bishops were present, all of which facts go to prove that at a very early date there was a church established in the country, true in its teaching, independent in its action— not dependant on the Church of Rome, or forming a branch of that Church, but a true branch of Christ's Church, and springing not from the Church of the West, but rather from the Church of the East—from the Church of Jerusalem, not from the Church of Rome. This is testified by the Roman Catholic historian, Dr. langard, who admits candidly that in the third century, within 200 years of the death of Christ, Christianity had spread through- out the length and breadth of the land, and Jerome says that the Church of England was then independent and suf- ficient for salvation. When England, 40 years after the departure of the Romans (about 409 A.D.), was overrun by the Saxons (450-681 AD.), who were at that time Pagans, the English Church and its monuments were in great part 11 swept away. There remained, however, sufficient to show 1, that it was quite an independent church, and was untainted by the later corruptions of Rome. During the period com- prised between 409 A D. and 449 A.D. the clergy largely guided the nation, and Gibbon thinks there were as many as 30 or 40 bishops. In 596 the arrival of Augustine as agent of the Pope of Rome took place; but let it not be thought that England then received Chris- tianity for the first time. On the contrary Augustine found British Bishops here, who, though they welcomed him in a fraternal spirit., studiously refused to put themselves under either him or his master. The following, which is recorded as the anrpver. of the Abbot of Bangor to Augustine, is worth keeping in remembrasce :—" We are all and every- one of us obedient and subject to the Church of God, and to the Pope of Rome, and to every godly Christian, to love everyone in his degree, in perfect charity, and to help every- one of them, by word and deed, to be the children of God; and other obedience than this Ido not know due unto him whom you name to be Pope. . . Besides, we are under the Government of the Bishop of Caerlon-upon-Uske, who is to oversee, under God, for us, to cause us to keep the way spiritual." (The Bishop of Caerleon-upon-Uske, it will be remembered, was one of the three Bishops who attended the before mentioned council at Arles.) "The interference of Rome at this time," says a writer, " must be looked upon as the friendly succour of a more flourishing sister towards a sister in distress, not as the authoritative assistance of a mother towards a daughter, owing existence te her at the first and bound to pay her due submission for the future." It must never be forgotten that not only in England, but in Scotland, in Ireland, and in Wales, an immense amount of mispiociary we* had been performed by what may be called the Celtic' Church, long anterior to Augastine's *ch. The influences set on foot by Augustine 4,teire, no doubt, very useful, and must not be underrated. But his mission was not by any means a success. It is true that in addition to the sees of Canterbary and London, he founded the see of Rochester, but the bishops he ap- pointed were compelled to abandon their pesitions and leave the country, and the people within their dioceses relapsed again into idolatry. How then were the conver- sions brought about?—not by those who received the teachings of Augultiae and his monks, but by those of the old 13, itish enurch, who had retired, some into Ireland and some into ezcotland ; from Scotland, missionaries came south and spread the truth amongst the Saxons, who had taken possession of the soil; therefore, when we spoke of our Christianity, we looked not to Rome, but to lona and to Lindisfarne. Those missionaries spread over the whole of what was called the kingdom of Mercia, and we have evidences in many of the older parishes of their visits. (To be continued.)

WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The usual fortnightly meeting of the Warringtoi Board of Guardians was held at the Board-room at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning, under the presidency of Mr. Green- ing. There were also present Mr. E. C. Cooper (vice-chair- man). Alderman Harrison (the Mayor), Major Cartwright, and Messrs. Greene'', Hunt. Boonell, Wa'matey, W. Houghton, J. Houghton, Forster, Humphreys, Derbyshire, Appleton, Ki'shall, Brown, Grange, Caldwell, Blackhurst, Jolley, and J. C. Sutton (clerk). The minutes of the House Committee, which contained nothin,l of special interest, were passed without com- ment.

comment or explanation. The cost of out-door relief, and the comparatively new item of school fees, practically con- done at a uniform rate, forming, of course, important items of expenditure. The various changes effected in thq administration of relief have proved generally bene- ficial. The service given by Guardians on committees has eased the work at Board meetings. Applications for school fees are beard and recommended or otherwise by committees separately from the grant of out-relief. The Latchford and a portion of the Warrington pauper cases are now heard in the second board-room. The Newton and Haydock poor at- tend before a district committee sitting at Newton in lieu of tramping to Warrington. The aged pour and inform and chronic cases, save when such cases neon revision by altered circumstances, are dealt with half-yearly at special meet- ings held other than on Board days. This last arrangement was suggested by Mr. Bleckley, when chairman of the Board, but by him conditionally only, upon arrangements whereby increased visitation of the recipients of relief would be secured. The reference of other important union work to committees and the changes referred to enabled - the Guardians on the recommendation of the Bury Uaion, where general convenience had been found to result from a similar change, to hold fortnightly in lieu of weekly meetings. By this change an improvement has been effected in the work of every depart- ment immediately connected with the business performed at Board meetings, and has also enabled two extra days of each fortnight to be given by the several relieving officers to the important and necessary work of visiting the poor. It may be useful to explain that the surrounding Lancashire and Cheshire Boards of Guardians, namely, the Altrincham, Barton-upon-Irivell, Leigh, Preecot, Runcorn, and Wigan also now meet fortnightly; that of 29 Lancashire Unions 21J meet fortnightly; of 61 Yorkshire 49 meet fortnightly and that but three Cheshire Unions meet weekly, about a ,similar average applying to the whold country. The exceptions are the Unions possessed of WI" tral Board rooms and offices, and where the district (such as Manchester) are very populous, and of comparatively small area; and the Guardians, as a rule, are ordinarily within a short distance of the central buildings. Formerly the work of a Board of Guardians was almost limited to the granting of relief, and matters pertaining thereto. It is now of a much more extended character, whilst with increase of population and rateable value, there , is a constant growth of labour. The changes and new • system introduced by the Central Authority to secure im- • proved administration, and bythe legislature, add materially , to the Union work generally. The increase of the popula- tion of this union in the last decade was close upon 16,000, a number exceeding the total population of many poor law I unions; and in the same period the rateable value has in- creased by more than a third of the total Union assessment. It had, therefore, become im- practicable and most inconvenient and unjust to the poor to crowd into the proceedings of a weekly t Board rreetiog the work of a poor law union extending, as this does, from the boundaries of Lynam and High Leigh, in Cheshire, to those of Widnes, St. Helens, Golborne, and. Cadishead, in Lancashire, and governed by 30 elected Guardians, indepandent ot those who are es-officio. I Your Board, moreover, is practically the School Board for the rural portions of the Union, inclusivemow of very pupa- lone portions, and this work is also given to a committee. The Rural Sanitary Authority are practically, the Local Bard or the municipal authority for a very large area, out-p iris of which now require the execution of important drainage • works, street making, &z. The work of the Assessment r Committee is of great and increasing importance' and need - constant consideration and attention. A new Industrial I Schools Committee, which has been remarkably well at- I tended, and has been well assisted by useful t sub-committees, finds constant opportunity for their ' labour of love. These are of course exclusive of the House and other important committees, the whole sriou taiing the energies and trespassing upon the time 3 of doardiand. It was anticinated, that fora period during , the winter months weekly retellings of your Board might be necessary for relief, and had the tinCeesity arisen the par- -3 pose would be easily affected by adjournments of Board ? meetings for the administration of relief, I without disturbances of other departmental work. 1 The occasion has not, however, arisen, and the business of 1 the Board has usually been got through at a reasonable / hour. Beyond the ordinary work of the Board and com- mittees there is now almost conrantly arising work of a specially impo-tint character reviring great attention and consideratien, connected with magistrate's cases, settle- • meats and removals, valuations and assessments of pro- perty, drainage contracts, audits, dm, do. The opportunity of devoting each alternativs week to work of this special • character, often involvin4 important Union interests, has t been attended with great benefit to the Union."—The report was adopted.

TUESDAY. —Before H Brig-h—t and Mr. A. Gladstone. A NAMELESS CART.—William WhiVng was tined 2s. ed. and costa for having used & cart without any name painted on it on the 7th inst at Rohy. THE CHESHIRE POISONING MYSTERY.

At Knutsford, on Wednesday, the extraordinary case in which Margaret Wilkinson, aged 44, married woman, was charged with attempting to administer oxalic acid to her son and daughter-in-law, with intent to murder, came on for hearing for the sixth time. The prisoner was again pre- vented by illness from being present, she being still confined in the prison hospital. Mr. Harris, of altrincham now ap- peared for the first time to prosecute on behalf of the police; and Mr. Fletcher, of Northwich, again defended. The court was crowded.—M.. Harris, in applying for a remand, said he had received notice that Mr. Fletcher would made an applioation to have the case proceeded with in the absence of the prisoner. Such a course, he contended, was contrary to all law and practice, and for this reason he (Mr. Earns) had not brought his witnesses. Mr. Fletcher, on the other hand, urged that the prisoner had already been incarcerated for a long time, and was suffering seriously in health, while the prosecution bad failed to bring any evidence against her. If Mr. Harris had fresh evidence, he might dis- close its nature, and so enable the magistrates to judge whether it was of such a character as to justify them in further detaining Mrs. Wilkinson in custody. This sug- gestion was adopted; and Mr. Harris having handed in his brief to the Bench, they retired to consider it. On their re- turn to court, the chairman (Major Hill) said they were unable to discover any new evidence. They had beard it all before. This investigation (he continued) was very properly instituted by the police. After giving the case patient attention and consideration, the Bench had come to the conclusion that oxalic acid was by some per- son surreptitiously introduced into the kettle with an un- lawful intent, but the case of the prosecution as against the accused rested mainly upon suspicion, coupled with the obtaining of life policies, and supported only by the uncorroborated testim• ny of the son of the prisoner, whose character and antecedents were not favourably known to the court. The Bench did not feel justified in sending Wilkinson for trial. At the same time, they could not too strongly condemn the lax and vicious syst rn of life insurances, whereby policies were obtained upon proposals signed without the knowledge of the assured and without medical examination. From this system, if allowed te continue, the most pernicious results might be anticipated.—This decision was received with evident satis- faction by the crowded court. ^ry —The

The usual fortnightly meeting of this Board was held in the Workhouse, Whiston, on Thursday morning, Mr. W. Tyrer presiding. There were also present :—Messrs. John Fidler, John Matthews, W. Gilbody, W. A. Meadows, T. llobell, J. T. Hall, John Leatherbarrow. W. Gerrard, T. Sadler, James Buckley, R. Leigh, W. B. Longtoo, E. Syder' the Revs. T. Finegan, T. Chambers, and J. Barnacle; and Mr. S. H. Hartley (clerk).

REPAYMENT BY LOCAL GOTERMIENT BOARD. The CLERK read a letter from the Loci! Government Board intimating that they had paid Mr. C. C. White, trea- surer to the Guardians, the sum of .£3l 10s, the amount re- payable in respect of additional fees paid to the registrar of births and deaths. THE NEW RELIEVING OFFICER. • . .

A letter was read from the Local Government Board in- quiring as to whether the newly-appointed relieving officer at St. Helens, Mr. 0. M. Barton, was now residing in his district. —A. letter was also read from Mr. Barton, stating that he had removed to Dunriding-lane, which was in his district, and Mr. Hartley said he had informed the local Government Board of this fact. —Mr. DOBELL asked if the new relieving officer understood that he was to give the whole of his time to the business of the Board.—The CLERK said he did not know that Mr. Berton had any other busi- ness; the auditor of the Local Government Board required a relieving officer to give the whole of his time to the Guardians.—Mr. CnAmeaneas said there would perhaps be no objection to his playing an organ on the Sundays, but it would be different if he taught music on week days.—Mr. Firetnn said Mr. Barton did not teach music.—The subject then dropped.

ANOTHER REMITTANCE. The CLBRI read a letter from the Local Government Board, stating that they had remitted to Mr. White, the treasurer, the sum of £1,558 12s in respect of the Jost of maintenance of pauper lunatics in county and borough asylums and licensed houses. He (the clerk) wished for authority to ask for an explanation wit'a respect to this re- mittance. The Board claimed .£1,565 16s, but for some reaeon or other the Local Government Beard had taken CT 4s off. He could only imagine that that sum had been taken off Because the Guardians excused a man named Torbay, owing to his being too poor to pay. That Board, he thought, ought to be the best judge as to the ability or non-ability of a man to pay for his wife in the asylum.— Mr. CHAMBERS said it was the man's daughter who was in the asylum. The man lived in Halewood, and he himself knew that he was too poor to pay. He would move that the Clerk should write to ask for an explanation from the Local Government Board.—Father FINEGA.N seconded the pro- posal, which was carried. , THE AUDITOR AND THE GUARDIANS. A letter was read from the Local Government Board, stating that an extract from the Auditor's report relative to the production before the auditor of the registers of the public vaccinators of the Prescot Union, was enclosed, and asking for the observations of the Guardians as to the mat- ter. The extract from the auditor's report stated that a, his adjourned audit on the 29th nit., the Clerk told him that the Board of Guardians at their previous meeting had passed a resolution declining to produce the registers. Under these circumstances he (the auditor) deemed it advisable to adjourn the audit till the 22nd March.—Mr. NEWSOME : What observations do they Want? I propose we make no observations.—Mr. FIDIJIR thought they ought not to cross the Luca( Government Board on that subject. —The Catunrami, remarked that the auditor ' seemed to have his own opinion about these thiggitThe CLERIC said he would suggest that they inform the Local Government Board that the Guardians were pleased to and that they did not think they were required to produce the books. The Local Government Board said before that it was the duty of the Guardians to produce these books, but upon the Guardians questioning their ruling and asking for the statute under which they were compelled to produce the books, they were bound to admit that they were not aware of any statutory obligation to produce them.. The Guardians said they would not produce the books, then the auditor sad, "I obeli take such steps as will make you, and then he (the Clerk) said, "I shall not be your mes- senger or servant." If the auditor would ask to be obliged by having the books, then they plight Produce them, for they had withing to Conceal, but when he demanded them he (the Clerk)." told him that he was not obliged to run but the country after them.—The matter was left in the hands of the Clerk. • LIBERAL REVIVAL IN ST. HELENS. Daring the past week a series of meetings have been held in the various wards in St. Helens, in connection with the Liberal Association. These meetings were held for the purpose of appointing five residents in each ward as repre- sentative members of the association, and two others as re- presentatives upon its council. The first meeting was held on Monday evening at the Liberal Club, when the Liberals resident in Hardsbaw ward appointed their representatives. Mr. John Cotton was elected to the chair. Mr. A. Sinclair, who was present, explained that for a good many years the St. Helens Liberal Association had had no members except those who subscribed to its funds, and the number of these, he was sorry to say, was not very large. They had felt, however, that the whole of the Liberals of the town ought to be represented in the association, especially as the day was not far distant, after the passing of the Franchise Bill, when they would have a member of their own. Those , who subscribed to the association bad not the slightest wish that they should be expected to pick candidates for them- selves. They only wanted that the whole of the Liberals of the district should_ come and work with them. Therefore about a month ago they altered a rule of the association and provided that, while the subscribing members of the association still elected the president and 20 members, the whole of the district should be divided into so many divi- sions, and that each of these divisions should be asked to hold a public meeting every year to appoint five deputa- tions, and send two more to the Council. Their enemies called this a caucus, but it really was simply an arrangement by which the whole mass of the electors should have a voice as to who a candidate shall be. This, he added, would form the association on lines similar to those on which the Liberal Associations of Birmingham' Leeds, Liverpool, and other large places were conducted. The St. Helens district would be divided into nine divisions, Viz., Hardshaw, Windle, Parr, East Sutton, West Sutton, Ecclesten, Eccles- ton Rural, Windle Rural, and Rainford, each of which would appoint five representatives and two members of the Councjl.—The appointment of representatives was then pro- ceeded with, and the following gentlemen were appointed: —To the Council: Mr. Abel, Hardshaw-street, and Mr. Foster, Hall-street. As representatives : Mr. Geo. Benson, Church-street; Mr. Twist, Upper Parr-street; Mr. Ashton, eorporation-street ; Mr. Donnelly, Bickerstaffe-street ; and Mr. Farrell, Hall-street.—On Tuesday evening a largely I attended meeting of the Liberals living in Windle division was held in the Club Rooms. Mr. H. Martin presided, and Mr. Sinclair was also present, and explained the objects of the meeting. The following gentlemen were then appointed: —To the Council : Mr. John Booth and Mr. Robert Clarke. As representatives: Mr. James L. Shepherd, Mr. A. Slater, Mr. James Brockbank, Mr. John Crowenlock, and Mr. An- drew Muir. On Wednesday evening another meeting for Ecclestod division was held in the Old. Mill, Liverpool-road. Mr. Win. Fletcher presided. The representatives elected were as follows:—For the Council; Mr. Wm. Fletcher and Mr. Thomas Brown ; as representatives: Messrs. P. Wright, W. Powell, W. Fletcher, W. H. Foster, and John Leith.—Mr. Dnomemoraz, in moving a vote of thanks to the chairman, said if the meeting had been a larger one he should have suggested that a vote of confidence in the ministry be passed —(applause)—and that they be urged under present circumstances to exercise considerable determination in carrying the Franchise Bill through the House of Com- mons. (Applause.) He was sure he ' was speaking the sentiments of all present, and perhaps of the whole of the township, in saying that they were most anxious that that system of obstruction which had been persevered in by the' Opposition party should be controlled by public opinion outside, and that an expression of public opinion should go from every meeting of Liberals wherever they might be assembled. He did not know any other way in which this system of delaying business and defrauding the people of their rights by putting off the enfranchisement of the country was to be met except by persons coming forward at public meetings and demanding that this sort of thing be put a stop to. He did hope that when those elected got to the Council of that association they would be able to tell them that a public meeting in the town was necess cry so that the voice of St. Helens, being an unenfranchised one, must be heard. It was time that it should have a voice in the representation of the country. So long as there were two millions of people who were not enfranchised, and a large number of females whe deserved to be enfran- chised, so long should St. Helens be deprived of its repre- sentation in the House of Common's. It would be some time—perhaps it might be difficult within this session—to carry the Franchise Bill, and after that it would be ROM time before they should get a redistribution of seats. If the course now being pursued week by week by the Opposition succeeded they should not get the Franchise Bill this ses- sion, and if that harassing sort of obstruction went on it might end at last in the Liberal Government appealing to the,coußtry, and then they could all of them see what an amount of evil that would bring upon them. (Hear, hear.) —Dr. McNrcceet, in seconding the vote of thanks to the chairman, said he must confess he had not any very great tare for politics at any time, and really if one were inclined to take disgust and retire, the present state ef affairs would afford a good opportunity. He sometimes wondered that many more members of Parliament, many of whom were men of culture and men of taste, did not give up a warfare which seemed so discreditable to Parliament, which ought to be an assemblage of gentlemen, and retire to give themselves up to those tastes and study the poets and other writers and make themselves happy instead of worrying themselves and throwing themselves into the heat of battle. He would not say that the blame was altogether on the part of the Con- servatives—(" Lord Randolph ")—but really it appeared that the present discreditable state of party warfare was due mainly if not exclusively to the Conservative side. (Hear, hear.) He had in a way read politics for 50 years, and he could remember when men used to fight in a manly open -manner and not make absurd imputations. Nothing was easier than to impute bad motives. The best of actors in the world might have a bad construction put upon them, and there was sadly too much of that at the present time. Some people thoutht they ought to have more meetings in St. • Helens, but he was of opinion that theie was much latent beat, a great deal of slumbering energy amongat the Liberal , party in the town. He thought that if there was anything likes contest they would be found shoulder to shoulder, and lanyb dy who had a weakness or a whim-wham would lay it aside for the general good. In the late fight in the Soudan the battle was nearly lost because the square was broken, but he hoped the Liberal party would keep square and that iSt. Helens would take part in the general victory which he doubted not would wait upon the Liberal banner. div.head: SCHOOL COMMITTES.
div.p: SCHOOL COMMITTES.

This committee reported that all the children were well, with the exception of one boy, who WAS suffering from in- flammation of the lungs. The committee wished to thank Mr. Humphreys for the gift of a number of books and ma- gazines for the use of the cbildren.—Mr. DARBYSHIRB moved the adoption of the report. -He tendered his thanks to Mr. Elumphreys for his gift, and hoped thtt what that gentleman had initiated would be followed by other gentle- men who had any each articles to spare, which would be very thankfully received.—Mr. BL/LCKIIIIRST seconded, and it was carried without discussion.

div.head: SCHOOL FEES COMMITTEE.
div.p: SCHOOL FEES COMMITTEE.

This committee reported that 48 old cases and five new cases had been attended to.—ln proposing the adoption of the report, which was carried, Mr. BLACHRUBST remarked that considering the amount of distress that there was in the town, and the number of people who were out of work, there had been far less applications than might have been expected.

THE VACCINATION RETURNS. The CLERK read the following letter received from the Local Government Board :—"I am directed by the Local Government Board to inform you that on examining the return for the period January to June 1853, recently re- ceived from the Vaccination Officer of the Warrington Union, the Baard find that of the 1,078 children whose births were registered during that period, 143 were unaccounted for as regards vaccination. The Board also observe from the supplemental return for 1882, that, of the 1,958 children born during that year, 22 are still similarly unaccounted for, in addition to 134 children who are stated to bave removed from the district, or who have not been found. lam to re- quest that the Guardi ins will obtain from the Vaccination Officer,and fore ard to the Board,an explanation of this omis- sion to account for these cases. Dm Board will also be glad to be furnished with any observations which the Guardians may desire to make with reference to such explanation. I am at the same time to state that the Board have had before them the returns for the above-named periods in respect of the Warrington district, and they trust that Mr. Cooper, the new vaccination officer, will do his best to clear off the large amount of arrears existing in this district. lam to request that Mr. Cooper may be instructed to forward to the Board, after the April attendances for vaccination are over, and not later that the 19th May next, fresh returns on the enclosed forms, showing the then state of vaccination in his district as regards the children whose births were registered therein during 1882 and the first half of IBB3."—The CLERK said that he had communicated the contents of the letter to the vaccination officers of the Union, and the subject than dropped.

div.head: FISH DINNERS AT THE WORKHOUSE.
div.p: FISH DINNERS AT THE WORKHOUSE.

The CLERK read a letter received from the Local Govern- ment Board referring to the report of the Medical Officer of the Warrington Union with regard to the fish dinners sup- plied to the inmates of the Rouse. The Board stated that, assuming that the Guardians proposed to continue the fish dinners weekly, the Board would sanction its permanent adoption as an alternative diet.—The letter was simply received.

div.head: MEDICAL APPOINTMENT.
div.p: MEDICAL APPOINTMENT.

Mr. BROWN, in accordance with notice, submitted the following resolution :—" That, inasmuch as Dr. Joseph, medical officer of the No. 1 district of the Union, has hitherto acted in that capacity to the satisfaction of the Guardians, and that his present residence and surgery are within a very convenient distance from his district, and that ne duly qualified medical man, resident within the said district has applied for the office, he be re-appointed medical officer of the said district, at the salary hitherto paid him, viz.: £lOO per annum, for a further period of three years, terminating upon the 25th day of March, 1887, subject to the approval of the Local Government Board."—Mr. BLACKHURST seconded, and the resolution was carried without dis- cussion.

div.head: SUND&Y CLOSING _QUESTION.
div.p: THE SUND&Y CLOSING _QUESTION.

- .. The CLERK reported the receipt of a communication rrom an association asking the Board to send a petition Parlia- ment setting forth their opinion that the sale of intoxicating liquors on Sundays" was a fruitful source of intemperance, domestic misery, and crime," and petitioning for the closing of public-houses on the Sunday.—The CHAIRMAN slid that similar petitions had been sent to the Board on various occasions before. He thought that it was a very proper petition for the Board to send to the House. Individually he should be very much pleased to see public-houses closed on a Sunday, like bread shops and other places of business. When he went to, aud returned from, church, on Sundays, he saw people going into the public-houses in all directions; he saw people drunk and kicking up rows on Sundays, and all sorts et immorally going on in consequence. If he wanted a loaf of bread, which was a necessary, on a Sunday, he could not get it legally. (A member: Oh, yes.) Well, if he could it was illicit trading, and was not the usual custom. He thought that it would be for the well-being of the country if the public-houses were closed on the Sabbath, and he proposed that the petition be forwarded as was re- quested.—Mr. DARBYSHIRE seconded the motion. He thought that the least that the Board could do was to try and put a stop to the sale of intoxicating liquors on Sundays. If they were to keep holy the Sabbath day, it could not be done with the public-houses open.— Mr. JOLLEY thought that it was somewhat inconsistent on the part of a Beard of Ouardians to petition Parliament to close public-houses on Sundays. He maintained that this WAS a free country, although no one, he said, bad a greater objection to drunkenness, or excess of any sort, than he had. (Hear, hear.) If he went a five miles walk in the country on the Sunday, he was a bona fide traveller and wanted same refreshment as a matter of course. He thought it would be interfering with the liberty of the subject if such a course as the petition desired was adopted. It was a special busi- ness, and publicans paid licenses for the privilege of selling their goods. If they petitioned Parliament to curtail one day out of seven, he said that they should at the same time accompany it with a memorial that the licenses should be reduced one-sixth.--The CIIIIRmiN remarked that the petition said" except for bona fide travellers on Sunday."— Major CARTWRIGHT observed that there were arguments to be used on both aides. Everyone (addressing the chairman) knew that he would be in favour of shutting up public- houses altogether.—The CHAIRMAN: I never expressed my- self so; but I think it would be a good job for the country if they were.—Major CARTwRIGHT : lam not going to contra- dict you, but I do not know where you would get the revenue from.—The CHAIRMAN: Not out of crime.—Major CARTWRIGHT, continuing, said that there' ' "'Were thousands of people who were moderate men; and did not require the law to protect them. While be spoke in favour of the curtailment of the hours during which public-houses were opened, be thought that if they were closed the same law should be made applicable to clubs— (hear, bear)—which were increasing all over the country, and were open on Sanders all day through. If they checked it in one direction let them check it in another. He did not Intend to ,move an amendment, but should like an expression of opinion as to what was the unanimous opinion of the Board. He should have no objection in supporting a modified petition lot...reducing the hours of opening.—The VICE-CHAIRMAN did not think that the question was one for the Board of livardiane to considor at all. He thought that if the petition were passed it would be a great encroachnyint on the rights of the working people of the country. It would be all very well for gentlemen who kept a'barrel of beer in their houses, but what would the working man have to do for his drop of beer for his Sunday's diuner.—Mr. WALstsmie thought if they had Sunday closing it should be Sunday closing, and the bona fide ' traveller should be left out, so that the publicans would be free for the day.—The discussion was continued by Mr. Caldwell and the Chair- man.—On the question being put to the vote, eight members voted in favour of the adoption of the petition and eleven against, the motitm of the Chairman thus being lost. oONTRACTS FOR MAINS.

div.head: --ESTIMATES.

BLIND SINGERS AT EARLESTOWN. The Viaduct Institute, Eariestown, was nicely filled on Monday evening last, when Mr. H. J. Darman, organist of • St. John's Church, Earlestown, gave a vocal and instru- mental concert. An unusual and attractive feature of the gathering was the fact that the performers were blind, and another great cause of the success which attended it is to be found in Mr. Durman's popularity. As to his merits as ' a musician there cannot be two opinions, while his kind and genial charcter to all won him the respect and esteem of those with whom he had been brought in contact. The artistes were from Liverpool and Manchester, and their efforts to give satisfaction to the audience met with hearty commendation. The glees by the party were rendered in an impressive manner, and raised the enthusiasm of those present. The pieces they sung were" Dawn of day. " (Reay), " Sweet and low" (Barnby), " Farewell to the forest" (Mendelssohn), and "0, hush thee, my babie " (Sullivan). The male party, assisted by Mr. IL J. Dur- man, capitally acquitted themselves in their selec- tions, " Die lifeboat" (Hatton) being rapturously applauded, while "The Tar's song " (Hatton) was deservedly encored. They also gave Hatton's amusing piece, "Beware," and Bishop's "Forester, sound the cheer- ful horn." Miss Pemberton and Miss Edgar gave an effec- tive and pleasing rendering of the duet, "May-bells and flowers" (Mendelssohn). The songs, When the heart is young" ( Dudley Back) and "The old cottage clock" Mol- ley), were nicely given by Miss Pemberton, and Miss Edgar very sweetly sang" The eld and the young Marie" (Cowen) and "Sunshine and Rain" (Blurecnthal). A hearty and deserved recall was accorded to Mr. W. D. Evans, whose Strong bass voice was heard to advantage in " The Desert' (Emmanuel); and he also equally well acquitted himself in "The Suliote War Song" (Brinley Richards), and was again recalled. Mr. H. J. Durman it it; almost needless to say, was very warmly received, and his rendering of the amusing piece, "The little scrub," created much enthusiasm. On being recalled he repeated the two last verses. A pianoforte duet by Mr. H. A. Aeplatt and Mr. W. Chastise wlso gave the overture to " Tancredi" (Rossini), was brilliantly ex- ecuted, and the performance was heartily enc,red. Mr. Asplet, in a subsequent pianoforte solo," En route" (SydnelY Smith) splendidly acquitted himself. He also gave, with telling effect, two violin solos, entitled "The harp tha,p once thro' Tara's hall" (Farmer) and "Blue Bells of scot- land" (Farmer): At the close of the concert Mr. Darman Stepped forward and thanked the audience for the very kind manner in which they had suppotted them that evening. Considerable expense at- tended the getting up of a concert, and people could readily see that when they bad to pay two or three guineas for an artiste they would have to sell a good many tickets before they could pay for one singer. His blind friends, who had been singing that evening, were all school mates of his, and they had kindly come forward and given their services. (Applause.) It had been a very great pleasure to them to come before the audience, and be received in such a kind manner as they had been. Mr. Durman then proceeded to give an e=ol4nAii9n of the scene at the church on the pree vious day, and P. rotor kl '11! he found reported in another column.

For hawking fire-screens without a certificate in Naylor- street, on Tuesday, Rose Marron, a respectable looking young woman, was fined 2s. 6d. and costs at the St. Helens Police Court on Wednesday. STEALING A Rya AT PRESCOT.—Ann Dutton, a middle- aged woman, was on Tuesday charged at the Preseot Police Court with having stolen a rug, valued at 7s 6, the property of Mr. Morton, pawnbroker, Prescot. The tug, it seemed, had been hanging at Mr. Morton's door on OP 15th inst., when the prisoner was seen to, wa.k off with it.—Se was sent to gaol for 14 days. CHURCH OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE SOCIETY (JUVENILE BRANCH), PRESCOT.—The usual fortnightly meeting of this society was held in the Houghton-street Schools, on Mon- day evenirg, and was presided over by the Rev. F. R. Lee There were also present Mr. J. Case and Mr. F. Halsal I, and a large number of members, many of whom contributed to the enjoyment of the evening by recitations and glees. PRESOOT WORKING MEN'S IMPROVEMENT AND RECREA- TION SOCIETY.—The 15th of these popular entertainments was given on Monday evening last, in the Town Hall, Pres- cot. The Rev. H. A. Macnaughten, vicar of Prescott occu- pied the chair, and a very excellent programme was gone through by the following artistes Thompson' Misses Kimpton, Lea, A. Morris, and A. Scarisbrick, and ,Messrs. T. H. Mawdsley, G. Merrick, W. Jackson, Joseph Lyon, and J. B. Wood. Miss Harriette Wood was the accompanist.

ST. HELENS NEWS. ASSAULTING A T.411E-LIGHTER AT S. HELENS.—On Mon- day, at St. Helens Police Court, Thomas White, a burly collier, was charged with having assaulted William Finney, a lamp-lighter, in the employ of the Corporation.—Tbe complainant, who lives in Duke-street, said thai the 11th inst. the defendant accosted him, and after a few threatert- ing words, struck him violently in the mouth.—Defendant denied having struck complainant, and the case was dis- missed. CRUELTY TO A HORSE AT ST. HELENS —At the St. Helens Police Court, on Monday, Richard Ashton was charged with having worked a horse whilst in an uafit state, and John Benyon was charged with having allowed the Same to he worked.—Sergeant Callister said that he had seen the horse in question being driven along Orrel-lane by the de- fendant Ashton. It seemed to be in pain, and on examining it he found several sores on its shoulders.—Ashton was fined 28 6d and cots, and Benyon 7s 6d and costs. THEFTS IN ST. HELENS MARBET.—Mary Ann McGhee a young woman, was on Menday charged, at St. Helens Ponce Court, with having stolen some articles from the stall of Thomas Hargreaves, general dealer, 29, Robson-street, Liverpool.—On Saturday last the prosecutor, who keeps a stall in St. Helens Marketplace, saw the prisoner pick the ' articles mentioned off his stall, and concealing them on her person, walk away. She was, however, apprehended.— Prisoner was also charged with having stolen a pair of drawers from the shop of B. A. Dromgoole, pawnbroker; and a still further charge of having stolen a purse and lead pencil from the stall of Peter McKinley was also preferred against her.—Prisoner had been previously convicted of theft and drunkenness and she was committed for seven days on each charge. A Gosstteetel NEIGHBOUR.—ThOnIaS MulrOV, a decrepit old man, was on Friday charged at the St. Helens Police Coart with having been upon licensed premises during pro- hibited hours.—P.C. Mather said that about half-past four on the Sunday afternoon previous he and P.C. Carter were near the Bowling Green Inn, Suttonewhen they saw the de- fendant go into the house. They waited a short time and then f ollowed defendant, whom they found standing in the kitchen. They asked him what he was doing there sad he replied that he did not know, and Mrs. Ashton, the landlady of the public-house, also said that she did not know what defendant had come in for.—The defendant said he had only gone into the public-house to see Mrs. Ashton's son-in-law that was going to be married.—The case was dismissed. ASSAULT ON CONSTABLES AT ST. HELENS.—At the St. Helens Police Court, on Monday, Thomas Kelly was charged with having refused to quit the Victoria Hotel, Market-place; and also with having assaulted P.C. Walsh. —P.C. Massey said that at eight o'clock on Saturday night he with Sergeant Callister went to the Victoria Hotel, and on going into the tap-room they saw seven or eight fighting together. Prisoner, who was very drunk, was requested to quit but refused to do so, and went up to Sergeant Callister, who, had another man in charge, and struck him.. Prisoner then rushed at Massey, struck at and knocked bins down, and them jumped upon him. Sergeant Callister was at length compelled to let his prisoner go in order to assist Massey.—Prisoner was fined ss. and costs for refusing to quit, and £1 and costs for the assault, or in default five weeks' imprisonment.--Andrew Welsh, a young man from Rainford, was similarly charged, the assault having been committed upon P.C. Beardswood. These offences were stated to have taken place at the same hotel, and were similar in their circumstances to those above described. Similar penalties were likewise imposed.--Michael Synott, a middle-aged man, was charged with having been drunk and disorderilr, and with having assaulted P.C. Rat- cliffe, and was fined se. and costs on the firefcharge and 10s. and costs in the second, or three weeks' imprisonment. CHURCH PASTORAL Am SOCIETY.—On the morning and evening of Sundae; last sermons were preached in the Parish Church, St. Helens, by his Grace the Bishop of Liver- pool, in aid of the Church Pastoral Aid Society. On both occasions there were large congregations. In the morning ' his Lordship took as a text 1 Cur., 13 c., 13 v.: "Now abideth faith, hope, and charity; but the greatest of these is charity." He believed there were few chapters in the Epistles of the New Testament which were better known and more valued than that chapter. He had been told that atheists, agnostics, and infidels, who professed to despise the religion of the Bible, thought it a grand chapter, be- cause it was the most perfect picture that ever was drawn of that glorious grace, the grace of charity. His Lordship then went onto point out that the true meanine of the word charity, and in what respects it wasgreater than the two other graces of faith and hope. In concluding his dis- course, he referred to the Pastoral Aid Society. The society, he said, furnished assistance to the vicars of large over- grown parishes, and thus enabled them to reach and to help those they could not otherwise have reached and helped. The society had now been in elistence 45 years or more, and the populous counties of Lancashire, Yorkshire, and Cheshire, and large manufacturing places like St. Helens, Liverpool, and Manchester, owed it a heavy debt.—ln the evening his Lordship preached from Hebrews, c. 12, v. 2: "Looking unto Jesus.".—The collections in the morning amounted to £lB3s 24. and in the evening to £l.l 170.—0 n Monday evening, a well attended meeting in aid of the same society was held in the schoolroom adjoining the Parish Church. The Rev. Canon Carr presided, and addresses were delivered by the Rev. Canon Rycroft, the Rev. F. B. B T yrer (Liverpool), and Mr. Clarke Aspinall. PROSECUTING # PUBLICAN AT S. Hseeres.—At the St. Helens Police Court, on Friday, David Kenny, landlord of the Running Horses public-house, was charged with having sold intoxicating liquor to John Iveson and William Seddon during prohibited hours.—P.C. Hurst said that at a quarter past 12 on the morning of Thursday, the 6th inst., he was standing in the doorway of the Queen Vaults, when he saw William Iveson, William Seddon, and John Iveson coming down Bridge-street. They went about 10 yarde past the Running Horses, when they stopped for about two minutes, and then turned back and went along Smith's entry. Not seeing them return, the officer went up the entry, and when he got about half-way up he heard a knock at the defen- dant's back-door. lie went to the back-door, which was partly open, and listened for about two minutes, and heard William Seddon and John Iveson call for two glasses of beer. Afterwards be heard the rattle of money thrown en the counter. Witness then went inside. and found Mrs Kenny along with William Seddon and John Iveson in the bar, the two men having each a glass of beer before them. He asked Mrs. Kenny what the two men were doing there, and she replied that they were lodgers, and had come from Liverpool. The two men also asked witness to say nothing about it, and wanted to stand him some drink.—ln defence, it was stated that defendant and two other men bad made arrangements to go early the morning after this occurrence I was said to have taken place to Downed Green for a day a rabbit shooting. It was arranged that Seddon, who is an unmarried man, should stay that night with the defendant, and on his arrival with Iveson from Liverpool (where they had been) by the last train, he persuaded the latter to also go to defendant to stay the night. Defendant himself was out when they went to his house, but Mrs. Kenny came downstairs partially dreesed to let them in, and then went upstairs to re-dress. While she was upstairs Ivreon and Seddon served themselves with a glasa of beer each, and it was after they had clout, this that the officer came in.—The case was dismissed

THE ATTEMPTED MURDER AND SUICIDE AT WESTON. CENJURE ON THE HUSBAND. On Saturday afternoon an inquiry was held at the Pros- pect Inn, Weston, near Runcorn, by the county coroner, as to the death of Fanny Eccleston, aged 40 years, the wife of , William Eccleston, weigher at the Runcorn Chemical Works, who on Monday last was found to have cut her tkroat, and that of her infant child, born at the beginning of the month. Mrs. Eccleston was attended by Dr M‘Daugall, of Runcorn, and great practical sympathy was shown to her by the neighbours; but she died on Friday shoat noon. The case was in charge of Inspector Uniting- worth, of Runcorn. Mary Anu Hulse deposed that she was the wife of a labourer, livieg at the Village Inn. She occasionally acted as midwife, arid attended deceaeed during her confinement, and for nine days after wards. She did not notice anything mentally wrong about her. Certainly she was a little fret- ful ose day, and upon being asked the cause she Slid they bed received notice to leave the apartments they occupied, as the person keeping the house where they lived was leav- isg. She observed nothing in deceased's manner to cause Let to suppose she would take away her life. After Mrs. Eecleston had cut her throat, witness went to the house and inquired what had caused her to do it. She replied, "Be- cause I was upset about having to leave the house." Alice Butler, servant at Mr. Dawson's, grocer, Colliers' Building!, stated that she had seen the deceased regularly during her confinement, and she seemed happy until Mon- day morning. About twenty minutes past eight on the morning in question she took Mrs. Eccleston a cup of tea from Mee. Dawson. She found her out of bed, undressed, sitting in a chair iu the front room downstairs, where there Was a bed. Mrs. Eccleston asked her to go home twice, and seemed anxious to get rid of her, though she had never dons so before. Witness then described being called to the -toese by deceased s little girl, and giving the alarm to her

yesterday, at the Prospect Inn, Weston, by Mr. E. J. Wore- ley, the deputy coroner. Mr. Edward Aaron was the fore- man of the jury. William Mayhew, Eccleston, said be now lived at 17, Thomas-street, Runcorn, but at the time the child died he resided at Collier's-row, Weston. The deceased was his son, named Isaac, and 18 days old. He died on Wednesday night last. Witness was not present when the child died. M.rs. Somerville had attended to the child since it was in- jured. He had seen it once every day. Dr. \lacßougall deposed that he was a duly qualified practitioner, practising in Runcorn. He was first called in to see the child on the morning of the 10th ' inst. At that time the child was being attended to by Mrs. Somerville. The child had an incised wound across the throat. He had attended the child until i's death, which occurred on the evening of the 19th inst. The cause of death was convulsion. The wound in the throat was very early healed. He had since made a post-mortem examination of the body. All the organs were fairly healthy; and the child seemed to have partaken of a fair quantity of nourishing food. ' The Coroner: There is one important question which is really the question which we have to consider—Do you think that you could say that the convulsions were conse- quent upon the wound ? The Witness : I could not Artificial fed children are very prone to convulsions. This was an artificially fed child from the 10th inst. . . . .
The Coroner : Was the wound in the throat doing very well? . .

Witness : Very well indeed. There was very little of it left unhealed—about an inch and a half of the skin on the right side. The wound on the left side of the neck, which was not so deep, had quite healed up. Mrs. Somer. villa attended the child from the day of the accident at his request, and she had nursed it with the greatest possible care and tenderness to the hour of its death. The Coroner: That is very pleasing. Have you attended the family of the father of the child in past years? Witness: I attended the mother in her first confinement, and he believed one of the children also, but he had not a distinct recollection of his attendance on the child. The Coroner: Do you know whether any of them are liable to convulsions? Witness: I have been informed that one of Eccleston's children died from convulsions. The Coroner: When did you perceive the symptoms of which the child died coming on? Witness: On the Tuesday. Up to Monday the child was uncommonly we'l. I was in the greatest hopes that the child would get better. I should say the child would have got better but for these unfortunate convulsions setting in. The Coroner :Can you venture to assign any cause for

mistress. Mrs. Mary Ann Dawson said she had sent food into the h else, nct because she thought deceased was really in want of tee necessaries of life, but because she considered a con- Enemeut an expensive matter. Mrs. Eccleston had also LOU her some weeks she only got 16s from her husband, and occasionally 17s. From conversation with deceased, she knew that her hu4aand did not give her enough money. Pars. Eccleston told her that if she could get about £1 per week from her husband on which to keep the house, she would feel very happy. Deceased appeared to be much afraid of losing the apartments she and her husband occu- pied, as she said she did not know how they were to buy fewniture, though she admitted her husband had been down re Runcorn *boat some. Mrs. Eccleston sometimes refer- red to the fact that her husband, who received 20s per reek, did not remain in the house during the evenings. She added that if Eccleston WOUIEI take her (deceased's) advice, "they would be different." After Annie Williams, servant, Collier's-row, had given evidence, Police-constable Joseph Cooper was called. lie proved examining the house after deceased had cut her thrcat. He found on the mantelpiece, which was a painted one, the word "Trouble" written in pile ink, and 4s 6d. There was very little indeed in the house in the way of provision for a woman in such a condition. Deceased's husband had often been out late at nights. The wound was one which it was quite possible was self-inflicted. In reply to a juryman, witness said he would rather not reaee any remarks as to the state of anything in the house. The Coroner said he must reemest the doctor to answer the juryman's question, if he was of opinion that his replies would throw eny light upon the sad occurrence. Dr. hi'Dougall remarked that he certainli went out of his previace to address some observations to the husband daring Monday afternoon. He told Eccleston that it would he his duty to provide certain things for his wife, Nebo WAS in such a delicate state that she could not take rough, plain fare. He advised him that if he was not In a pecuniary petition to get what was required be had better see Mrs. Cawson, who had been exceptionally kind to deceased, as to what could be done. On inquiry, he found that the husband had not done this. He (witness) then told the pelicemen on duty to make arrangements with Mrs. Dawson, and he (witness) would make himself responsible for every- thing supplied to her from that time up to her decease. Witness spoke in the highest terms of the groat kindness shown to deceased by the neighbours. William Eccleston, husband of the deceased, said that on the morning of her death be left the house at half-past edght. Before doing so he made her some tea and gave her same food, lie was up attending to tbe child several times during the night, and on every occasion when it cried his wife put her hands up to her head as if in pain. The child of Mrs. Eccleston died about seven o'clock on f Wedneeday mailing, and the inquest en the body was bold

the convulsions? The witness: I should say flatulence, distension and irri- tation of the bowels. If the convulsions were due to the wound, they would, in his opinion, have followed immedia- tely after the infliction of the wound or a reasonable time afterwards. The child was free from convulsions until Tuesday. All the important blood vessels affected were healed up. Maria Somerville said she wts the wife of David Sotner ville, stonemason, Weston. She took charge of the de- ceased on the 10th instant, by the request of Dr. Mac- Dougall, who attended the child up to the time of death : sometimes twice a day. The child died on Wednesday night. The Coroner said: After what the doctor has said, I am very much relieved to find that you will be spared a very painful task. Had the evidence been such that the doctor had found that death resulted from the wounds inflicted on the 10th instant, you would have had a very painful duty— I a very painful duty. lam thankful to say that that duty has been spared you. You will observe that after the doctor had given his evidenco we have said nothing much about the wounds received on the 10th instant beyond de- scribing them as wounds. I don't think they come into the Case, and I don't wish to say more about them. I think you will have no difficulty ia Coming to the conclusion that this poor child being deprived of its mother on the 10th inst. was taken the greatest possible care of by Mrs. Somerville, but that on the 19th inst. it died of convulsions. I think that will probably be your verdict. _ . .
I wish myself, and I think you will wish, t& say that we censider Mrs. Somerville behaved very handsomely. She took care of the child when it was in a most disastrous con-

and according to the evidence of the doctor she seems to have done everything that could be done, and I should like, if it is your wish, to tell her Co. The Foreman observed that Mrs. Somerville was deserv- ing of all possible praise for her great and disinterested kindness. He added: It is a hundred thousand pities that the law does not give us power to punish the father! Mr. Ford (a juryman): I think he has been pretty well punished, Mr. Aaron. Mrs. Somerville was then called into the room, and the Coroner paid her a la'gh eulogy for her conduct. She replied that she had only done her duty; and the Coroner said that impressed the jury more than all. After Mrs. Somerville had retired, the jurymen showed their apprecia- tion of Mrs. Somerville's kindness by each placing the fee they bad received for attendance upon tbe table, and requested the Coroner to band the 12s. to Mrs. Somerville. The Coroner graciously did so, and Mrs. Somerville ex- pressed her thanks.

literature is being used in great profusion, but so far noth- SERMON BY THE REV. R. FILCHER M A OF tog out of the ordinary has been issued. The Owners' and , . WARRINGTOX.
