Handley, "and them only." It is claimed that these eventag by the Rev. R. Filcher, 8.A., who took for his text candidates have a large and varied experience, and that second chapter St. Paul's Epistle to the Romans, 14th and their reelection will result in the efficient management of , the town's affairs and economy in the rates. The Rate- following verses—" For not the hearers of the law are just i I [ payers' Association ask the ratepayers to exercise their before God, but the doers of the law shall be justified. suffrages in favour of Messrs. J Bsech, Samuel Sadler, Wm. For when the Gentiles which have no law, do by nature the Sadler, and Samuel White. These gentlemen, the Oster things of the law, these having no law are a law unto them- states, have pledged themselves to continue the policy Of selves in that they show the work of the la* written in economy urged upon the Board three years ago by the Bate- their hearts, their conscience bearing witness therewith, and payers' Association, and commenced two years ago in pran- their thogghts one with another accusing or else excusing tice by the men, who, by an overwhelming mejority, they them." The preacher, in the course of his remarks, said: sent to represent their interests who reversed the policy of In the Manchester Guardian on the 10th March appeared blundering pursued for so many years which had created one of the most remarkable letters that has been seen for grievous burdens in increased rates and costly covenants many years. It is a challenge by G. J. Holyoake to the unfulfilled. As returning officer, Me o•Kesete, has fixed the electors of Leicester to return him to Parliament. The election to take place on the Bth April. letter, as an expression of pure Liberalism, would be in it- - self remarkable. As a challenge to try the right to affirm in Parliament and to force on the abolition of Oaths not by trickery or surprise, but (as every reform in this country has been carried) by fixed principle, and, above all, by the vindication of morality as against mere expediency, I think this letter makes al most an epoch in our history. It has been a source of constant reproach to me by some of my Secularistic friends that I have not supported Mr. Bradlaugh as they think I ought to have done, and I must plead guilty to a large extent to the accusation. I have always upheld the right of constituen- cies to return to Parliament persons whom they think proner. I have always condemned the action of the majority of the House of Commons. They have,' think, strained the con- stitution to the verge of wrong-doing, and sure lam that they have committed a huge folly. As a question of morals, however, they are in the right and Mr. Bradlaugh, in my judgment, in the wrong. Either ti. Oath has value in his eyes or it has not. By value I mean that the Oath has a binding power upon him in the sense in which it is binding upon the Christians who have drawn it up. If it has; if it binds him in the sense that it binds the Christians who take the Oath he ought, in my judgment, to have taken it at the outset and to have saved us all this great scandel and trouble. He knew well he would not be allowed to affirm; he knew as wall as any man living that so far as Parliament is concerned the Oath is still exacted, excepting so far as Quakers, dm., are concerned, and that is only slightly altered in the Case of Jews. He knew that so well-known a man as himself would be challenged at once. It will, of course, be said that other Atheists have been Admitted to the House notably Mr. J. Stuart Mill and Mr. Grote that the majority has strained out the gnat in rejecting him aid swallowed the camel in accepting them. True! but their wrong cannot and does not make Mr. Bradlaugh right. If on the other hand the Oath has no value in his eyes; if, as Mr. Holy- oake expresses it, he holds to "the validity of an unsworn word ; " if he holds that a man's word should be as good as his bond; if he holds that an appeal to God is either irreverent or superstitious or useless, then in my judgment , he should not take the Oath even if he has to wait as long as Baron Rothschild did on behalf of the Jews, when the in- fluence of Disraeli had no force on this question with the Tory party. The men of the maj wity believe in God— believe also that God will punish them if they take the Oath to a lie. They are superstitious if you will, but still that is their belief. Now, for a man believing just the opposite to take the Oath is sheer profanity. "I would not " (says Mr. Holyoake), "I would not profane the Oath in the opinion of r men of Christian conviction by solemnly repeating words which indicated no corresponding belief in my mind,nor would I, like the late Emperor Napoleon, demoralise public faith and Public trust by taking the Oath as a formality." Now, to profane, means to empty of all sacrednees, Bet how can Mr. Bradlaugh profane the Oath? Simply by emptying it of all truthfulness! For truthfulness is seeing things exactly as they are—and to be truthful is to desire to see things exactly as they are, and earnestly to try to describe them as they are. The chief value of the work that the men of science have done for this generation lies in their upholding the cause of truth" as against "edification" so dear to some of the popular churches. Now, truthfulness in the individual implies trustfulness in all others and sic, versa. They feel that they can rely upon him. They feel as Mr. Holyoake expresses it, "Public faith and public trust,"--nor, says he in con- tinuation, "would I like the late Emperor Napoleon demoralise public faith and pr)lic trust by taking the oath as a formality." For the benefit of the younger members Mr. Filcher sketched the treachery to his Oath of Napoleon 111. on the 2nd December, 1851, and the 17 years of most corrupt rile which ended in the debased character of his statesnaen and the ruin of his dynasty. Well may Mr. Holyeake say, "The history of nations tells us plainly that In all that makes the character of statesmen or the security if the people conscience is higher than 'right,' or 'law,' or any worldly advantage." For conscience is the inward knowledge of men. It is the highest factor in the forma- tion of character. Mr. Filcher then examined in detail the various factors (or circumstances) which do this, and con- tinned :—We inherit from our aocestors tendencies both good and bad. This increases enormously the responsibility of all crime. The preacher then instanced cases in which men rose above adverse circumstances of race, climate, ate. Hereditary tendencies, be continued, can be recognised, can be modified, and their heart of evil can be killed out. Killed? Yes! killed by starvation. "When the non-Jew has not the Jewish law to guide him, he is a law unto him- self." The truths which underlie all law are writteu on their beerte. In other words, individual cen;cience recog- nises these universal truths ;." bears witness therewith their reasonings one with another accusing or else excusing them." Their reasonings from past experiences, i.e, from history. For history is but the recorded experiences of our race. Here I must again read you what Mr. Holyoake says: —"The history of a nation tells us plainly that in all that makes the character of statesmen or the security of the people conscience is higher than right, or Jew, or any worldly advantage." We bear within us, then, the power of insight into men and into things. To the universal law of these our insight is a witness. By this insight into the universel law of things we test all men and things, and by this same power we art enabled in ourselves to choose that which is right an& good and to reject that which is wrong or bad. The measure in which we strive to do this is the measure of our love of truth—is the measure of oar truthfulness. The greatest factor in the formation of character is conscience. " Conscience," says our great seer, " doth make cowards of us all." Yes, but it also makes men heroes, martyrs, and saints. We may say with Shakespeare, slightly altering his words— " Enterprises of great path and moment, leo conscience have their currents male more strong, T. take the name of action." Especially is conscience an important factor in the character of statesmen—in the moulding of the will of statesmen—of the leaders of thought and action. It is especially impor- tant, bee cuss upon them depends the security of the people. The seeurity of the people ; the freedom from care. Care not only as to shelter and bread, but as to the national honour, justice, truth, and the like, that the people miy be secure that the policy of the coun- try," again, as Mr. Holyoake expresses it, " may be just without sentimentality, brave without swagger, which keeps faith with treaties adversaries have made fights with English courage for English honour, and does not knowingly murder for pres•ige." It is in my judgment of vital importance that we should be able to trust our leaders; that we shall be free from care about them ; that we shall be able to feel that they are faithful to their best know- ledge; that they are not ready to swear if not allowed to affirm, so long as they get that which they may desire, but, that they are ready to go without their hearts desire until by force of the manifest justice of their claim, until by the force of public opinion the knowledge of men may be lifted up to theirs, until their adversaries become at last aware of the startling truth that they, the oppsnents of reform, "having eyes saw not and having ears they could not hear," and that the ve-y law of reform demanded had been all the time " written on their hearts." It is because Mr. Bradlaugh has not been willing to do this that I for one have been unable to uphold him ; it is because Mr. tiolyoake is willing to do all this and to uphold conscience above everything as against mere expediency, that I rejoice to read his letter and wish him all success. Not ignorance but faithlessness is crime, and not ignorance but faithless- ness should be our dread and our hate.
FRODSHANI MUSICAL SOCIETY. MENDELSSOHN'S " ELIJAH."

On Wednesday evening the Frodsham Musical Society gave the oratorio, "Elijah," in the Town Hall, for the first time in Frodsham, and were assisted by Madame Billinie Porter, Miss Frances Armstrong, Mr. R. R. Ambler, Mr. H. V. Black, 8.A., and a capital band, of which Mr. J. W. Cal- houn was the leader, the number of band and chorus being about eighty. The difficult and elaborate character cf this masterpiece of oratorios was apparent, and required every effort of each individual member of the chorus; it could not be expected that the Society would be perfect, but consider- ing the small number et voices in proportion to the number of instrumentalists required to give effect, the performance must be considered as the crowning success of the season, and was due in a great measure to the spirited conductor- ship of Mr. W. J. Argent, who fairly carried the chorus through. Abe chorus, "Baal, we cry to thee," was rendered with precision, if we may except the faulty start made by the bass voices, and probably due to the cue given to the instrumentalists being taken. In "Beheld! God the Lord passed by," all the parts were promptly taken up, and it went well with the exception of the middle portion. The remaining choruses were given in a very creditable manner. The principals kindly gave their services, and each showed power of a special order to cope with the difficulties of oratorio. Miss Kate Rigby took part in the trio, " Lift thine eyes," and Miss Emily Riley and Miss Barker also assisted in the quartette, "Holy, holy, holy."

div.head: REMOTAL AND SALE OF ANIMALS. SWINE FEVER AF LYMM.
div.p: THE REMOTAL AND SALE OF ANIMALS. SWINE FEVER AF LYMM.

At the Lymm Petty Sessions, yesterday, before Messrs. P. Stubbs (chairman), R. H. Joynson, H. Stanton, and W. Long, Hugh Bradbury, Knutsford, cattle dealer, was sum- moned for, on the Bth of February, at Bollington, " being then and there the owner of certain animals, to wit, six pigs, unlawfully did expose such animals at a certain pri- vate sale of animals, on certain premises, to wit, a public highway there situate, such animals not having been on the said premises for fourteen clear days immediately be- fore the day on which such sale was held, and such sale not being held under a license of the Local Authority of the county of Chester."—Mr. Jenkins defended.—Superintendent Leighton said that on the Bth of February the defendant brought six pigs to the road outside the house of Mrs. Evans, at thllington. After parleying financially for some time with the Evans's. he sold the six pigs to them at 555. each. Three days afterwards they noticed that one of the pigs was unwell, and on the following morning they found it dead in the cote. It was afterwards found to have been affected with swine fever.--Mr. Jenkins tOOk a technical objection to tbe summons. The proceedings were taken under the 3rd clause of the Bth section of an Order made by the Privy Council on the 30th of November last, and the whole of the section qualified the mode in which public or private sales of animals were to be conducted. One conditisn was that 'the animal or animals exposed at the sale should have been on the farm or premises not less than 14 clear days imme- diately before the day on which the sale was held. The defendant wee charged with exposing the pigs for sale on certain premises, to wit, a public highway, such animals not having been on the said premises, the public highway, for 14 clear days, Sm. He (Mr. Jenkins) contended that that allegation was not within the terms of the clause in question, for it could not be intended that a person should keep animals for 14 days on the public highway; that would be impossible. He submitted that the terms of the offence as shown in the summons were illogical, for clearly the words meant by the clause were the words "farm or premises," and must be taken to mean premises in the nature of farm buildings, cattle sheds, fields, or other places ordinarily used by persons for the safe keeping of animals, and not the public highway. How could the defendant possibly comply with those those terms, and keep the pigs on the highway for 14 days ?—The Chairman asked if the sum- mons restricted the offence to clause 3 of the section.—The Magistrates' Clerk read the interpretation of the clause, and remarked that no doubt the arguments of Mr. Jenkins,was a good one, and required consideration.—Mr. Jenkins again submitted that a public highway did not come within the meaning of the terms. Further than that, he would state that the defendant kept his pigs on his premises at Knots. ford for more than 14 days previously, so that actually he had complied with the order.—Aftar same further conversa- tion on the point, the Chairman said that considering that the highway was a place over which the public had a pas- sage only, and that the freehold of it did not belong to the public, but to the owners of the land on either side; it seemed to him that the Clerk was right in contending that the highway was not a place on which sales could be held at all.—lt was then decided to proceed with the case.—Jane Evans, shopkeeper, Bollington, said that on the Bth of February the defendant called at her house with six pigs in a cart. Ile asked if they wanted any pigs, and witness bought them, giving him £l6 10f. for the six. Nothing was the matter with the pigs then, but on the Monday fol- lowing, the 11th, she noticed that one of the pigs in par- ticular was changing colour. It was a bluish colour, which went all over it. On the next day the pig was found dead in the cote, and witness got a veterinary surgeon to examine it. Some of the other pigs were "sickly," and one of them was changing colour and was slaughtered; it was not going blue like the other, but was rather of a reddish colour. Cross-examined: The whole of the pigs appeared to be very healthy when she bought them. They were "beautiful " pigs, and she thought that they were -worth the money she gave for them—By the Magistrates' Clerk: The bargain was made in the yard.—The Magistrates' Clerk said that if Mr. Jen- kins continued his objection he should suggest that it would be proper to amend the summons.—Mr. Jenkies de- cided to withdraw his objection, and the summons was amended to "premises of Mrs. Evans."—Evidence was then given showing that the pigs had been affected with swine fever, Mr. Msnroe,V.S., stating that he had examined the pigs and was decidedly of opinion that they had been so affected In answer to Mr. Jenkins, witness said it was possible that the defendant when in possession of the pigs at Knutsford would not be able to see any indications of the disease. it would only have been by a cereful examination with a barometer that even a scientific man would have been able to detect the symptoms, as the pigs would then be in the incubatory stage. At the close of the incnbatory stage—six or seven days--the disease rapidly developed, and the symptoms became observable.—Mr. Jenkins conten- ded that the meaning of the clause was that the animals should have been 14 days on the premises from which the vendor took them to sell them. He then called evidence to prove that the pigs bad been kept above that period of time on the premises of the defendant, and that they were apparently quite healthy when he removed them for sale.—The Chairman said that if the pigs had been sold on the defendant's own premises it would have been all right, but to remove them to another place where they had not been kept 14 days was an offence, in his opinion, against both the spirit and the letter of the law.—Mr. Jenkins asked for a small penalty, urging the difficulty of a proper inter- pretation of the order to show that the defendant had not intended an offance.—The Chairman said that the intention of the order evidently was to prevent people taking cattle indiscriminately about the country, and thus spreading dis- ease.—Superintendent Leighton said that the defendant had previously been summoned for an infringement of the Con- tagious Diseases (Animals) Act.—The Chairman said that the Bench considered that an offence had been committed, but they were inclined to take a lenient view of it. He would be fined Ss and cpsts, 42s in all. Whenever there was any doubt in such cases he should get advice; aek the police.—Superintendent Leighton said that the police were always ready to give the public all the information that they could.—Mr. Jenkins said that it had been his intention to ask the Bench to state a case, but as they had been so lenient he would leave it as it was.

div.p: LATEST NEWS.
THE MERCHANT SHIPPING BILL. IMPORTANT DECLARATION BY MR.

CHAMBhRLAIN. Mr. H. G. Reid, of Middlesborough, yesterday received the following letter from the President of the Board of Trade :-40, Princes Gardens, W., March I9.—Dear Sir,—l beg to acknowledge through you receipt of the resolution from the North Riding Liberal Association, and also from the Middlesborough Trades Council in favour of the Mer- chant Shipping Bill, and of its reference to a Grand Com- mittee. In the last fortnight I have received scores of similar resolutions and innumerable private letters, all testi- fying to the deep interest in the subject which is felt by impartial people throughout the country. lam sorry that the delay in the business of Parliament has hitherto pre- vented the discussion on the second reading of the bill. ' Whenever I get the opportunity of making my speech I shall be prepared to prove the absolute accuracy of the statements I have already made, and to justify the case by facts and ?targuments that will carry conviction to the minds of all disinterested persons. In the meantime I am ready, as I always have been, to con- sider formally any practical proposals for the amendment of the bill provided they do not conflict with its main prin- ciples and objects. I have never supposed that it was a , Perfect measure, and I have asked for the co-operation of all respectable shipowners in order that defects may be , pointed out and removed. I cannot, however, be a party to any proposal which is intended to shelve the question for as indefinite time, and if this is to be the result the responsi- bility must rest on the right shoulders, believing as Ido that there is a great and unnecessary waste of human life, and this is largely due to bad legislation, I will not have it on my conscience that I have voluntarily abandoned the hope of a remedy. Sooner or later a reckoning will be de- manded, and when that time comes it is right that the coun- try bmold know who has been to blame for the delay and for all the misery and suffering which will result from it.— I am, yours very truly, J. CHAMBERLAIN. H. G. Reid, Esq."

Cip`ain 'Rayner was yesterday selected Conservative can- didate for Anglesea. Early yesterday morning the Fowler mill at Warley, near Halifax, occupied by Mr. Balwin, wersttd spinner, WO totally destroyed by fire. The damage is estimated at £7OOO. FEVER AND DEFICIENT WATER SUPPLY.—The Sand- beet' Local Board have again been threatened by the Local Government Board, for neglecting to provide a proper water supply and sewerage arrangements. For years the Board have been considering schemes, but they cannot make up their minds. Fever is now epidemic, and public schools in the town are closed. The medical officer says that the provision of a water supply would do more to stamp out disease than anything the Board are doing now. Curators DETECTION OF A HOUSEBREAKER.—At Hyde, yesterday morning, a youthful housebreaker, named Eli Brown, was committed for trial at Chester Assizes. A police-constable met the prisoner at half-past one this morning, and noticing blood dripping from one of his hands he stopped him, searched him, and found upon him a con- siderable number of articles which the prisoner admitted having sl'oien. Subsequent inquiries elucidated the fact that three tradesmen's shops had been robbed, and in breaking the windows the prisoner sustained his injuries. EXCITING SCENE AT A FlLM—lntelligence has reached Chester of a fire on Thursday night at Burnardsley, on the Broxfon Hills, Cheshire, which will probably terminate in loss of life. Thothatched roof of a cottage occupied by George Price, a labourer, was ignited, it is supposed, by a spark from the chimney of a neighbouring tenement. The roof was spsedilv in a blaze and the hones in flames. It was then stated that a decrepit old man, eighty years of age, lay ill in bed. Some of the neighbours rushed into the house and thence into the bedroom, and there found the bed burning beneath the old man. They hastily rolled blankets and sheets about him, but before they could raise him the sheets were burned off his body. The burning thatch had also fallen around inflicting dreadful injuries. He is not expected to recover. TILE BANDA AND KIRWEIS PRIZE MONEY. The Court of Appeal consisting of Lords Justice Cotton, Bowen, and Fry. gave judgment yesterday upon the appeal of the Rev. A. Kinloch, from the decision of Mr. Justice Kay, allowing the demurrer of the Crown and the Sec-etary of State for India to his petition of right. Mr. Kinloch was chaplain to Sir G. Whiteleck's division, which served throughout the Indian mutiny in 1858, and which captured the towns of Banda and Kir wee, with a booty of £700,000. That was granted to the troops, and about £500,000 of it had been distributed among them. The petition of right asked that the balance of £200,000 retained by the Indian Govern- ment, might be divided in the same way. Their lordships, however, held that, the grant being in the nature of a bounty, the troops had only such interest as Her Majesty was pleased to order, and could bays no independent right of property in the booty. The Court, therefore, sustained the judgment of the Court below. ABM:7C HON OF A FEMALE GYSINAST.—At Birmingham yesterday, Samuel Neale, wholesale newsagent, was charged On remand with abducting Florence May Lillo Stone, other- wise Dillon, professionally known as " Lillo," of the Lillo &sin and Echo troupe of female gymnasts, the girl being I under 16 years of age. The defendant was also charged ; with felony by ins3rting in a register of marriage a false , entry relating to the age of his bride. WARRINGTON TEMPERANCE UNION. The annual meeting of the above union was held on Tuesday evening, at the Workmen's Club, Market-place, when there was a moderate attendance. Mr. Robt. Garnett presided, and was supported by the Revs. J. Yonge, W. Mules, W. Pilling, W. Reid (Levenshulme), G. H. Murray (Preston), J. McTurk, T. Rippon, and ethers. During the evening several musical contributions were rendered by the members of the choir. The Crum:dew, after the meeting had been opened with singing and prayer, said that they were determined to go on still with the same fight that they had been engaged in for years past. They were sot weary of well-doing, for if they fainted not, in due time they would reap. They had had much to encourage them hitherto, and he supposed that they had now probably something like le millions of total ab- stainers in the country, which was a wonderful change. (Applause.) While they were thankful for this fact, they were thankful without resting. (Applause.) Their pur- pose was to go on, and continue in the fight so long as the demon of drink was committing such devastation in our midst. It was a solemn and terrible thing that no matter wherever they went, in every town and village, in the home, at the fireside, and even in the House of God they found people under its most mischievous influence. Wherever I they went it was staring them in the face. The result was that the gaole and asylums of the country, if not filled, were largely replenished with the effects of drunkenness and im- providence. It was often said that it was no crime to be poor, and he believed that there were cases in which it was no crime, but he did believe, and every day's experience seemed to add conviction to the belief that crime' improvidence' drunkenness and poverty, were very often found band in hand. (Applause.) They complained, and very justly, in the town of Warrington, about the poor-rate, which was no donbt very heavy, but one substan- tial feature in connection with the poor-rate was simply and solely brought about by improvidence end drink. They wished to do something in their day, and to leave the world better than they came to it. It was for this that friends of temperance had so long been labouring, often in the face of great difficulties and dangers. In regard to the political aspect of the question the Chairman said that he was very much afraid that the Local Option question would stand a very fair chance of being elbowed out for the present, but at the same time they were bound to give the Governrilent credit for a wish and desire to do something in that way. (Applause.) Mr. W. ROBERTS (secrelary) read the 49th annual report, from which it appeared that the meetings of the Union had been well attended, and that the work during the year had been of a very encouraging nature. The Rev. W. MULES proposed the adoption of the report, which would be, he thought, te all except the publicans and their allies, a very encouraging one indeed. He thought that the fact that the work had been done without a lot of noise and clatter was not the least encourag- ing aspect of the else. They all knew that some of the greatest physical forces of the world were the most silent, and it was a 'most encouraging thing to him that the work of the past year had been done so quietly and unostentatiously. Spasmodic effort bad never been successful yet in producing any very beneficial effect. Tbe thing that was of mushroom growth was generally of mushroom duration, whilst a Work that, like the mik, grew slowly but surely, must, like the oak, endure when other things that had laughed at its slow development had fallen a prey to the ravages of time. (Applause.) The expression in the report that there was need of much more harmony and united effort upon the part of the temperance societies atruck him forcibly. Was the fact that there were some matters upon which religious bodies could not join issue a reason why they should not join hand in hand in prosecuting such a great and glorious work as temperance? Me trusted that the time was not far distant when the War- rington Temperance Union would include all the temper- ance societies in the town, that they might join their hands and their hearts in trying to destroy the evil of drink. He hoped that the result of the naeeting

The tota!,number of members at the close of 18 83 was 36,540, an inarease of 8,168 in the year. The expenditure had been ever. £33,000. There were B,2s3,cases of disablement during the year, and 84 members of the Society were killed. The fatalmecidents threw upon the Society 44. widows and 88 children, and at the close of the year 310 widows and 731 children were re- ceiving regular relief from. the funds. The disbursements for medical al amounted to £4,474, and £17437 was paid to members disabled by accidents in mines. div.head: THEFT IN THE WARRINGTON MARKET. A CAUTION_ TO ?ALI. HOLDERS.
div.p: THEFT IN THE WARRINGTON MARKET. A CAUTION_ TO ?ALI. HOLDERS.

At the Warrington Borough Police court, on Thursday, before Captain Litton (in the chair), and Alierman Webster, a married woman named Violetta Wordsworth, who lives with her husband off Charles-street, was charged with stealing from a stall in the new market, on Wednes• day, 2i yards of black cashmere,of the value of 2s Bd, the property of Israel Guisbere, of Manchester.—On baing brought up prisoner had a fainting fit, and it was sometime before the Case could he proceeded with.—Mr Place, market Inspector, said that at about noon on Wednesday last the prisoner was pointed out to him in the market as going about in a suspicious manner, and he asked her where she got some cashmere that she had in her possession. She re- plied that she would take him to the stall where she bought it, but on his asking the owner of the stall if he had sold the cashmere he replied that he had not, but that he had been looking for it. Prisoner said that th 3 man was too by for her to pay for it at the time, arid she then pulled out her purse and offered to pay.—The chairman remarked that the pros cutor had base at the court several times before when be bad had property stolen from his stall ; was there no negligence on his part in not taking proper care of the stall? Mr. Place said that the stall was Liid out in a proper manner but when Mr. Guisberg had had ten or fifteen customer'. round he could not look after them all at ence.—The Chair- man remarked that if Mr. Guisberg led people into unneces- sary temptation he should take the consequences or not be allowed to have a stall.—alelerman Webster said it appeared as though there were great- facilities for steeling from this particular stall than any of the others.—Mr. Place said that he thought many people Came to the market for nothing else but to eteal.—,:onsidering the good character of the pri- soner, and the temptation to which she had been subjected, the Bench only int:tic:Ed a penalty of 204. including caste. —The Bench informed the prosecutor that he should have assistance, and warned him teat if he had not, it would be a question far the Markets Committee to consider whether it was worth while having him As a tenant.

- - - THE OPENING OF MUSEUMS ON SUNDAYS.—Lord Trtnatow moved a resolution in favour of the opening of national libraries and museums to the working classes on a Sunday.— Earl SHAFTESBURY proposed an amendment limiting the opening of the Britkb Museum and National. Gallery to week-day evenings.—The House divided on Lord Thurlow's motion, which was lost by 48 to 38.—Earl Shaftesbury, yielding to an appeal from the Marquis 0 Salisbury, withdrew his amendment.—The House adjourned at eight o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS. THE MINISTER FOR SCOTLAND. Sir W. HArtnOtm, replying to a question, said the Bill for establishing a minister for Scotland was ready, and would be introduced before Easter. COLONEL BURNABY.—Lord Harertwororf, replying to Mr. Buchanan, said that supposing the newspaper reports were true as to tbe action of Colonel Burnaby at the battle of El Teb, he did not see he bad done anything opposed to the usages of war, and, therefore, he did not propose to take any further action in the matter. KHARTOUM : OUR POLICY IN EGYTT.—Lord HearrilsoTolt, replying to Mr. Bourke, said that no additional information ; from Khartoum had been received. The district around Berber was disturbed, and telegraphic communication be- tween Cairo and Khartoum had not yet been restored.—Sir STAFFORD Nownicont gave notice that on Monday he 'Mould ask when it was proposed by the Government to make the promised statement as to their policy in Egypt. Tam Coarreorocs DISEASES (ANIMALS) BILL.—The ad- journed debate on the Contagious Diseases (Animate) Bill was resumed bw Sir A. GORDON, who wished the duration of the bill te be five years instead of two.—Sir IC H. BmACH said if the bill was amended as was that proposed by the Government, it would become quite unacceptable to the agrmultural interests of the country. He defended the amendments made in the bill be the Lime at Lords, and

furged the House to retain those introduced by the Duke of Richmond.—The discussion was continued by Mr. Duck- barn, Sir W. Bartellot, Colonel Kingscote, and others.—The bill was read a second time without a division. THE EXPENSE OF THE AFGHAN WAR.—On the motion for going into Committee on the Consolidated Fund Bill, Lord G. Ifelmmotr criticised the financial arrangements of the Government, more particularly that as regards the payments of the contribution to expenses of the Afghan war. Mr. COURTNEY defended the arrangement that had been made, and denied that it was an attempt on the part of the . Government to manufacture a surplus for the years t 1884-s.—The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER defended the plan adopted with regard to the payment of the present instalments.--Sir S. NORTHCOTE objected to the alteration of an arrangement made by Parliament, and the taking of a burden on the year which did not originally belong to it. Lord R. Cwuracutra. said there was no necessity to show the great extravagance of the present Government, as that was apparent to the country, but what he did object to was the political dishoneety of the Government in under estimating the expenditure it_ order to make the country be- lieve they were following out an economical policy.—A dis- cussion followed, in which Sir It. CROSS and Mr. STHART WORTLEY took part.—Mr. SEXTON condemned the policy of the Tory party in ransacking English and Indian finance, in order to eke out the afternoon's discussions, and thus I prevent the small Bill for revising jurors' and voters' lists in Ireland passing one of its stages.—Mr. GORST denied that the time devoted to the present discussion had been wasted. —Eventually these went into committee. The clauses of the Bill were agreed to, and the report was ordered to be brought up on Monday. JURORS' AND VOTERS' LISTS BILL.—OR the motion to go into committee on the revision of the Jurors' and Voters' Lists (Dublin County) Bill, Mr. Pratexav moved the ad- journment of the debate.—The House divided, when there voted for adjourning the debate, 77; against, 127.—1 t being ten minutes to seven the debate stood adjourned until the evening sitting.—The sitting was suspended.

At the Warrington Borough Police Conrt, on Monday, before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) in the chair, and Alderman Davies, the Magistrates' Clerk (Mr. White) called on the case of the Whitecross Wire and Iron Cowper!! against Joseph Brayon, and no one answering, he informed the Bench that he believed that the summonses that had been taken out by the Company against a number of their apprentices had been settled out of court. In answer tO Alderman Davies, Mr. White said that he thought the ap- prentices had returned to work. The apprentices were sum- moned under the Employers' and Workmen's Act, 1975, by the Whitecross Don anel Wire Company, vrhce claimed 101 in each case as compensation, for the defen lams having ab- sented themselves from work on tlae 4th last without jest or lawful excuse.--Phe following are the names of those summoned : Joseph Benyon, 58, Allen-street Joseph May- bury, 27, Hoyle-street; William Wright, Chorley-street C. A. Lea, Jones's-buildings ; Henry Emerson, 3, James- street ; Peter Peers, gO, Church-street; G. H. Hall, Priest/ey- street ; Thomas Jellsv, lei, Allen-street; Thomas Hill, 0, Wakefield-street ; Thomas Owen, 4, Aikin-street ; Robert Heves, 71, Howley-lane; W. T. Robinson, 8. Milner-street ; J. T. Thornley, 20, Pierpoint-street ; John Edw irdson, g 2. Pierpoint-street ; Joseph Monks, 5, Lovely-lane; and Arthur Lingard, 37, Hopwood-street.

On Tuesday, the representatives of the masters met those of the men now on et, ilte in Warrington, and of those who are still working in Birmingham, Sheffield, and Manchester, with the object of settling the dispute. Ttte men's deler- gates presented a list of prices, which was refused by the representatives of the masters. The men's delegates were invited to an expression of their views on any partica;lar point in the list proposed by tho masters, but they were not prepared to discuss it in detail, being only instructed by their union to argue on the question of their own proposal. The meeting therefore broke up, no settlement being arrived at. We understand th4t the list submitted by the men showed that they were willing to aubmit to a reduction of 14 p.c. on the obilist, thereby meeting the masters half way. The employers offered, we believe, to increase the speed'. and to introduce one or two other features of a technical character with the view of recouping the men for the redac- tion proposed: The men are in their resist.ance receiving support, It is said, from many outside their trade.

HELENS.—TO ARCHITECTS, BUILDERS, PROPERTY OWNERS, and OTHERS.— The Corporation desire to draw attention to the provhnons of their bye-laws requiring the depesit of plans and sections. by persons intending to erect any new building or erection, and particularly to the provision that with sualo plans and sections there shall be left at the Borough Surveyor's Office a BLOCK PLAN showing the position of the bulloings and appurtenances of the properties immediately adjoining, the width and level of the street, the level of the lowest floor of the intended building, and of the yard or ground belonging thereto.
